knowledge_statements.title: Linear Programming Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous relaxation of a linear mixed-integer minimization formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ x_i\in\mathbb Z\text{ for every }i\in I\}\), and let the objective be \(c^\top x\). The linear-programming relaxation is \(R_{\mathrm{LP}}=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\), obtained by deleting the integrality restrictions. Thus \(P\subseteq R_{\mathrm{LP}}\). With the convention \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\), its value \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=\inf_{x\in R_{\mathrm{LP}}}c^\top x\) satisfies \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le z_P=\inf_{x\in P}c^\top x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping integrality from a linear mixed-integer minimization model produces a polyhedral superset whose optimal value is a valid lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The problem uses the minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\subseteq R_{\mathrm{LP}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}\le z_P\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Infeasibility and Optimality Transfer from a Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic consequences of a valid relaxation: relaxation infeasibility transfers to the original problem, while a relaxation optimizer transfers optimality only under original feasibility and objective agreement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(RP\) be a relaxation of an integer problem \(IP\), whose feasible set is \(X\), with relaxation objective \(f\) and original objective \(c\). Then: (i) if \(RP\) is infeasible, \(IP\) is infeasible; (ii) if \(x^*\) is optimal for \(RP\), \(x^*\in X\), and \(f(x^*)=c(x^*)\), then \(x^*\) is optimal for \(IP\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a valid relaxation is infeasible, the original integer problem is infeasible. An optimal relaxation solution is optimal for the original problem only when it is feasible for the original problem and the two objective values agree at that solution.
assumptions_latex: RP\text{ is a relaxation of }IP
X\text{ is the feasible set of }IP
f\text{ and }c\text{ are respectively the relaxation and original objectives}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: RP\text{ infeasible}\Rightarrow IP\text{ infeasible};\qquad [x^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}RP,\ x^*\in X,\ f(x^*)=c(x^*)]\Rightarrow x^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}IP

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Programming Relaxation of an Integer Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The continuous relaxation obtained by removing integrality from the stated nonnegative linear formulation while retaining its constraints and objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the integer program \(Z=\max\{c^\top x:x\in P\cap\mathbb Z^n\}\), where \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:Ax\le b\}\), the linear programming relaxation is \(Z^{LP}=\max\{c^\top x:x\in P\}\). Because \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n\subseteq P\) and the objective is unchanged, this is a relaxation of the integer program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The LP relaxation removes the integrality restriction from the stated linear integer program while retaining the objective and all other constraints. Its feasible set therefore contains the integer-feasible set.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:Ax\le b\}
Z=\max\{c^\top x:x\in P\cap\mathbb Z^n\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Z^{LP}=\max\{c^\top x:x\in P\},\qquad P\cap\mathbb Z^n\subseteq P

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Formulation Inclusion Orders LP Relaxation Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a maximization integer program, inclusion of formulation polyhedra orders the corresponding LP upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) be formulations of \(\max\{c^\top x:x\in X\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\}\), and suppose \(P_1\subset P_2\). If \(Z_i^{LP}=\max\{c^\top x:x\in P_i\}\) for \(i=1,2\), then \(Z_1^{LP}\le Z_2^{LP}\) for every \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a maximization integer program, an LP formulation contained in another formulation produces an LP bound no larger than the bound from the larger formulation, for every linear objective.

P_1\text{ and }P_2\text{ are formulations of }X
P_1\subset P_2
Z_i^{LP}=\max\{c^\top x:x\in P_i\},\quad i=1,2
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall c,\quad Z_1^{LP}\le Z_2^{LP}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear relaxation and natural LP relaxation of a mixed-integer set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The general definition requires containment; the natural relaxation specifically removes integrality while retaining the original inequalities and nonnegativity restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^p\), a linear relaxation of \(S\) is a set \(P':=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p:A'x+G'y\le b'\}\) such that \(S\subseteq P'\). The corresponding linear-programming relaxation maximizes the original linear objective over \(P'\). For \(S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z_+^n\times\mathbb R_+^p:Ax+Gy\le b\}\), the natural linear relaxation is \(P_0:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R_+^n\times\mathbb R_+^p:Ax+Gy\le b\}\), obtained by discarding the integrality restriction on \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear relaxation is a linearly described continuous set containing the mixed-integer set. Its LP relaxation optimizes the original objective over that containing set. The natural relaxation keeps the original constraints and nonnegativity conditions but treats the integer variables as continuous.
assumptions_latex: S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^p
P'=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p:A'x+G'y\le b'\}
S\subseteq P'
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{cx+hy:(x,y)\in P'\}\text{ is a linear-programming relaxation; for the stated mixed-integer linear set, }P_0:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R_+^n\times\mathbb R_+^p:Ax+Gy\le b\}\text{ is the natural relaxation.}

children.title: Convex Nonlinear Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Convex bounding models for mixed-integer nonlinear formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Nonlinear Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex feasible-set and objective-underestimator relaxation for mixed-integer nonlinear minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the feasible set of a mixed-integer nonlinear problem with objective \(f:F\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). A convex nonlinear relaxation is a pair \((C,\ell)\) such that \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex, \(F\subseteq C\), and \(\ell:C\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is convex with \(\ell(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). Its relaxation value \(z_C=\inf_{x\in C}\ell(x)\) is therefore no greater than \(z_F=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex superset paired with a convex objective underestimator yields a valid lower bound for nonlinear mixed-integer minimization.
assumptions_latex: \(F\ne\varnothing\).
The extended-real infimum convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_C\le z_F\).

notation.meaning: convex underestimator of the original objective on feasible points

source_refs.locator: Matrix relaxations in combinatorial optimization p. 483

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{q\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{q\times p}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^q\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). Define \(Q_K=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p:Ax+By-b\in K\}\). This lifted system is a conic relaxation of \(F\) when \(F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_K)\). Its linear-objective minimization value \(z_K=\inf\{c^\top x:(x,y)\in Q_K\}\) satisfies \(z_K\le\inf_{x\in F}c^\top x\). Standard choices of \(K\) include products of nonnegative orthants, second-order cones, and positive-semidefinite cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted conic system whose projection contains the original feasible set provides a valid lower bound for a linear minimization objective in the original variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint relaxation retaining the original discrete or combinatorial domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a discrete or otherwise combinatorially structured set and \(F=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\le0\text{ for every }i\in I\}\). For \(J\subseteq I\), the combinatorial relaxation associated with \(J\) is \(R_J=\{x\in X:g_i(x)\le0\text{ for every }i\in J\}\). Because \(F\subseteq R_J\), its minimization value \(z_J=\inf_{x\in R_J}f(x)\) is a valid lower bound on \(z_F=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), while membership in \(X\) preserves the selected combinatorial structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Removing selected constraints while retaining the structured discrete domain creates a combinatorial relaxation and a valid minimization lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(J\subseteq I\).
The same objective \(f\) is used on \(F\) and \(R_J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq R_J\) and \(z_J\le z_F\).

notation.meaning: relaxation retaining constraints indexed by J

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: deleting constraints preserves feasible-set containment while retaining the discrete domain
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Constraint deletion gives the displayed containment and lower bound, but no inspectable source supports the use and scope of the term “combinatorial relaxation” for this particular construction. A source is needed before selecting this mathematical version for the leaf.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General definition based on the type of optimization problem produced by a relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be a relaxation whose resulting relaxed problem is \(P_{\mathcal R}\). The relaxation \(\mathcal R\) is called a \emph{combinatorial relaxation} when \(P_{\mathcal R}\) is a combinatorial optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation is called a combinatorial relaxation when the relaxed problem it produces is a combinatorial optimization problem.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal R\text{ is a relaxation producing a relaxed problem }P_{\mathcal R}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathcal R}\text{ is a combinatorial optimization problem}\implies \mathcal R\text{ is called a combinatorial relaxation}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty set, let \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), let \(g:X\to\mathbb R^m\), and define \(z_P=\inf\{f(x):x\in X,\ g(x)\le0\}\). For each \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\), the Lagrangian relaxation value is \(L(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in X}\{f(x)+\lambda^\top g(x)\}\), and the Lagrangian dual value is \(z_D=\sup_{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m}L(\lambda)\). The weak-duality relations are \(L(\lambda)\le z_D\le z_P\) for every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dualizing inequality constraints with nonnegative multipliers produces lower bounds, and maximizing those bounds gives a Lagrangian dual value no greater than the primal minimization value.

children.title: Complementary Relaxation Bounds
children.top_down_role: Comparative use of combinatorial versus Lagrangian bounds across structured instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementary Relaxation Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregation of combinatorial and Lagrangian lower bounds for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_P\) be the infimum of a minimization problem. Suppose a combinatorial relaxation provides \(b_C\le z_P\), and a Lagrangian relaxation at multiplier \(\lambda\ge0\) provides \(b_L(\lambda)\le z_P\). Their complementary aggregate is \(b_{CL}(\lambda)=\max\{b_C,b_L(\lambda)\}\). It remains a valid lower bound and weakly dominates each constituent bound: \(b_C\le b_{CL}(\lambda)\le z_P\) and \(b_L(\lambda)\le b_{CL}(\lambda)\le z_P\). Optimizing the Lagrangian component gives \(\max\{b_C,\sup_{\lambda\ge0}b_L(\lambda)\}\le z_P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of valid combinatorial and Lagrangian lower bounds is valid and at least as strong as either constituent bound.
assumptions_latex: \(b_C\le z_P\).
\(b_L(\lambda)\le z_P\) for every admissible \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{b_C,b_L(\lambda)\}\le z_P\).

notation.meaning: Lagrangian lower bound at multiplier lambda

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the maximum of lower bounds is a lower bound and dominates each component
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The maximum of two valid lower bounds is mathematically valid and dominates each constituent. However, no source supports calling this elementary aggregation a “complementary relaxation bound” or establishes that it is the intended local sense of the terminal container.

children.title: Common-Space Relaxation Dominance
children.top_down_role: Strength ordering for relaxations expressed in a shared variable space.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Space Relaxation Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-inclusion strength order for minimization relaxations in identical variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq R_1\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(F\subseteq R_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be relaxations expressed in the same variable space. Relaxation \(R_1\) dominates \(R_2\) when \(R_1\subseteq R_2\); dominance is strict when the inclusion is proper. For every objective \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), the corresponding minimization bounds satisfy \(\inf_{x\in R_2}f(x)\le\inf_{x\in R_1}f(x)\le\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\). Thus the smaller relaxation supplies the no-weaker lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among relaxations in one variable space, set inclusion defines dominance: the smaller feasible region yields a no-weaker minimization bound.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq R_1\cap R_2\).
All three problems use the same minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\subseteq R_2\Longrightarrow \inf_{R_2}f\le\inf_{R_1}f\le\inf_F f\).

notation.meaning: relaxations in the common variable space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: minimization infima are monotone under set inclusion
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inclusion and infimum inequalities are correct for common-space minimization relaxations. An inspectable source is still needed to confirm the selected dominance convention and its exact terminology for this leaf.

children.title: Projected Relaxation Dominance
children.top_down_role: Strength ordering after auxiliary variables are projected away.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Relaxation Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominance comparison for lifted relaxations after eliminating auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(Q_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^{p_i}\) satisfy \(F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_i)\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\). The lifted relaxation \(Q_1\) projectively dominates \(Q_2\) when \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_1)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_2)\). Consequently, for every objective \(f\) depending only on \(x\), \(\inf_{(x,y_2)\in Q_2}f(x)\le\inf_{(x,y_1)\in Q_1}f(x)\le\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\). Auxiliary-variable dimensions and descriptions need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted relaxation dominates another when its projection onto original variables is smaller, yielding no weaker bounds for objectives in those variables.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_1)\cap\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_2)\).
The objective depends only on the original variable \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_1)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q_2)\Longrightarrow \inf_{Q_2}f(x)\le\inf_{Q_1}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: lifted relaxation with its own auxiliary variables
projection of the lifted set onto original variables

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: projected set inclusion induces bound dominance for objectives on original variables
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Projected set inclusion yields the displayed ordering for objectives depending only on the original variables. A source is needed to establish that this is the intended formal definition of projected relaxation dominance in the taxonomy.

children.title: Optimization Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Agreement of formulation optima for a specified optimization setting.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value equivalence of two relaxations over a specified objective class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_1,R_2\subseteq X\) and let \(\mathcal C\) be a class of extended-real objective functions on \(X\). The formulations are optimization-equivalent over \(\mathcal C\) when, for every \(f\in\mathcal C\), their minimization values coincide: \(\inf_{x\in R_1}f(x)=\inf_{x\in R_2}f(x)\), using \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). This definition concerns optimal values only; it does not require \(R_1=R_2\), equality of minimizer sets, or equivalence for objectives outside \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two formulations are optimization-equivalent on an objective class when they have equal infimal values for every objective in that class.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1,R_2\subseteq X\).
Every \(f\in\mathcal C\) is defined on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall f\in\mathcal C,\ \inf_{x\in R_1}f(x)=\inf_{x\in R_2}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: feasible regions of the compared formulations

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: equality of value functions on a prescribed objective family defines objective-restricted optimization equivalence
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record clearly defines value equivalence over an objective class and distinguishes it from feasible-set or optimizer-set equivalence. Because “optimization equivalence” admits multiple conventions, an authoritative source is needed to support this exact value-only notion.

children.title: Objective-Class Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Families of objectives over which formulation comparisons are intended to hold.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Class Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissibility condition delimiting objectives used in formulation comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the common original-variable space. An objective-class restriction is a specified subset \(\mathcal C\subseteq\{f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\}\) together with any declared structural requirements, such as \(\mathcal C=\{x\mapsto c^\top x:c\in D\}\) for a coefficient set \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). A dominance or equivalence assertion restricted to \(\mathcal C\) quantifies only over \(f\in\mathcal C\); it makes no assertion for objectives outside that set. Objectives in lifted formulations must be evaluated through the common original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective-class restriction explicitly identifies the objectives over which formulation dominance or equivalence is asserted.
assumptions_latex: All compared formulations expose variables in the common space \(X\), possibly by projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in\mathcal C\) is the complete admissibility predicate for the restricted comparison.

notation.meaning: admissible coefficient set in the linear-objective example

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: restricted comparison requires explicit quantification over a declared objective family
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restriction is internally coherent and correctly limits subsequent quantification to the declared objective family. No source supports this precise formalism or confirms it as the intended condition for the terminal container.

children.title: Objective-Class Dominance
children.top_down_role: Formulation orderings that depend on the permitted objective family.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Class Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bound-strength ordering restricted to a declared minimization objective class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_1,R_2\subseteq X\), let \(\mathcal C\) be an objective class, and define \(v_i(f)=\inf_{x\in R_i}f(x)\). Formulation \(R_1\) dominates \(R_2\) over \(\mathcal C\) when \(v_1(f)\ge v_2(f)\) for every \(f\in\mathcal C\). Dominance is strict over \(\mathcal C\) when this inequality holds throughout \(\mathcal C\) and is strict for at least one member. Mutual dominance is equivalent to optimization equivalence over \(\mathcal C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimization, one formulation dominates another on an objective class when it gives a no-smaller bound for every admitted objective.
assumptions_latex: The comparison uses minimization values.
Every \(f\in\mathcal C\) is defined on the common space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\succeq_{\mathcal C}R_2\Longleftrightarrow \forall f\in\mathcal C,\ v_1(f)\ge v_2(f)\).

notation.meaning: infimal value of objective f over formulation i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: minimization-bound dominance is pointwise ordering of value functions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise value-function ordering is correct for minimization, and mutual dominance gives equality on the objective class. A source is required to confirm this exact convention and terminology.

children.title: Equivalence Failure beyond the Objective Class
children.top_down_role: Loss of optimization agreement when objectives leave the designated family.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalence Failure beyond the Objective Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of restricted value equivalence under objective-class enlargement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take \(X=\mathbb R^2\), \(R_1=\{(0,0)\}\), \(R_2=\{(0,1)\}\), and \(\mathcal C=\{f_a(x)=a x_1:a\in\mathbb R\}\). For every \(f_a\in\mathcal C\), \(\inf_{x\in R_1}f_a(x)=0=\inf_{x\in R_2}f_a(x)\), so the formulations are optimization-equivalent over \(\mathcal C\). For the objective \(h(x)=x_2\notin\mathcal C\), however, \(\inf_{x\in R_1}h(x)=0\) while \(\inf_{x\in R_2}h(x)=1\). Hence restricted equivalence need not survive enlargement of the objective class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two singleton formulations agree for every objective using only the first coordinate but differ for an objective using the second coordinate.
assumptions_latex: Optimization equivalence means equality of infimal values, not equality of feasible or optimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\equiv_{\mathcal C}R_2\) but \(\inf_{R_1}h\ne\inf_{R_2}h\).

notation.meaning: linear objectives depending only on the first coordinate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed finite counterexample is directly verifiable
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Incomparable Formulations
children.top_down_role: Formulations whose relative strength changes across objectives or projected regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomparable Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-inclusion incomparability after projection to a common variable space; the objective-witness characterization is stated for compact convex relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_1,P_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the projected relaxations of two formulations of the same minimization problem. The formulations are incomparable when \(P_1\nsubseteq P_2\) and \(P_2\nsubseteq P_1\). If \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are nonempty, compact, and convex, there exist \(c_1,c_2\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(\min_{x\in P_1}c_1^\top x<\min_{x\in P_2}c_1^\top x\) and \(\min_{x\in P_2}c_2^\top x<\min_{x\in P_1}c_2^\top x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two formulations are incomparable when neither projected relaxation contains the other. For nonempty compact convex relaxations, different linear objectives can rank them in opposite directions.
assumptions_latex: The two formulations describe the same integer feasible set after projection to a common variable space.
Their projected relaxations \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) lie in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
For the objective-witness characterization, \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are nonempty, compact, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither formulation dominates the other in the projected-relaxation ordering; under the compact-convex hypothesis, each failed inclusion has a finite linear-objective witness.

notation.meaning: linear objective vectors witnessing the two failed inclusions

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

children.title: Primal-Dual Bound Certificate System
children.top_down_role: Primal feasible information and relaxation-based dual information as complementary optimization certificates.

children.title: Primal-Bound Sources
children.top_down_role: Feasible solutions and incumbents viewed as sources of primal bounds.

assumptions_latex: The optimization problem is a minimization problem with nonempty feasible set \(X\).
The reported feasible point has a finite objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible incumbent supplies a valid upper bound on the optimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal bounds use the minimization convention; inequalities reverse for maximization.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in X\}\), every feasible point \(\bar x\in X\) with finite \(f(\bar x)\) yields the primal bound \(z^*\le f(\bar x)\). An incumbent set \(I\subseteq X\) yields \(U=\inf_{x\in I}f(x)\), with \(z^*\le U\); when the infimum is attained, an attaining incumbent verifies the bound by direct feasibility and objective evaluation. Better feasible solutions decrease \(U\) without invalidating earlier bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any feasible solution gives an upper bound for a minimization problem, and the best incumbent value is the strongest bound obtained from known feasible solutions.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Bound Sources

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

children.title: Dual-Bound Relaxation Sources
children.top_down_role: Continuous, combinatorial, and dual relaxations viewed as sources of dual bounds.

children.title: Continuous-Relaxation Sources
children.top_down_role: Dual-bound information supplied by continuous relaxations of discrete formulations.

assumptions_latex: The mixed-integer problem is a minimization problem.
The continuous relaxation is obtained by dropping integrality while retaining all other constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The continuous-relaxation optimum is a valid dual bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-bound source for minimization through feasible-set enlargement.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Continuous relaxation p. 24
6.1 Continuous-Relaxation-Based Branch-and-Bound Methods p. 150

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq R\) and define \(z^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) and \(L_R=\inf_{x\in R}f(x)\). Feasible-set inclusion gives \(L_R\le z^*\), so every certified lower bound on \(L_R\), and in particular an exactly computed finite value \(L_R\), is a valid dual bound for the mixed-integer problem. If \(R=\varnothing\), then \(X=\varnothing\), certifying infeasibility rather than a finite objective bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping integrality enlarges the feasible set, so the continuous-relaxation value lower-bounds the mixed-integer optimum and relaxation infeasibility proves original infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Relaxation Sources

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Continuous relaxation p. 24
6.1 Continuous-Relaxation-Based Branch-and-Bound Methods p. 150

children.title: Combinatorial-Relaxation Sources
children.top_down_role: Dual-bound information supplied by tractable combinatorial relaxations.

assumptions_latex: The original minimization problem has feasible set \(X\).
A tractable combinatorial relaxation has feasible set \(C\) containing \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimizing over the combinatorial relaxation supplies a valid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers discrete supersets, restricted constraint families, and tractable combinatorial surrogate problems.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq C\) and let both problems use the same objective \(f\). For \(z^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\) and \(L_C=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\), one has \(L_C\le z^*\). Thus an exact solution of the combinatorial relaxation, or any independently certified lower bound \(\ell\le L_C\), yields the valid dual bound \(\ell\le z^*\). Validity depends on the inclusion \(X\subseteq C\), not on whether \(C\) is continuous or discrete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any tractable combinatorial feasible-set superset gives a lower bound for minimization; validity follows from containment of every original feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial-Relaxation Sources

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

children.title: Lagrangian Dual Sources
children.top_down_role: Dual-bound information supplied by constraint relaxation through penalties.

assumptions_latex: The problem is \(\inf\{f(x):x\in Y,\ g(x)\le0\}\).
Multipliers for the relaxed inequalities are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Lagrangian dual value is a valid lower bound on the primal optimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak Lagrangian duality for inequality-constrained minimization.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.2 Lagrangian relaxation p. 25
3.3 Lagrangian relaxation p. 24
source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\), define \(q(\lambda)=\inf_{x\in Y}\{f(x)+\lambda^\top g(x)\}\) and \(d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}q(\lambda)\). Every feasible \(x\in Y\) satisfying \(g(x)\le0\) obeys \(q(\lambda)\le f(x)\); hence \(q(\lambda)\le d^*\le z^*\), where \(z^*=\inf\{f(x):x\in Y,\ g(x)\le0\}\). Therefore either a multiplier value \(q(\lambda)\) or a certified dual value supplies a valid lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative Lagrange multipliers produce lower bounds for minimization, and maximizing those bounds gives the Lagrangian dual value, which cannot exceed the primal optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Dual Sources

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.2 Lagrangian relaxation p. 25
3.3 Lagrangian relaxation p. 24
source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

children.title: Dual-Bound Comparability
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing meaningful comparison among bounds from different relaxation sources.

assumptions_latex: All bounds refer to the same minimization instance, objective, and objective scaling.
Each source has independently established validity as a lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Valid dual bounds are numerically comparable, and their maximum is the strongest combined bound.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparability requires identical instance, objective direction, units, scaling, and bound semantics.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.3 Continuous bound versus Lagrangian bound p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dual bounds \(L_1\) and \(L_2\) are directly comparable only when they bound the same optimal value \(z^*\), use the same minimization or maximization convention, and are expressed under the same affine objective scaling. Under the minimization convention, \(L_1\le z^*\) and \(L_2\le z^*\), the larger value is stronger, and \(\max\{L_1,L_2\}\le z^*\). Bounds from different scalings must first be transformed to a common objective scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual bounds can be ranked only after aligning instance, objective direction, and scaling; for minimization, the larger valid lower bound is stronger.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Bound Comparability

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.3 Continuous bound versus Lagrangian bound p. 26

children.title: Bound-Gap Conventions
children.top_down_role: Absolute, relative, and normalized measures used to compare compatible primal and dual bounds.

assumptions_latex: The primal and dual bounds satisfy \(L\le U\) for the same minimization problem.
The normalization scale is positive whenever a normalized gap is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Absolute and relative gaps are nonnegative and vanish exactly when the compatible bounds agree.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gap values are meaningful only with an explicit denominator and common objective scale.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For compatible finite bounds \(L\le U\), the absolute gap is \(g_{\mathrm{abs}}=U-L\). Given an explicitly declared scale \(s(L,U)>0\), the normalized gap is \(g_{\mathrm{rel}}=(U-L)/s(L,U)\). Common choices include \(s(L,U)=\max\{1,|U|\}\) and \(s(L,U)=\max\{1,|L|,|U|\}\); these conventions are not numerically interchangeable. Both gaps are nonnegative, and each equals zero exactly when \(L=U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The absolute gap is upper minus lower bound; a relative gap divides this difference by a declared positive scale, whose convention must accompany every comparison.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Gap Conventions

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

children.title: Bound-Based Optimality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certification regimes based on agreement or prescribed proximity of compatible bounds.

assumptions_latex: A feasible incumbent has objective value \(U\).
An independently valid dual bound \(L\) satisfies \(L\le z^*\le U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality certifies exact optimality; a prescribed small gap certifies bounded suboptimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and additive-tolerance certificates for minimization; relative certificates require a declared normalization.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\bar x\) be feasible with \(U=f(\bar x)\), and let \(L\) be a valid lower bound, so \(L\le z^*\le U\). If \(U=L\), then \(f(\bar x)=z^*\), certifying exact optimality. If \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon\ge0\), then \(0\le f(\bar x)-z^*\le\varepsilon\), certifying additive \(\varepsilon\)-optimality. Likewise, a declared normalized-gap inequality certifies the corresponding relative tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent and compatible lower bound certify exact optimality when equal, or additive and relative near-optimality when their declared gap meets tolerance.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Based Optimality Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

children.title: Relaxation-Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance-level, family-level, and pathological regimes for interpreting formulation strength.

children.title: Instance-Level Root-Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relaxation quality for a fixed instance and objective before search.

children.title: Root-Node Gaps
children.top_down_role: Relaxation quality measured before branching or other search refinements.

assumptions_latex: Branch-and-bound is applied to a fixed minimization instance.
The root relaxation is solved or bounded before branching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root-node gap measures the separation between the root dual bound and a compatible primal reference value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance-level gap before branching, using a stated primal reference and normalization.

source_refs.locator: 6.1 Continuous-Relaxation-Based Branch-and-Bound Methods p. 150

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_0\) be the valid dual bound obtained from the root-node relaxation of a fixed minimization instance, and let \(U_0\) be a compatible finite primal reference, such as the root incumbent or known optimum. The absolute root-node gap is \(g_0=U_0-L_0\). For a declared positive scale \(s_0\), the normalized root gap is \(g_0/s_0\). The reported value must identify both the root relaxation and the chosen primal reference.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A root-node gap compares the root relaxation's lower bound with a stated compatible incumbent or known optimum before any branching occurs.
knowledge_statements.title: Root-Node Gaps

source_witnesses.locator: 6.1 Continuous-Relaxation-Based Branch-and-Bound Methods p. 150

children.title: Fixed-Instance Gaps
children.top_down_role: Gap behavior tied to one model instance under a designated objective.

assumptions_latex: One problem instance, formulation, objective, and relaxation are held fixed.
A compatible finite primal reference value is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fixed-instance gap is a scalar property of the specified instance-formulation-objective tuple.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates within-instance measurement from claims uniform over an instance family.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed minimization instance \(I\), let \(L(I)\) be the value of a specified relaxation and let \(U(I)\) be a compatible finite primal reference. The absolute fixed-instance gap is \(g(I)=U(I)-L(I)\). A normalized gap is \(g(I)/s(I)\) for an explicitly specified \(s(I)>0\). Changing the instance, formulation, objective coefficients, relaxation, primal reference, or normalization produces a different gap quantity and cannot be treated as the same measurement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-instance gap belongs to one fully specified instance, formulation, objective, relaxation, primal reference, and normalization; changing any component changes the measured quantity.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Instance Gaps

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

children.title: Objective-Specific Root Gaps
children.top_down_role: Dependence of root relaxation quality on the selected objective.

assumptions_latex: A fixed feasible set and root relaxation are evaluated under objective vector \(c\).
The integer and relaxation values are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The root gap is indexed by the objective and may change when the objective changes.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The same relaxation geometry can exhibit different gaps under different linear objectives.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Continuous relaxation p. 24

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(X\subseteq R\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and objective \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(z(c)=\inf_{x\in X}c^\top x\), \(r(c)=\inf_{x\in R}c^\top x\), and \(g(c)=z(c)-r(c)\ge0\), when both values are finite. This root gap is objective-specific: replacing \(c\) by \(d\) may change both its magnitude and the relative ranking of competing relaxations. Under positive scaling, \(g(\alpha c)=\alpha g(c)\) for every \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A root gap depends on the objective vector, can rank relaxations differently under another objective, and scales linearly when the objective is positively rescaled.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Specific Root Gaps

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.1 Continuous relaxation p. 24

children.title: Cross-Instance Gap Comparability
children.top_down_role: Limits on comparing root-gap measurements across differently scaled instances.

assumptions_latex: Each instance uses compatible primal and dual references.
Objective units, scaling, gap denominator, and treatment of zero or infinite values are uniform across instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-instance numerical comparisons are valid only under a common gap protocol.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the protocol required before aggregating or ranking gaps across heterogeneous instances.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For instances indexed by \(i\), let \(L_i\le U_i\) be compatible bounds and define \(\gamma_i=(U_i-L_i)/s_i\) with \(s_i>0\). Values \(\gamma_i\) are cross-instance comparable only when the same rules determine objective scaling, \(U_i\), \(L_i\), and \(s_i\), and when zero, infeasible, unbounded, and unsolved cases receive a common treatment. Without these conditions, rankings or aggregates of \(\gamma_i\) can reflect conventions rather than formulation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaps across instances are comparable only under uniform objective scaling, bound references, normalization, and exceptional-case rules; otherwise rankings may be artifacts of convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Instance Gap Comparability

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Optimality, Relaxation and General Solution Procedures p. 13

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed protocol is mathematically coherent and fits the condition container, but the cited general chapter locator does not specifically support the asserted cross-instance comparability requirements or exceptional-case policy. A benchmarking, solver-reporting, or formulation-comparison source with a direct section or page locator is required.

children.title: Integrality-Gap Families
children.top_down_role: Worst-case and asymptotic gaps over structured classes of instances.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N_{\ge 1}\), and \(\mathcal F_n\) is a nonempty family of minimization instances having size parameter \(n\).
For every \(I\in\mathcal F_n\), the values \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)\) and \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\) are finite and satisfy \(0<z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\le z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)\).
When an asymptotic rate is stated, \(h:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_n=\sup_{I\in\mathcal F_n}z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)/z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\), with asymptotic behavior expressible through \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}G_n\) or, when matching bounds hold, \(G_n=\Theta(h(n))\).

notation.meaning: integer and relaxation optimal values for instance I
worst-case multiplicative integrality gap at size n
positive comparison function for an asymptotic rate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the multiplicative gap for positive-valued minimization families; additive or maximization conventions require separate normalization.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Comparing the Strength of Different Formulations p. 70

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\), let \(\mathcal F_n\) be a nonempty structured family of minimization instances. For each \(I\in\mathcal F_n\), define \(g(I):=z_{\mathrm{IP}}(I)/z_{\mathrm{LP}}(I)\). The family integrality gap is \[G_n:=\sup_{I\in\mathcal F_n}g(I).\] A uniform gap bound is a constant \(C\) satisfying \(G_n\le C\) for every \(n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\). Asymptotic behavior may be summarized by \(\limsup_{n\to\infty}G_n\), or by \(G_n=\Theta(h(n))\) for a function \(h:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) when matching upper and lower bounds hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each positive integer size, a family gap is the worst integer-to-relaxation objective ratio among the structured instances; the resulting sequence can be bounded uniformly or studied asymptotically.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality-Gap Families

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Comparing the Strength of Different Formulations p. 70

children.title: Objective Exactness without Ideality
children.top_down_role: Zero-gap objectives occurring in formulations whose relaxation is not geometrically ideal.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is the integer-feasible set and \(Q\supseteq\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is a relaxation.
\(c\in\mathbb R^d\) has finite minima over \(S\) and \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in Q}c^\top x=\min_{x\in S}c^\top x\) does not imply \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exactness for one objective from geometric exactness for all linear objectives.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Comparing the Strength of Different Formulations p. 70

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A relaxation \(Q\) is objective-exact for \(c\) when \[\min_{x\in Q}c^\top x=\min_{x\in S}c^\top x.\] Objective exactness without ideality occurs when this equality holds but \(Q\ne\operatorname{conv}(S)\). Equivalently, the relaxation contains some \(\bar x\notin\operatorname{conv}(S)\), yet no such extra point improves the chosen objective below the integer optimum. Thus a zero objective gap for one \(c\) does not certify geometric ideality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonideal relaxation may have zero gap for a particular objective because its extra fractional points do not improve that objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Exactness without Ideality

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Comparing the Strength of Different Formulations p. 70

children.title: Pathological Gap-Metric Regimes
children.top_down_role: Gap measures compromised by objective signs, scaling, missing incumbents, or unbounded relaxations.

children.title: Undefined Relative Gaps
children.top_down_role: Gap ratios rendered unusable by zero, sign-changing, or otherwise unsuitable reference values.

assumptions_latex: \(L,U\in\mathbb R\) are respectively a valid lower bound and incumbent value for a minimization problem.
The reported relative gap is \(r=(U-L)/|U|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U=0\Rightarrow r\text{ is undefined}\), even when \(U-L\) is finite.

notation.meaning: lower bound and incumbent objective value

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses incumbent-magnitude normalization; other denominators have analogous zero-denominator boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the convention \[r:=\frac{U-L}{|U|},\] the relative gap is defined only when \(U\ne0\). If \(U=0\), division by zero makes \(r\) undefined regardless of whether the additive gap \(U-L\) is finite or zero. Consequently, a reporting rule must retain the additive gap, adopt an explicitly positive scaling denominator, or return an undefined status; assigning a finite percentage without such a convention is not mathematically justified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incumbent-normalized relative gap is undefined when the incumbent value is zero, although the additive gap may remain meaningful.
knowledge_statements.title: Undefined Relative Gaps

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-denominator failure is mathematically correct under the explicitly selected incumbent-normalized convention, and failure_boundary fits the container. No inspectable source is supplied for that convention or its reporting implications.

children.title: Scale-Distorted Gap Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparisons whose apparent quality changes materially under objective rescaling.

assumptions_latex: \(L<U\) are finite lower and incumbent values for a minimization problem.
An objective translation replaces every value \(v\) by \(v+\beta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_\beta=(U-L)/|U+\beta|\) can vary arbitrarily although \(U-L\) and all optimizers are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Demonstrates translation distortion for incumbent-normalized relative gaps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Translate an objective by a constant \(\beta\), so that the bound pair becomes \((L+\beta,U+\beta)\). Feasible solutions, optimizers, and the additive gap remain unchanged because \[(U+\beta)-(L+\beta)=U-L.\] However, the incumbent-normalized relative gap becomes \[r_\beta:=\frac{U-L}{|U+\beta|}.\] As \(|\beta|\to\infty\), \(r_\beta\to0\); at \(\beta=-U\), it is undefined. Hence relative-gap comparisons can be arbitrarily distorted by an optimization-equivalent change of objective origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a constant preserves solutions and additive gaps but can make an incumbent-normalized relative gap arbitrarily small or undefined.
knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Distorted Gap Comparisons

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The translation example correctly preserves optimizers and the additive gap while allowing the selected relative gap to approach zero, become arbitrarily large near the zero denominator, or become undefined. The counterexample kind fits, but no source supports the normalization and invariance discussion.

children.title: Missing-Incumbent Gap Failures
children.top_down_role: Gap reporting regimes lacking a valid primal reference value.

assumptions_latex: \(L\in\mathbb R\) is a valid lower bound for a minimization problem.
No feasible incumbent objective value \(U\in\mathbb R\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quantities \(U-L\) and \((U-L)/|U|\) cannot be evaluated as finite primal-dual gaps.

notation.meaning: available dual or relaxation lower bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes absence of an incumbent from a large but finite optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite primal-dual gap requires both a valid bound \(L\) and the objective value \(U\) of a known feasible solution. Before any incumbent exists, \(U\) is unavailable rather than merely large. Therefore neither the additive expression \(U-L\) nor the relative expression \((U-L)/|U|\) is a finite computable certificate. Replacing the missing incumbent by \(+\infty\) may encode algorithmic state, but it does not produce a finite gap or an approximation guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a feasible incumbent, bound information alone cannot yield a finite primal-dual gap or relative optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing-Incumbent Gap Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly distinguishes a missing incumbent from a finite incumbent with a large gap, and failure_boundary is the appropriate role. An authoritative source for primal-dual gap reporting when no incumbent exists is absent.

children.title: Unbounded-Relaxation Gap Failures
children.top_down_role: Gap measures invalidated by an unbounded relaxation.

assumptions_latex: The integer minimization problem has finite optimum \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}\in\mathbb R\).
Its stated relaxation is feasible and unbounded below, so \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{\mathrm{IP}}-z_{\mathrm{LP}}=+\infty\), and no finite relaxation-gap ratio is certified.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers a finite integer optimum paired with a relaxation unbounded in the improving direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the integer optimum is finite but the minimization relaxation satisfies \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}=-\infty\), then its additive integrality gap is \[z_{\mathrm{IP}}-z_{\mathrm{LP}}=+\infty.\] A multiplicative expression involving \(z_{\mathrm{LP}}\) is likewise not a finite strength measure. Thus the relaxation supplies no finite objective-gap certificate, even though the original integer problem is well posed; finite gap analysis first requires a relaxation bounded in the objective direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation unbounded below has infinite additive gap against a finite integer optimum and yields no finite strength certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Relaxation Gap Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For a finite integer optimum and a relaxation unbounded below, the extended-real additive gap is infinite and no finite multiplicative certificate follows. The mathematical role and scope are appropriate, but the record supplies no source.

children.title: Misleading Aggregate Gap Summaries
children.top_down_role: Benchmark summaries that obscure sign, scale, or instance heterogeneity.

assumptions_latex: For each \(n\ge3\), a benchmark contains \(n\) valid nonnegative instance gaps.
The summary reports their arithmetic mean, median, or maximum using the conventional order-statistic median.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the gaps \(0,\ldots,0,n\), the mean is \(1\), the median is \(0\), and the maximum is \(n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete family showing that central summaries need not control worst-case formulation weakness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer \(n\ge3\), consider the instance gaps \[g_1=\cdots=g_{n-1}=0,\qquad g_n=n.\] Their arithmetic mean is \(1\), their conventional median is \(0\), and their maximum is \(n\). Hence a constant mean and a zero median can coexist with an unbounded worst-case gap. Aggregate reporting without the sample size, tail statistics, and a declared treatment of undefined or infinite gaps can therefore conceal severe relaxation weakness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For benchmarks of at least three instances, the displayed gap family has mean one and median zero while its worst-case gap grows without bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Misleading Aggregate Gap Summaries

children.title: Ideal Formulations
children.top_down_role: Formulations whose relevant relaxation vertices satisfy the designated integrality structure.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{d+k}\) is the polyhedral continuous relaxation of a valid mixed-integer formulation.
\(I\) is the finite index set of variables designated integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\text{ is ideal}\iff v_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\) for every \(v\in\operatorname{ext}(Q)\).

notation.meaning: polyhedral relaxation in original and auxiliary variables

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses vertex integrality in all designated integer coordinates for a polyhedral mixed-integer formulation.

source_refs.locator: 1.7 Good and Ideal Formulations p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{d+k}\) be the polyhedral continuous relaxation of a valid mixed-integer formulation, and let \(I\) be the finite index set of its designated integer variables. The formulation is ideal when every extreme point \(v\in\operatorname{ext}(Q)\) satisfies \(v_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\). Ideality concerns the designated integrality structure at the vertices of the lifted relaxation itself, not merely exactness after projection onto the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyhedral mixed-integer formulation is ideal when every relaxation vertex is integral in all variables designated as integer.
knowledge_statements.title: Ideal Formulations

source_witnesses.locator: 1.7 Good and Ideal Formulations p. 15

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent full-space characterization for nonempty bounded polyhedral relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a nonempty polytope and let \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Then
\[
\bigl(v_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\ \text{for every }v\in\operatorname{ext}(Q)\bigr)
\iff
Q=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(Q\cap\{z:z_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\}\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty polytope, vertex integrality in the designated coordinates is equivalent to being the convex hull of the points satisfying those integrality restrictions.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a nonempty polytope.
\(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) indexes the designated integer coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\text{ is ideal on }I\iff Q=\operatorname{conv}(Q\cap\{z:z_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\})\).
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Convex-Hull Characterization of Ideality

children.title: Perfect Original-Space Formulations
children.top_down_role: Exact descriptions expressed in the original decision space.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\) is the original-space feasible set.
\(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\) is a polyhedron containing \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is perfect for }S\iff P=\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restricts perfectness to linear descriptions using only the original decision variables.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Convex Hulls and Perfect Formulations p. 20
Chapter 4. Perfect Formulations p. 129

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An original-space linear formulation \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\le b\}\) is perfect for \(S\) when \[P=\operatorname{conv}(S).\] It then contains no points beyond convex combinations of integer-feasible solutions, and for every \(c\in\mathbb R^d\) having a finite minimum, \[\min_{x\in P}c^\top x=\min_{x\in S}c^\top x.\] The qualification original-space excludes auxiliary variables and projection from the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perfect original-space formulation describes exactly the convex hull of feasible integer points without auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Perfect Original-Space Formulations

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Convex Hulls and Perfect Formulations p. 20
Chapter 4. Perfect Formulations p. 129

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rational mixed-integer hulls and perfect formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rational-polyhedral convex hulls and exact original-space formulations for rational mixed-integer linear sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z_+^n\times\mathbb R_+^p:Ax+Gy\leq b\},\] where \(A,G,b\) have rational entries. There exist rational \(A',G',b'\) such that \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=P:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{n+p}:A'x+G'y\leq b'\}.\] Consequently, every linear objective has the same supremum over \(S\) and \(P\). If the linear program over \(P\) is feasible and bounded, the common optimum is attained over \(S\). The system defining \(P\) is a perfect formulation of \(S\); when \(p=0\), \(P\) is an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of a rational mixed-integer linear set has a rational linear description. This description is a perfect formulation: its linear relaxation gives the same value for every linear objective, and a feasible bounded relaxation yields an attained mixed-integer optimum. In the pure-integer case the resulting polyhedron is integral.
assumptions_latex: S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb Z_+^n\times\mathbb R_+^p:Ax+Gy\leq b\}
A,G,b\text{ have rational entries}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists A',G',b'\text{ rational}:\ \operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,y):A'x+G'y\leq b'\},\quad \sup_{(x,y)\in S}(c^\top x+h^\top y)=\sup_{(x,y)\in\operatorname{conv}(S)}(c^\top x+h^\top y)

source_evidence.locator: Getting Started / 1.4. Convex Hulls and Perfect Formulations / Definition 1.4-extra-2

source_refs.locator: Getting Started / 1.4. Convex Hulls and Perfect Formulations / Definition 1.4-extra-2

children.title: Sharp Formulations
children.top_down_role: Formulations exact after projection onto the original variables without requiring lifted-space ideality.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is the original feasible set.
\(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{d+k}\) is a valid lifted relaxation with projection \(\pi_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\text{ is sharp}\iff\pi_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
review_flags: terminology may vary across formulation literature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines sharpness as convex-hull exactness after projection, independently of lifted-space vertex integrality.

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Comparing the Strength of Different Formulations p. 70

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lifted formulation \(Q\) is sharp for \(S\) when its original-variable projection satisfies \[\pi_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(S).\] Therefore every linear objective depending only on \(x\) has the same relaxation value as optimization over \(S\), whenever that value is finite. Sharpness does not require every extreme point of \(Q\) to satisfy the designated lifted-space integrality conditions; it requires only exactness of the projected relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted formulation is sharp when projecting its relaxation onto the original variables gives exactly the feasible-set convex hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Formulations

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Comparing the Strength of Different Formulations p. 70

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict separation between projected hull exactness and lifted-space vertex integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the original feasible set be \(S=\{0,1\}\), designate \(x\) as integer, and set
\[
Q:=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(1,0),(\tfrac12,1)\}\subseteq\mathbb R^2.
\]
Then
\[
\pi_x(Q)=[0,1]=\operatorname{conv}(S),
\]
so \(Q\) is sharp for \(S\). However, \((\tfrac12,1)\) is a vertex of \(Q\) with fractional designated coordinate \(x=\tfrac12\); hence the formulation is not ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted relaxation can project exactly to the original convex hull while possessing a fractional lifted-space vertex in a designated integer coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(S=\{0,1\}\subseteq\mathbb R\).
The coordinate \(x\) is designated integer and the second coordinate is continuous.
\(Q=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(1,0),(\tfrac12,1)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is sharp for \(S\) but is not ideal.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness Does Not Imply Ideality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent characterization when both the projected relaxation and target hull are nonempty closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P:=\pi_x(Q)\) and \(H:=\operatorname{conv}(S)\), and suppose \(P\) and \(H\) are nonempty closed convex sets. Then
\[
P=H
\iff
\inf_{x\in P}c^\top x=\inf_{x\in H}c^\top x\quad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb R^d,
\]
where the infima may take the value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty closed convex projected and target sets, sharpness is equivalent to equality of every linear minimization value.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\pi_x(Q)\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(H=\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(S)\iff \inf_{x\in\pi_x(Q)}c^\top x=\inf_{s\in S}c^\top s\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Objective Characterization of Sharpness

children.title: Locally Ideal Formulations
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer formulations whose relaxation has the intended local integrality behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(S=\{x:x\in S_t\text{ for every }t\in T\}\) is assembled from local feasible sets.
\(Q_t\) is a mixed-integer formulation of \(S_t\) with designated local integer coordinates \(I_t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local ideality requires \(v_{I_t}\in\mathbb Z^{|I_t|}\) for every \(t\in T\) and every \(v\in\operatorname{ext}(Q_t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses subsystem-wise vertex integrality; the assembled intersection need not be globally ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Relative to a specified decomposition into local subsystems \(t\in T\), a formulation is locally ideal when each isolated relaxation \(Q_t\) is ideal in its designated local integer coordinates: \[v_{I_t}\in\mathbb Z^{|I_t|}\quad\text{for every }v\in\operatorname{ext}(Q_t).\] This property is local to the declared subsystems. It does not by itself imply that the combined relaxation \(\bigcap_{t\in T}Q_t\) is ideal, because intersecting locally ideal polyhedra may create new fractional extreme points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each declared subsystem has integral relaxation vertices locally, although their combined formulation may still have fractional vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Locally Ideal Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Subsystem-wise vertex integrality is internally plausible and the definition kind fits the proposed container, but locally ideal has context-dependent meanings. No authority is cited, and the ambient spaces and embeddings needed for the displayed combined intersection are not specified sufficiently to establish that this is the intended standard notion.

children.title: Branch-Persistent Exactness
children.top_down_role: Sharpness or related strength properties intended to survive natural branching restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) has a lifted relaxation \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{d+k}\).
\(\mathcal B\) is a declared family of branching regions in the original variable space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_x(Q\cap\pi_x^{-1}(B))=\operatorname{conv}(S\cap B)\) for every \(B\in\mathcal B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes persistence of projected convex-hull exactness under every declared natural branch restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sharp formulation \(Q\) is branch-persistently exact with respect to \(\mathcal B\) when, for every branch region \(B\in\mathcal B\), restricting the formulation and then projecting remains exact: \[\pi_x\!\left(Q\cap\pi_x^{-1}(B)\right)=\operatorname{conv}(S\cap B).\] The property is relative to the specified branch family, such as variable-bound or split branches. Root-node sharpness alone is insufficient, since intersection with a branch region need not commute with taking the projected convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactness persists after every allowed branch when the restricted relaxation projects to the restricted feasible set's convex hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Persistent Exactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a coherent definition of projected convex-hull exactness after restrictions from a declared branch family, and definition fits the container. However, branch-persistent exactness is not sourced, and the admissible structure of the branch regions must be tied to an authoritative formulation-theory convention before this candidate is reliable.

children.title: Convex-Hull Formulation Principle
children.top_down_role: The convex hull as the canonical geometric target for strongest continuous formulation strength.

children.title: Original-Space Hull Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Hull representations using only the original decision variables.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
\(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}(S)\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of the feasible set
polyhedron described in the original variables

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear descriptions without auxiliary variables.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. The Convex Hull of a Disjunctive Set p. 17

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An original-space hull description of \(S\) is a system \(Ax\leq b\) in the variables \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that
\[
P:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}=\operatorname{conv}(S).
\]
It is therefore exact precisely when every point satisfying the inequalities is a finite convex combination of points of \(S\), and every point of \(S\) satisfies the inequalities. If the intended target is the closed convex hull, the defining equality must instead be stated with \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An original-variable inequality system is a hull description exactly when its feasible region equals the convex hull of the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Original-Space Hull Descriptions

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. The Convex Hull of a Disjunctive Set p. 17

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replacement of linear optimization over a feasible set by a linear program over a known compact original-space description of its convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A problem class has the explicit convex hull property when a compact description of \(\operatorname{conv}(X)\) is known, so that an instance \(\max\{cx:x\in X\}\) can in principle be replaced by the linear program \(\max\{cx:x\in\operatorname{conv}(X)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the convex hull has a known compact description in the original variables, linear optimization over the feasible set can in principle be replaced by linear programming over that convex hull.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n
\operatorname{conv}(X)\text{ has a known compact description}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{cx:x\in X\}\text{ can in principle be replaced by }\max\{cx:x\in\operatorname{conv}(X)\}.

children.title: Lifted Hull Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Hull representations obtained with auxiliary variables and projection.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
\(p,r\geq1\) are integers, \(G\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n}\), \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times p}\), and \(h\in\mathbb{R}^r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended formulations whose projection gives the finite convex hull.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 The Convex Hull Via Lifting and Projection p. 17

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A lifted hull description of \(S\) is the polyhedron
\[
Q:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^p:Gx+Hy\leq h\}
\]
whose projection onto the original coordinates satisfies
\[
\operatorname{proj}_x(Q):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p\text{ such that }(x,y)\in Q\}=\operatorname{conv}(S).
\]
The variables \(y\) are auxiliary. If the intended target is \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\), that equality must be stated explicitly because the projection of a closed convex set need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lifted hull description introduces auxiliary variables and is exact when projection onto the original variables equals the finite convex hull of the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Hull Descriptions

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 The Convex Hull Via Lifting and Projection p. 17

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear-Objective Transfer Through a Hull Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization of objectives depending only on the original coordinates over an exact lifted hull description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(S)\), then for every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), with extended-real infima allowed,
\[
\inf_{(x,y)\in Q}c^\top x=\inf_{x\in\operatorname{conv}(S)}c^\top x=\inf_{s\in S}c^\top s.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact lifted hull description preserves every linear optimization value whose objective uses only the original variables.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.
\(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) satisfies \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{(x,y)\in Q}c^\top x=\inf_{s\in S}c^\top s\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: linear objective vector on the original coordinates

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Objective Transfer Through a Hull Lifting

children.title: Closed Convex-Hull Targets
children.top_down_role: Closure-sensitive convex targets used for exact formulation comparisons.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean closed convex hull, distinguished from the finite convex hull.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed convex-hull target generated by \(S\) is
\[
H:=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S),
\]
where closure is taken in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Equivalently, \(H\) is the intersection of all closed convex subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) containing \(S\). Thus a formulation targeting \(H\) may contain limit points absent from \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\); the two targets coincide exactly when \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex-hull target is the Euclidean closure of the finite convex hull and may include additional limit points.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convex-Hull Targets

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4

children.title: Limit-Point Geometry
children.top_down_role: Boundary points arising through convergent feasible sequences.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{x:\exists (x^k),\ x^k\in\operatorname{conv}(S),\ x^k\to x\}\).

notation.meaning: a sequence of finite convex combinations from the set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) belongs to the closed convex hull of \(S\) if and only if there exists a sequence \((x^k)_{k\geq1}\) with \(x^k\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) and \(x^k\to x\). Equivalently, for every \(k\geq1\), one may choose finitely many points \(s_{k1},\ldots,s_{kr_k}\in S\) and coefficients \(\lambda_{kj}\geq0\) satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^{r_k}\lambda_{kj}=1\), such that
\[
x^k=\sum_{j=1}^{r_k}\lambda_{kj}s_{kj}\longrightarrow x.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed-hull points are exactly limits of sequences of finite convex combinations of feasible points.
knowledge_statements.title: Limit-Point Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4
source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform bound on the number of source points needed at each stage of a closed-hull approximating sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), every \(x\in\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\) admits points \(s_{k0},\ldots,s_{kn}\in S\) and coefficients \(\lambda_{kj}\ge0\), \(\sum_{j=0}^n\lambda_{kj}=1\), such that \(\sum_{j=0}^n\lambda_{kj}s_{kj}\to x\). Repeated points or zero coefficients may be used when fewer than \(n+1\) points suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every closed-hull point is a limit of convex combinations using at most n+1 source points per approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.
\(x\in\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\lambda_{kj},s_{kj}:\quad \sum_{j=0}^{n}\lambda_{kj}s_{kj}\longrightarrow x.

notation.meaning: source points in the kth convex combination

children.title: Nonclosed Hull Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where the ordinary convex hull omits relevant limiting points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Noncompact Source with Nonclosed Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary bounded example showing that boundedness without closedness does not prevent a closure gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2<1\}\). Then \(S\) is convex and \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=S\), while \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{x:\|x\|_2\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open Euclidean unit ball is bounded and convex but has a strictly larger closed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(S)=\{x:\|x\|_2<1\}\subsetneq\{x:\|x\|_2\le1\}=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S).
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Noncompact Source with Nonclosed Hull

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact geometric criterion distinguishing an ordinary convex hull from its closed-hull target.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is in a nonclosed-hull regime when \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is not closed, equivalently when \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\). The set \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\setminus\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is its closure gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed-hull regime occurs exactly when closing the ordinary convex hull adds points.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(S)\text{ is nonclosed}\iff\operatorname{conv}(S)\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Convex-Hull Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness Rules Out a Closure Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sufficient condition excluding nonclosed convex hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is compact, then \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is compact and hence closed. Therefore a nonclosed convex hull in finite-dimensional space requires a noncompact generating set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact generating sets have closed convex hulls, so nonclosed-hull behavior requires a noncompact source set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete distinction between a convex hull and its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
S:=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\geq x^2\}\setminus\{(0,0)\}.
\]
The removed point is an extreme point of the epigraph, so \(S\) remains convex and hence \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=S\). Nevertheless, the sequence \((1/k,1/k^2)\in S\) converges to \((0,0)\notin S\). Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{conv}(S)=S\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y\geq x^2\}.
\]
Thus replacing a hull by its closure can strictly enlarge the formulation target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting the origin from the quadratic epigraph leaves a convex but nonclosed set whose closed hull restores the missing origin.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Hull Regimes

Define the horizon cone by

C^\infty:=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists (x^k)_{k\geq1}\subseteq C,\ \exists (t_k)_{k\geq1}\subseteq(0,\infty),\ t_k\downarrow0,\ t_kx^k\to d\}.

Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\). Then

\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:Ax\le b\}\text{ is integral for every }b\in\mathbb Z^m.
