knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral matrix is totally unimodular exactly when every associated nonnegative inequality system is integral for every integer right-hand side.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total-unimodularity certificate for a pure-integer linear formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose every square subdeterminant of \(A\) belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\). Then total unimodularity of \(A\), together with integrality of \(b\), certifies that
\[
P:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\leq b\}
\]
is integral: every nonempty face of \(P\) contains an integer point, equivalently
\[
P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n).
\]
Thus the continuous relaxation already gives the integer hull. The certificate is checkable from the matrix structure and the right-hand side; it does not extend automatically to nonintegral right-hand sides.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: TDI certificate for rational inequality systems with integral right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The system \(Ax\leq b\) is totally dual integral if, for every \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\) for which
\[
\max\{c^Tx:Ax\leq b\}
\]
has a finite optimum, the dual problem
\[
\min\{b^Ty:A^Ty=c,\ y\geq0\}
\]
has an integral optimal solution \(y\). If the system is totally dual integral and \(b\) is integral, then \(P\) is integral:
\[
P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n).
\]
Total dual integrality is a property of the displayed system, not merely of the polyhedron it represents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A TDI inequality system with an integer right-hand side certifies integrality through integer optimal dual solutions for every integer objective.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Integrality Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reeve Simplex: Integrality Does Not Imply IDP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation between polyhedral integrality and the integer decomposition property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(m\in\mathbb Z\), \(m\ge2\), let
\[
R_m=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(1,1,m)\}.
\]
The lattice points of \(R_m\) are its four vertices, but \((1,1,1)\in2R_m\cap\mathbb Z^3\) is not the sum of two lattice points of \(R_m\). Hence \(R_m\) is integral but lacks the integer decomposition property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Reeve simplex has integral vertices but fails integer decomposition, so IDP is strictly stronger than integrality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_m\text{ is integral but does not have IDP}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer-decomposition certificate for rational polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume the stated integer decomposition property. For any vertex \(v\) of \(P\), rationality provides an integer \(k\geq1\) such that \(kv\in\mathbb{Z}^n\). The decomposition certificate supplies
\[
kv=z^1+\cdots+z^k,
\qquad z^j\in P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n.
\]
Thus \(v=k^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^kz^j\). Extremality of \(v\) forces \(z^1=\\cdots=z^k=v\), so \(v\in\mathbb{Z}^n\). Consequently every vertex is integral and
\[
P=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every integer point in every dilation decomposes into integer points of the original rational polytope, then all vertices are integral.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Decomposition Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed-Cycle Obstruction to the Path Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acyclicity is essential for the uncapacitated unit-flow system to equal a bounded path polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider arcs \(s\to a\), \(a\to t\), \(a\to b\), and \(b\to a\). If \(p=(s,a,t)\) and \(C=(a,b,a)\), then
\[
\chi^p+\lambda\chi^C\in\{x\in\mathbb R_+^E:Bx=b^{st}\}\quad(\lambda\ge0).
\]
Hence this unit-flow set is unbounded and is not the convex hull of directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path incidence vectors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed path-polytope certificate on acyclic graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\) be the node-arc incidence matrix and let \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^V\) have value \(-1\) at \(s\), value \(1\) at \(t\), and value \(0\) elsewhere, using the head-minus-tail convention. Then
\[
P_{st}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^E:Bx=b\}
\]
is bounded because \(D\) is acyclic. Total unimodularity makes every vertex integral, and conservation with one unit of flow makes each integral vertex the incidence vector \(\chi^p\) of a directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) path. Therefore
\[
P_{st}=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^p:p\text{ is a directed }s\text{-to-}t\text{ path}\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a directed acyclic graph, the nonnegative unit-flow formulation is exactly the convex hull of directed source-to-sink path incidence vectors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite matching ideality certified by total unimodularity of the vertex-edge incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}V,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph, and let \(A\) be its vertex-edge incidence matrix. Then \(A\) is totally unimodular. Consequently,
\[
P=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^{E}_{+}:\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le 1\quad(v\in U\cup V)\right\}
=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\text{ is a matching of }G\}.
\]
Thus total unimodularity of \(A\), together with the integral right-hand side, is a verifiable certificate that the degree formulation is ideal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bipartite graph, total unimodularity certifies that the nonnegative degree relaxation has exactly the matching incidence vectors as its vertices.
assumptions_latex: G=(U\mathbin{\dot\cup}V,E)\text{ is a finite bipartite graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\text{ is a matching of }G\}

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits the leaf, and the finite bipartite matching-polytope statement is mathematically precise. No source reference with an inspectable theorem, section, or page locator is supplied, so the total-unimodularity and hull claims remain unsupported.

children.title: Matroidal Certificates
children.top_down_role: Exactness evidence inherited from matroid or independence-system structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Base-polytope ideality transfers between a matroid and its dual by complementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\) be a finite matroid on \(E\) and \(M^*\) its dual. Then
\[
B(M^*)=\{\mathbf1-x:x\in B(M)\},
\qquad r_{M^*}(S)=|S|-r_M(E)+r_M(E\setminus S).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementing base incidence vectors maps a matroid base polytope affinely onto the base polytope of its dual.
assumptions_latex: M\text{ is a finite matroid on }E
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B(M^*)=\mathbf1-B(M)
knowledge_statements.title: Matroid-Dual Base-Polytope Transfer
Matroidal Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matroid rank inequalities certify integrality of the independent-set formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M=(E,\mathcal I)\) be a finite matroid with rank function \(r\). Its independent-set polytope satisfies
\[
P(M)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^{E}_{+}:x(F)\le r(F)\quad\text{for every }F\subseteq E\right\}
=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I\}.
\]
Hence identifying a set system as the independent sets of a matroid and verifying its rank inequalities certifies that every vertex of \(P(M)\) is integral. Adding \(x(E)=r(E)\) analogously yields the convex hull of incidence vectors of bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rank-inequality system of a finite matroid is integral and therefore certifies exact independent-set and base formulations.
assumptions_latex: M=(E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a finite matroid with rank function }r
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(M)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^I:I\in\mathcal I\}

notation.meaning: sum of x_e over elements e in F

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits the leaf, and the independent-set and base-polytope claims are standard and consistently stated. An authoritative matroid-polytope source with a specific theorem, section, or page locator is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General algorithmic characterization of matroids rather than a formulation-ideality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite hereditary independence system is a matroid if and only if weight-ordered greedy selection returns a maximum-weight independent set for every nonnegative weight vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Universal correctness of the independence-system greedy algorithm characterizes matroids.
assumptions_latex: E\text{ is finite}
\mathcal I\subseteq2^E\text{ is nonempty and hereditary}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (E,\mathcal I)\text{ is a matroid}\iff\text{greedy is optimal for every }w\in\mathbb R_+^E
knowledge_statements.title: Rado–Edmonds Greedy Characterization

intermediate_metadata.reason: The local inventory is rank-inequality integrality for independent sets and bases plus dual-matroid base transfer. The proposed greedy algorithm is deferred as algorithmic matroid theory. Matching, flow, path, and generic matrix certificates are excluded.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rank-inequality description for common independent sets of two matroids under a cardinality bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M_1=(N,r_1)\) and \(M_2=(N,r_2)\) be matroids on the same ground set, and let \(q\) be the cardinality bound. Then
\[
P_q=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_{j\in A}x_j\le r_1(A),\ \sum_{j\in A}x_j\le r_2(A)\ \forall A\subseteq N,\ \sum_{j\in N}x_j\le q\right\}
\]
is the convex hull of the incidence vectors of sets independent in both matroids and having cardinality at most \(q\). The displayed inequality system is totally dual integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two matroids on a common ground set, nonnegativity, both systems of rank inequalities, and the cardinality upper bound describe exactly the convex hull of their common independent sets of size at most q. The inequality system is totally dual integral.
assumptions_latex: M_1=(N,r_1)\text{ and }M_2=(N,r_2)\text{ are matroids on the same ground set }N
q\text{ is the stated cardinality bound}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_q=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^S:S\in\mathcal I(M_1)\cap\mathcal I(M_2),\ |S|\le q\},\qquad P_q\text{ is defined by a TDI inequality system}

children.title: Certificate Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on carrying structural integrality certificates into altered formulations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection Transfer Criterion for Integrality Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which integrality of a combinatorial lift transfers through projection and supports an intended hull claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^p\) be an integral polyhedron and let \(\pi(y)=Ty\) with \(T\in\mathbb Z^{n\times p}\). Then \[\pi(Q)=\operatorname{conv}\{Ty:y\in Q\cap\mathbb Z^p\},\] so \(\pi(Q)\) is integral. For an intended integer family \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\), exact hull representation requires \[\operatorname{conv}\{Ty:y\in Q\cap\mathbb Z^p\}=\operatorname{conv}(X).\] The stronger semantic condition \(\{Ty:y\in Q\cap\mathbb Z^p\}=X\) is sufficient and additionally certifies that the projected integer points are exactly the intended objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer linear image of an integral lift is integral, but intended-hull exactness still requires equality of the projected integer-point hull with the target hull.
assumptions_latex: Q\subseteq\mathbb R^p\text{ is an integral polyhedron}
T\in\mathbb Z^{n\times p}
\pi(y)=Ty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(T(Q\cap\mathbb Z^p));\quad \pi(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(X)\iff\operatorname{conv}(T(Q\cap\mathbb Z^p))=\operatorname{conv}(X)

notation.meaning: intended family of integer incidence vectors

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Transfer Criterion for Integrality Certificates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arbitrary Side Constraints Do Not Preserve Combinatorial Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General boundary on transferring flow, path, matching, or matroid certificates to augmented systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=\{x:Ax\le b\}\) be integral because its displayed system has a combinatorial integrality certificate, such as total unimodularity with integral right-hand side. For an additional system \(Dx\le d\), integrality of \[Q\cap\{x:Dx\le d\}\] does not follow from integrality of \(Q\). It transfers only after separately verifying an integrality-preserving condition for the augmented system, such as total unimodularity of the full constraint matrix with integral right-hand side. Integral coefficients alone are insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding side constraints to an integral combinatorial formulation can create fractional vertices; the augmented system needs its own valid integrality certificate.
assumptions_latex: Q=\{x:Ax\le b\}\text{ is integral}
Dx\le d\text{ is an added system}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ integral}\centernot\implies Q\cap\{x:Dx\le d\}\text{ integral}
knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrary Side Constraints Do Not Preserve Combinatorial Integrality
Certificate Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite matching certificates fail when transferred to nonbipartite graphs without odd-set inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be the triangle with edge set \(E=\{12,23,31\}\). The degree relaxation
\[
P=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_+^E:x_{12}+x_{31}\le1,\ x_{12}+x_{23}\le1,\ x_{23}+x_{31}\le1\right\}
\]
contains the fractional vertex \(\bar x=(1/2,1/2,1/2)\). Every matching of the triangle has at most one edge, whereas \(\bar x(E)=3/2\). Therefore \(P\) is not the matching polytope, and the bipartite total-unimodularity certificate does not transfer beyond bipartite graphs without additional odd-set inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The triangle’s degree relaxation has the fractional vertex (1/2,1/2,1/2), so the bipartite matching certificate cannot be transferred unchanged.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is the three-cycle}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\in P\setminus\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\text{ is a matching of }G\}

notation.meaning: nonnegative degree relaxation of the triangle
vector assigning one half to every edge

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The triangle is a correct counterexample establishing the stated transfer boundary, and counterexample is the appropriate content kind. No inspectable source locator supports the nonbipartite matching boundary or the need for odd-set inequalities.

children.title: Disjunctive-Hull Certificates
children.top_down_role: Exactness obtained by an explicit convexification of alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive-Hull Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balas lifting for the convex hull of a finite union of bounded polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty polytopes \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\le b_i\}\), indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,k\), define
\[
Q=\left\{(x,(x^i),(\lambda_i)):x=\sum_{i=1}^k x^i,\ A_i x^i\le b_i\lambda_i,\ \lambda_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\right).
\]
Accordingly, the displayed decomposition variables and multiplier constraints form an explicit certificate that the projected continuous relaxation is the disjunctive hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogenized copy of each bounded alternative, joined by convex multipliers, projects exactly onto the convex hull of their union.
assumptions_latex: P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\le b_i\}\text{ is a nonempty polytope for each }i
k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i)

notation.meaning: scaled copy of the point assigned to alternative i
nonnegative convex multiplier for alternative i

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. The Convex Hull of a Disjunctive Set p. 17; §2.1 The Convex Hull Via Lifting and Projection p. 17

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. The Convex Hull of a Disjunctive Set p. 17; §2.1 The Convex Hull Via Lifting and Projection p. 17

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Without recession compatibility, homogenization can produce the closure rather than the nonclosed convex hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
P_1=\{(0,y):y\ge0\},\qquad P_2=\{(x,1):x\ge0\}.
\]
Then \(\operatorname{conv}(P_1\cup P_2)\) excludes \((x,0)\) for every \(x>0\), although these points lie in its closure. The homogenized formulation permits a recession direction of \(P_2\) at multiplier zero and therefore contains these limit points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternatives with incompatible recession cones can have a nonclosed convex hull while the homogenized formulation contains its missing limit points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\ne\operatorname{conv}(P_1\cup P_2)
knowledge_statements.title: Unequal-Recession Closure Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded-polyhedral extension of the Balas formulation under a shared recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\le b_i\}\) be nonempty polyhedra with common recession cone \(C\). For
\[
Q=\left\{(x,(x^i),\lambda):x=\sum_i x^i,\ A_i x^i\le b_i\lambda_i,\ \lambda\ge0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1\right\},
\]
one has
\[
\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_iP_i\right),
\qquad \operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{proj}_xQ)=C.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The homogenized disjunctive formulation remains exact for nonempty unbounded polyhedra sharing one recession cone.
assumptions_latex: P_i\ne\varnothing\quad(i=1,\ldots,k)
\operatorname{rec}(P_i)=C\quad(i=1,\ldots,k)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Recession Disjunctive-Hull Formulation

children.title: Obstructions to Exact Formulations
children.top_down_role: Geometric and descriptive barriers preventing a practical explicit hull formulation.

children.title: Nonpolyhedral Hulls
children.top_down_role: Exact convex hulls not admitting finite linear descriptions in the selected space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Finite Linear Lift for a Nonpolyhedral Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extends the original-space obstruction to arbitrary finite-dimensional continuous linear extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and nonpolyhedral. There do not exist a finite-dimensional polyhedron \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+k}\) and a linear map \(\pi\) such that \[\pi(Q)=C.\] Every linear image of a polyhedron is a polyhedron. Thus auxiliary continuous variables cannot yield an exact finite linear formulation of a genuinely nonpolyhedral convex hull; nonlinear, conic, or mixed-integer representations are not ruled out.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonpolyhedral convex set cannot be the projection of a finite-dimensional polyhedron, so continuous linear lifting does not remove the obstruction.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is convex and nonpolyhedral}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\,Q\text{ polyhedral and linear }\pi\text{ with }\pi(Q)=C
knowledge_statements.title: No Finite Linear Lift for a Nonpolyhedral Convex Hull
Nonpolyhedral Hulls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonpolyhedral convex hull cannot have a finite linear formulation in the same finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
S=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb Z:\|x\|_2\le1,\ z=0\}.
\]
Its convex hull is
\[
\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,0):\|x\|_2\le1\},
\]
which is not a polyhedron because its two-dimensional unit-disk section has infinitely many extreme points. Hence no finite system of linear inequalities in the selected \((x,z)\)-space describes this hull exactly. The obstruction concerns finite linear descriptions; it does not preclude an exact conic or other nonpolyhedral formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit-disk mixed-integer set has a nonpolyhedral hull, ruling out any finite exact linear description in its original space.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathbb R^2
z\in\mathbb Z
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(S)\text{ is nonpolyhedral and has no finite linear description in the selected space}

notation.meaning: unit-disk feasible set with fixed integer coordinate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly gives a nonpolyhedral convex hull and therefore rules out a finite linear description in the selected finite-dimensional space. The failure-boundary kind fits the obstruction leaf, but no inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Exponentially Large Descriptions
children.top_down_role: Exact hull descriptions whose smallest known or possible representations are very large.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size measure underlying exponential lower bounds for exact linear descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polytope \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), its linear extension complexity is \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\min\{r:\exists\,Q=\{y:Ay\le b,\ Ey=f\}\text{ with }r\text{ inequalities and a linear map }\pi\text{ such that }\pi(Q)=P\}.\] Equations and auxiliary-variable dimension are not counted in \(r\) under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extension complexity is the minimum number of inequalities in any polyhedral lift projecting exactly to the polytope.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a polytope}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{xc}(P)\text{ is the minimum inequality count over exact polyhedral extensions of }P

notation.meaning: linear projection from the extension space

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Extension Complexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical algebraic characterization used to prove lower bounds for exact linear extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polytope with at least two points and let \(S\) be a complete facet–vertex slack matrix of \(P\). Then \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S),\] where \(\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\) is the least \(r\) for which \(S=TU\) with \(T,U\ge0\) and inner dimension \(r\). Thus lower bounds on nonnegative rank are exactly lower bounds on the number of inequalities in every linear extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum inequality count of an exact polyhedral lift equals the nonnegative rank of the polytope's slack matrix.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is a polytope with at least two points}
S\text{ is a complete facet--vertex slack matrix of }P
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S)

notation.meaning: complete facet–vertex slack matrix of P

knowledge_statements.title: Slack-Matrix Characterization of Extension Complexity
Exponentially Large Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perfect-matching polytopes exhibit exponential linear extension complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For even \(n\), let \(P_n\) be the perfect-matching polytope of the complete graph \(K_n\). In the linear extended-formulation model, where size is the number of inequalities defining a polyhedron \(Q\) with \(P_n=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\), there exists a constant \(c>0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{xc}(P_n)\ge 2^{cn}.
\]
Thus every exact linear extended formulation of this family has exponentially many inequalities, regardless of its number of auxiliary variables or the chosen linear projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perfect-matching polytope of the complete graph requires exponentially many inequalities in every exact linear extended formulation.
assumptions_latex: n\text{ is a positive even integer}
P_n\text{ is the perfect-matching polytope of }K_n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{xc}(P_n)=2^{\Omega(n)}

notation.meaning: perfect-matching polytope of the complete graph K_n
polyhedron in an extended variable space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the leaf, and the claimed exponential linear extension-complexity lower bound for complete-graph perfect-matching polytopes is a substantive theorem. It cannot be accepted without an authoritative source and exact theorem or page locator.

children.title: Closure-Recession Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Invalid hull constructions caused by omitted closure or incompatible recession behavior.

children.title: Missing-Closure Failures
children.top_down_role: Invalid hull descriptions caused by omission of required limiting points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Optimization Cannot Detect Omitted Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explains why objective-value tests may conceal a missing-closure error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and every \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\inf_{x\in S}c^\top x=\inf_{x\in\operatorname{conv}(S)}c^\top x=\inf_{x\in\overline{\operatorname{conv}(S)}}c^\top x.\] The infimum need not be attained on either of the first two sets. Consequently, equality of linear optimal values does not determine whether closure was omitted from a hull target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set, its convex hull, and its closed convex hull have the same linear infimum, although closure may add unattained boundary points.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne S\subseteq\mathbb R^n
c\in\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_S c^\top x=\inf_{\operatorname{conv}(S)}c^\top x=\inf_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}(S)}}c^\top x
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Optimization Cannot Detect Omitted Closure
Missing-Closure Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Omitting closure can make the purported hull incompatible with every finite linear extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=(0,1)\subset\mathbb R\). Then \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=(0,1)\), while its closed convex hull is \([0,1]\). Every set described by finitely many linear inequalities in an extended finite-dimensional space is a polyhedron, and its linear projection is again a polyhedron and therefore closed. Consequently, no such formulation can project exactly onto \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\); it can represent \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\) instead. Any exactness assertion that silently replaces a required closed hull by an unclosed convex hull may therefore fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The open interval equals its convex hull but cannot be the projection of a finite linear formulation because such projections are closed polyhedra.
assumptions_latex: S=(0,1)\subset\mathbb R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(S)\ne\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\text{ and no finite linear extended formulation projects onto }\operatorname{conv}(S)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The open-interval example correctly distinguishes convex hull from closed convex hull and uses the closedness of finite-dimensional polyhedral projections. The failure-boundary kind fits, but the projection-closedness claim lacks a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Recession-Cone Mismatches
children.top_down_role: Invalid constructions caused by incompatible unbounded directions among component sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Cone Mismatches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear projection need not commute with taking recession cones for general closed convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2:t\ge x^2\}
\]
and let \(L(x,t)=x\). Then \(L(C)=\mathbb R\), so \(\operatorname{rec}(L(C))=\mathbb R\). However,
\[
\operatorname{rec}(C)=\{(0,d):d\ge0\},
\qquad
L(\operatorname{rec}(C))=\{0\}.
\]
Therefore \(L(\operatorname{rec}(C))\subsetneq\operatorname{rec}(L(C))\). A projected formulation can consequently possess recession directions that are not projections of recession directions of the lifted convex set; recession compatibility must be checked rather than inferred from projection alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a parabolic epigraph onto its horizontal coordinate yields a line whose recession cone is larger than the projected lifted recession cone.
assumptions_latex: C=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2:t\ge x^2\}
L(x,t)=x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L(\operatorname{rec}(C))=\{0\}\subsetneq\mathbb R=\operatorname{rec}(L(C))

source_refs.locator: §3.6 Lineality Space and Recession Cone p. 97

source_witnesses.locator: §3.6 Lineality Space and Recession Cone p. 97

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive equality regime contrasting with the immutable general-convex counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron and \(L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear, then \[\operatorname{rec}(L(P))=L(\operatorname{rec}(P)).\] For a general nonempty convex set \(C\), only \[L(\operatorname{rec}(C))\subseteq\operatorname{rec}(L(C))\] is automatic, and the inclusion can be strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession cones commute with linear images for polyhedra, but only one-sided inclusion is guaranteed for general convex sets.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a nonempty polyhedron}
L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\text{ is linear}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rec}(L(P))=L(\operatorname{rec}(P))
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Projection Commutes with Recession

children.title: Nonclosed Projection Images
children.top_down_role: Projected representations whose images fail to retain required closure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A recession-kernel condition ensuring that a linear image of a closed convex set is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be linear. If \[\operatorname{rec}(C)\cap\ker L\] is a linear subspace, then \(L(C)\) is closed. In particular, every linear image of a polyhedron is a polyhedron and hence closed. Without an additional condition, a closed convex set can have a nonclosed linear image.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex image is closed when the recession directions invisible to the map form a subspace; polyhedral projections are always closed.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\text{ is linear}
\operatorname{rec}(C)\cap\ker L\text{ is a linear subspace}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L(C)\text{ is closed}

notation.meaning: kernel of the linear map L

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Image Sufficient Condition
Nonclosed Projection Images
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed convex set can have a nonclosed linear projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
C=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ t\ge 1/x\}.
\]
The set \(C\) is closed and convex in \(\mathbb R^2\): it is the epigraph of the convex function \(x\mapsto1/x\) on its positive domain, and no finite limit point occurs at \(x=0\). For the projection \(L(x,t)=x\),
\[
L(C)=(0,\infty),
\]
which is not closed. Thus closedness of a lifted convex feasible region alone does not certify closedness, or exact closed-hull representability, of its projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed epigraph of 1/x over positive x projects onto the nonclosed interval (0,∞).
assumptions_latex: C=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ t\ge1/x\}
L(x,t)=x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is closed and convex, but }L(C)=(0,\infty)\text{ is not closed}

notation.meaning: epigraph of the reciprocal function on the positive half-line

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reciprocal-epigraph example is a correct closed convex set with a nonclosed linear projection, and counterexample fits the leaf. No authoritative source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Closure–Recession Interaction
children.top_down_role: Coupled effects of limiting points plus unbounded directions on hull validity.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure–Recession Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Taking closure can add recession directions to a nonclosed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:y>0\}\cup\{(x,0):x\ge0\}.
\]
This set is convex and its closure is \(\overline C=\{(x,y):y\ge0\}\). Its recession cone is
\[
\operatorname{rec}(C)=\{(d_x,d_y):d_y>0\}\cup\{(d_x,0):d_x\ge0\},
\]
whereas
\[
\operatorname{rec}(\overline C)=\{(d_x,d_y):d_y\ge0\}.
\]
Hence \(\operatorname{rec}(C)\subsetneq\operatorname{rec}(\overline C)\). Closure and recession analysis cannot be interchanged without hypotheses ensuring equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a half-plane with only half its boundary present adds horizontal recession directions pointing left.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rec}(C)\subsetneq\operatorname{rec}(\overline C)

children.title: Objective-Specific False Exactness
children.top_down_role: Apparently exact optimization behavior that does not imply formulation ideality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp objective-independent boundary separating isolated value agreement from geometric exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets. Then \[C=D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\inf_{x\in C}c^\top x=\inf_{x\in D}c^\top x\quad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb R^n,\] with equality understood in the extended real line. Hence agreement for all linear objectives characterizes equality of closed convex feasible regions, whereas agreement for one objective or a proper restricted family generally does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonempty closed convex sets are equal exactly when every linear objective has the same infimum on both; agreement for one objective is insufficient.
assumptions_latex: C,D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ are nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C=D\iff(\forall c\in\mathbb R^n)\ \inf_C c^\top x=\inf_D c^\top x

notation.meaning: extended-real infimum of the objective over C

knowledge_statements.title: All-Objectives Criterion for Hull Equality
Objective-Specific False Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality of optimal values for one objective does not establish formulation ideality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=\{(0,0),(1,0)\}\) and let \(P=[0,1]^2\). For the objective \(c=(1,0)\),
\[
\min_{x\in S}c^\top x=0=\min_{x\in P}c^\top x.
\]
Nevertheless,
\[
\operatorname{conv}(S)=[0,1]\times\{0\}\subsetneq P,
\]
and \((0,1)\) is a fractional-relaxation point outside the hull. Thus agreement of an integer model and its relaxation for a single objective, or even for a restricted objective family, is not a certificate of ideality; hull equality is an objective-independent requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A square relaxation and a horizontal integer segment share the optimum for one objective although the relaxation strictly exceeds the integer hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in S}c^\top x=\min_{x\in P}c^\top x\text{ but }P\ne\operatorname{conv}(S)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted representation through auxiliary variables and projection, with all defining maps and dimensions explicit.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(p,m,q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), and let \(F:\mathbb R^{n+p}\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(H:\mathbb R^{n+p}\to\mathbb R^q\). Define
\[
Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p:F(x,y)\le0,\ H(x,y)=0\},
\]
where the inequality is componentwise. The set \(Q\) is an exact auxiliary-variable lifting of \(S\) when
\[
S=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^p\text{ such that }(x,y)\in Q\}.
\]
If the specified target is the closed convex hull of \(S\), exactness instead requires \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}(S))\); when \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is known to be closed, this equals \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An auxiliary-variable lifting introduces a finite-dimensional vector of auxiliary variables and is exact when projection of its feasible set equals the specified target set; for a closed-convex-hull target, the projection must equal the closure of the convex hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Projection Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-free definition of a linear image and its polyhedral lifting interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(X\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(P\subseteq E\), and let \(T:E\to X\) be linear. The projection of \(P\) under \(T\) is \[T(P)=\{x\in X: \exists z\in P,\ x=Tz\}.\] If \(E=X\times Y\) and \(T(x,y)=x\), then \(T\) is the coordinate projection \(\pi_X\), and \(P\) is an extended formulation of \(Q\subseteq X\) precisely when \(\pi_X(P)=Q\). A matrix representation \(Tz=Mz\) gives the equivalent image \(T(P)=\{Mz:z\in P\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear projection maps a lifted set to its linear image; an extended formulation is exact when that image equals the intended set.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(X\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(T:E\to X\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(P)=\{x\in X:\exists z\in P,\ x=Tz\}\).

children.title: Variable Elimination

knowledge_statements.title: Variable Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fourier–Motzkin elimination of one continuous variable from a finite linear inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given inequalities \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i y\le b_i\), partition their indices into \(I_+=\{i:c_i>0\}\), \(I_-=\{i:c_i<0\}\), and \(I_0=\{i:c_i=0\}\). Retain every row indexed by \(I_0\). For every \((i,j)\in I_+\times I_-\), add \[(-c_j)a_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i a_j^{\mathsf T}x\le (-c_j)b_i+c_i b_j.\] Optionally delete redundant rows and repeat for further variables. The resulting system in \(x\) describes exactly the projection of the original feasible set onto the \(x\)-space; infeasibility is represented by an inconsistent generated inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fourier–Motzkin elimination combines every upper bound with every lower bound and exactly removes one continuous variable.
assumptions_latex: The input is a finite system of non-strict linear inequalities.
The eliminated variable \(y\) is real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generated system has feasible region \(\{x:\exists y,\ a_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i y\le b_i\ \forall i\}\).

notation.meaning: Rows with positive, negative, and zero eliminated-variable coefficients.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary Fourier–Motzkin elimination does not preserve an integrality restriction on the eliminated variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real variable \(y\), Fourier–Motzkin elimination describes \(\{x:\exists y\in\mathbb R,\ Ax+By\le b\}\). If \(y\in\mathbb Z\), applying the same rule after dropping integrality can strictly enlarge the projection. For example, \(2y=x\), \(0\le y\le1\), \(y\in\mathbb Z\) projects to \(x\in\{0,2\}\), whereas continuous elimination gives \(0\le x\le2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fourier–Motzkin elimination is exact for real eliminated variables but may relax a projection when the eliminated variable is integral.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Induced Inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas-multiplier representation of inequalities valid for a nonempty polyhedral projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le b\}\) be nonempty and let \(Q=\pi_x(P)\). An inequality \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) is valid for \(Q\) if and only if there exists \(\lambda\ge0\) such that \[\lambda^{\mathsf T}A=\alpha^{\mathsf T},\qquad \lambda^{\mathsf T}B=0,\qquad \lambda^{\mathsf T}b\le\beta.\] Thus projected inequalities are precisely nonnegative combinations of lifted inequalities whose aggregate coefficient on every eliminated variable vanishes, with right-hand side no larger than the claimed bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected inequality is valid exactly when nonnegative multipliers cancel all auxiliary-variable coefficients and imply its original-variable coefficients and bound.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le b\}\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
\(x\) and \(y\) range over finite-dimensional real spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) is valid for \(\pi_x(P)\) exactly under the displayed multiplier conditions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonemptiness Is Essential for the Multiplier Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vacuous validity on an empty projection requires the separate Farkas infeasibility alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R:0x\le-1\}=\varnothing\). Every inequality, including \(x\le-1\), is valid for \(P\), but no \(\lambda\ge0\) satisfies \(\lambda\cdot0=1\). Thus the nonempty-projection coefficient-matching characterization does not extend unchanged to empty systems. Emptiness instead has the Farkas certificate \(\mu\ge0\), \(\mu^{\mathsf T}A=0\), \(\mu^{\mathsf T}B=0\), and \(\mu^{\mathsf T}b<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an empty projection every inequality is vacuously valid, so coefficient-matching multipliers must be supplemented by a separate infeasibility alternative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The seed's multiplier equivalence requires nonemptiness unless augmented by the Farkas infeasibility alternative.

children.title: Elimination Growth
children.top_down_role: Representation-size expansion associated with explicit elimination.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coarse arithmetic-size growth for integer Fourier-Motzkin cross-multiplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every coefficient and right-hand side before an elimination step is an integer of absolute value at most \(M\ge1\). Directly cross-multiplying a row with positive eliminated-variable coefficient and a row with negative eliminated-variable coefficient produces each new entry as a sum or difference of two products, so its absolute value is at most \(2M^2\). Consequently, if \(M_{t+1}\le2M_t^2\), then \[\log_2 M_k\le2^k(\log_2M_0+1)-1.\] This bounds unreduced intermediate integers; normalization and redundancy deletion may reduce the stored description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Naive cross-multiplication can double coefficient bit length at every elimination stage, giving a coarse exponential-in-the-number-of-eliminations bit-length bound.
assumptions_latex: The current system has integer coefficients and right-hand sides.
Elimination uses direct cross-multiplication, and the bound is measured before normalization.

notation.meaning: Maximum absolute intermediate integer at stage t.

knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient Growth Under Unnormalized Elimination
Elimination Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raw inequality growth in sequential Fourier–Motzkin elimination before redundancy removal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose one Fourier–Motzkin step processes \(p\) rows with positive, \(q\) rows with negative, and \(r\) rows with zero coefficient for the eliminated variable. The step generates at most \(pq+r\) inequalities before duplicate or redundancy removal. Consequently, if \(m_t\) is the number of rows before step \(t+1\), then \[m_{t+1}\le \left\lfloor m_t^2/4\right\rfloor+m_t,\] and hence \(m_k=O((m_0+4)^{2^k})\) is a valid coarse bound after eliminating \(k\) variables. The bound counts generated rows and does not assert that a minimal projected description is comparably large.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pairing positive and negative rows can square the raw inequality count at each elimination step, even when the final projection has a smaller description.
assumptions_latex: Fourier–Motzkin elimination is applied to real variables.
Generated inequalities are counted before redundancy removal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One step creates at most \(pq+r\) rows, with coarse recurrence \(m_{t+1}\le\lfloor m_t^2/4\rfloor+m_t\).

notation.meaning: Positive-, negative-, and zero-coefficient row counts.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Validity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier certificate that a lifted polyhedron projects inside a proposed outer description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{(x,y):Ax+By\le b\}\) be nonempty and let \(Q=\{x:Dx\le d\}\). For every row \(D_i x\le d_i\), suppose a vector \(\lambda_i\ge0\) is supplied with \[\lambda_i^{\mathsf T}A=D_i,\qquad \lambda_i^{\mathsf T}B=0,
\qquad \lambda_i^{\mathsf T}b\le d_i.\] Each triple of equalities and inequalities is directly checkable and implies validity of row \(i\) on \(\pi_x(P)\). The collection \(\{\lambda_i\}\) therefore certifies \(\pi_x(P)\subseteq Q\), but by itself does not certify the reverse containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Row-wise nonnegative multipliers certify that every projected lifted point satisfies the proposed target inequalities, establishing projection validity but not exactness.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
\(Q\) is given by finitely many linear inequalities.

children.title: Projection Exactness
children.top_down_role: Checks that the projected lifted set covers the full intended target.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient two-containment condition for an exact extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq X\times Y\) be a lifted feasible set and let \(Q\subseteq X\) be the intended set. The lifting is projection-exact if and only if \[\pi_X(P)=Q.\] Equivalently, both conditions hold: \[(x,y)\in P\Longrightarrow x\in Q,\] and \[x\in Q\Longrightarrow \exists y\in Y\text{ such that }(x,y)\in P.\] The first condition excludes extraneous projected points; the second guarantees a lifted witness for every intended point. For mixed-integer formulations, the sets and quantifiers must retain their declared integrality restrictions before projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection exactness requires both validity and liftability: no lifted point projects outside the target, and every target point has an admissible lift.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq X\times Y\) and \(Q\subseteq X\).
Any declared integrality restrictions are included in \(P\), \(Q\), and the quantifiers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_X(P)=Q\) exactly when both displayed containment conditions hold.

children.title: Projection Containment Gaps
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by projection images that are too large or too small.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Containment Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates outer and inner failures of a proposed projected representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a lifted set \(P\subseteq X\times Y\) and intended set \(Q\subseteq X\), define the outer and inner projection gaps by \[G_{\mathrm{out}}=\pi_X(P)\setminus Q,\qquad G_{\mathrm{in}}=Q\setminus\pi_X(P).\] A point in \(G_{\mathrm{out}}\) is an extraneous projected point and refutes projection validity. A point in \(G_{\mathrm{in}}\) is an intended point having no admissible auxiliary lift and refutes reverse containment. Projection exactness holds if and only if \(G_{\mathrm{out}}=G_{\mathrm{in}}=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer gaps are spurious projected points; inner gaps are target points lacking a lift. Exactness holds precisely when both gaps are empty.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq X\times Y\) and \(Q\subseteq X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_X(P)=Q\iff G_{\mathrm{out}}=G_{\mathrm{in}}=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Space Artifact Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Detects unbounded lifted behavior that is invisible in the projected variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{z:Hz\le h\}\) be a nonempty polyhedron and let \(Tz\) be its projected variable. A nonzero vector \(d\) satisfying \[Hd\le0,
\qquad Td=0,
\qquad d\ne0\] is a verifiable auxiliary-space artifact certificate. Indeed, \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap\ker T\), so for every \(z\in P\) and \(t\ge0\), the points \(z+td\) remain feasible while \(T(z+td)=Tz\). Thus the lifted formulation has an unbounded fiber invisible in the projected set, although this alone does not invalidate projection exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero feasible recession direction in the projection kernel certifies an unbounded auxiliary fiber invisible in the original variables.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{z:Hz\le h\}\) is nonempty.
\(T\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\ne d\in\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap\ker T\) certifies an invisible unbounded fiber.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes bounded fibers of a polyhedral linear projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a nonempty polyhedron, let \(T\) be linear, and define \(P_u=\{z\in P:Tz=u\}\). Every nonempty fiber satisfies \[\operatorname{rec}(P_u)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap\ker T.\] Consequently, every nonempty fiber is bounded if and only if \(\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap\ker T=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection fibers share the recession cone obtained by intersecting the lifted recession cone with the projection kernel, and they are bounded exactly when that cone is trivial.

\(T\) is linear.

knowledge_statements.title: Facial Structure under Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face lifting and the nonpreservation of facial rank under linear projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polyhedron, let \(T\) be linear, and set \(Q=T(P)\). If \(F\) is an exposed face of \(Q\), represented by \[F=\{x\in Q:c^{\mathsf T}x=\delta\},\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x\le\delta\text{ on }Q,\] then \[\widehat F=P\cap T^{-1}(F)=\{z\in P:(T^{\mathsf T}c)^{\mathsf T}z=\delta\}\] is an exposed face of \(P\), and \(T(\widehat F)=F\). Conversely, the image of a face of \(P\) need not be a face of \(Q\); dimensions and facet status may decrease under projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every projected face lifts to a face exposed by the pulled-back normal, but projecting an arbitrary lifted face need not preserve face or facet status.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polyhedron in a finite-dimensional real space.
\(T\) is linear and \(Q=T(P)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every exposed face \(F\) of \(Q\) has the exposed lift \(P\cap T^{-1}(F)\), while arbitrary face images need not be faces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Lifted Vertex Can Project to a Nonface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal polyhedral witness that images of lifted faces need not be faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(2,0),(1,1)\}\subseteq\mathbb R^2\) and let \(T(x,y)=x\). Then \(T(P)=[0,2]\). The singleton \(F=\{(1,1)\}\) is a vertex and hence a face of \(P\), but \(T(F)=\{1\}\) is not a face of \([0,2]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The apex of a triangle projects to an interior point of an interval, so even a lifted vertex need not project to a face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A linear image of a face need not be a face of the image polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.title: A Lifted Vertex Can Project to a Nonface

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-Dimension Formula for a Linear Image
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dimension loss caused by affine-hull directions annihilated by projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\ne\varnothing\), choose \(z_0\in P\), and set \(L=\operatorname{lin}(\operatorname{aff}(P)-z_0)\). For a linear map \(T\), \(\operatorname{aff}(T(P))=Tz_0+T(L)\), and therefore \[\dim T(P)=\dim P-\dim(L\cap\ker T).\] Projection preserves affine dimension exactly when \(T\) is injective on \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dimension lost under projection equals the dimension of affine-hull directions lying in the projection kernel.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is nonempty.
\(T\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim T(P)=\dim P-\dim(L\cap\ker T)\).

notation.meaning: Direction space of the affine hull of P.

children.title: Convex-Combination Liftings
children.top_down_role: Lifted representations based on convex combinations of points, alternatives, or component sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Combination Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balas-type lifting for the convex hull of a finite union of nonempty polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For nonempty polytopes \(P_i=\{x:A_i x\le b_i\}\), indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,k\), introduce \(x^i\) and \(\lambda_i\). Define \[R=\left\{(x,(x^i),(\lambda_i)):x=\sum_{i=1}^k x^i,
\ A_i x^i\le b_i\lambda_i,
\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1,
\ \lambda_i\ge0\right\}.\] Because each \(P_i\) is bounded, a zero weight forces the corresponding scaled component to contribute no recession vector. The projection satisfies \[\pi_x(R)=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaled copies of component polytopes, joined by simplex weights, project exactly to the convex hull of their union.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P_i=\{x:A_i x\le b_i\}\) is a nonempty polytope.
The index set \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_x(R)=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i)\).

notation.meaning: Scaled point contributed by component i.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 The Convex Hull Via Lifting and Projection p. 17

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 The Convex Hull Via Lifting and Projection p. 17

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barycentric lifting for the convex hull of a finite listed point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty points \(v^1,\ldots,v^k\in\mathbb R^n\), define \[R_V=\{(x,\lambda):x=\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_iv^i,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1,\ \lambda\ge0\}.\] Then \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R_V)=\operatorname{conv}\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}\). A feasible \(\lambda\) is a barycentric membership certificate; if \(\lambda\in\{0,1\}^k\), exactly one listed point is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simplex weights over finitely many points project exactly to their convex hull and provide a barycentric membership certificate.
assumptions_latex: The listed point family is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_x(R_V)=\operatorname{conv}\{v^1,\ldots,v^k\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Point Convex-Combination Lifting

children.title: Network-Flow Liftings
children.top_down_role: Lifted formulations whose auxiliary structure is a network flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Flow Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-flow extended formulation for convex hulls of path-feature vectors in an acyclic network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed acyclic graph with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and arc features \(g_a\in\mathbb R^n\). Define \[R=\left\{(x,f):f\ge0,
\ \sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}f_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}f_a=
\begin{cases}1&v=s,\\-1&v=t,\\0&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
\ x=\sum_{a\in A}g_a f_a\right\}.\] Unit-flow decomposition into directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths yields \[\pi_x(R)=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\sum_{a\in p}g_a:p\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit-flow polytope projects through arc features to the convex hull of feature vectors associated with source-to-sink paths.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph with source \(s\) and sink \(t\).
Each arc \(a\) has a feature vector \(g_a\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projected unit-flow formulation equals the convex hull of all \(s\)-\(t\) path-feature sums.

notation.meaning: Feature vector assigned to arc a.
Outgoing and incoming arcs at vertex v.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auxiliary Integrality of the Acyclic Flow Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integrality of the unit-flow variables in an acyclic path-feature lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the seed assumptions, let \(F=\{f\geq0:Nf=b\}\) be the unit \(s\)-\(t\) flow polytope. Then \(F=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^p:p\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\}\), and every vertex of \(F\) is a binary path-incidence vector. Consequently, the lifting \(R=\{(x,f):f\in F,\ x=\sum_ag_af_a\}\) needs no binary declarations on its auxiliary arc variables, including when distinct paths have the same projected feature vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The acyclic unit-flow relaxation has only path-incidence vertices, so its auxiliary arc variables need not be declared binary.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and acyclic with source \(s\) and sink \(t\).
\(b\) is the integral unit source-to-sink balance vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{vert}(F)\subseteq\{\chi^p:p\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{A}.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary Integrality of the Acyclic Flow Lifting

children.title: Path-Based Liftings
children.top_down_role: Lifted formulations whose feasible alternatives correspond to paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Based Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplex lifting indexed by feasible paths and projected through path-feature vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal P\) be the finite set of directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths in a finite acyclic network, and assign each path a vector \(v^p\in\mathbb R^n\). Introduce one variable \(\lambda_p\) per path and define \[R_{\mathcal P}=\left\{(x,\lambda):x=\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}v^p\lambda_p,
\ \sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\lambda_p=1,
\ \lambda_p\ge0\ \forall p\in\mathcal P\right\}.\] Then \[\pi_x(R_{\mathcal P})=\operatorname{conv}\{v^p:p\in\mathcal P\}.\] If \(v^p\) is the incidence or feature vector of path \(p\), this gives an exact path-indexed lifting of the corresponding path polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simplex weights on complete paths project exactly to the convex hull of their incidence or feature vectors.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a finite set of feasible paths.
Each path \(p\) has an assigned vector \(v^p\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi_x(R_{\mathcal P})=\operatorname{conv}\{v^p:p\in\mathcal P\}\).

notation.meaning: Convex weight assigned to path p.
Incidence or feature vector of path p.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-size boundary for the full path-simplex lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The full path-based lifting \(R_{\mathcal P}\) has \(|\mathcal P|\) nonnegative path variables, one convexity equation, and \(n\) linking equations, in addition to the \(n\) original variables. Its explicit size is therefore at least linear in \(|\mathcal P|\), which can be exponential in the size of an acyclic network. This does not alter its projection identity but distinguishes it from an equivalent arc-flow lifting with \(|A|\) auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full path-simplex lifting uses one variable per feasible path and may be exponential even when an equivalent arc-flow network is compact.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is explicitly enumerated and finite.
Each \(v^p\in\mathbb R^n\) is explicitly available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \#\operatorname{auxiliary\ variables}(R_{\mathcal P})=|\mathcal P|,\qquad \#\operatorname{linking/convexity\ equations}=n+1.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Path-Indexing Size Boundary

children.title: Layered-Network Liftings
children.top_down_role: Acyclic layered representations used to encode ordered choices or transitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Layered-Network Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-flow extended formulation for objects encoded by paths in a finite layered acyclic network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arc \(a\in A\), let \(y_a\geq 0\), and let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times |A|}\) be a decoding matrix such that \(x(P)=B\chi^P\) for every \(s\)-\(r\) path \(P\). Define \(Q=\{(x,y):x=By,\ \sum_{a\in\delta^+(s)}y_a=1,\ \sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}y_a=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}y_a\text{ for every }v\in V\setminus\{s,r\},\ y\geq0\}\). Then \(Q\) is a layered-network lifting and \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}\{x(P):P\text{ is an }s\text{-}r\text{ path in }G\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit-flow formulation on the layered network projects to the convex hull of the objects obtained by decoding its source-to-sink paths.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with ordered layers \(V_0,\ldots,V_T\), and every arc is directed from \(V_{t-1}\) to \(V_t\) for some \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\).
There are distinguished vertices \(s\in V_0\) and \(r\in V_T\), and flow conservation is imposed at every vertex other than \(s\) and \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}\{x(P):P\text{ is an }s\text{-}r\text{ path in }G\}\).

source_refs.locator: 3.7 Two Harder Network Flow Problems* p. 57

source_witnesses.locator: 3.7 Two Harder Network Flow Problems* p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Explicit Size of a Layered-Network Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Description size measured in the explicitly materialized layered graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the seed lifting on \(G=(V,A)\), there are \(|A|\) auxiliary flow variables and \(|A|\) nonnegativity inequalities, at most \(|V|-1\) independent source and conservation equations, and \(n\) decoding equations. Thus its network description has size \(O(|V|+|A|)\); when a dense decoding matrix \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times |A|}\) is written explicitly, its coefficient representation also contains \(O(n|A|)\) entries. These bounds are polynomial in the explicit graph size, which may nevertheless be exponential in the encoded size of the original instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A layered-network lifting is linear in its explicit graph, apart from decoder storage, but the graph itself may be exponentially large relative to the original input.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) and the decoding matrix \(B\) are explicitly represented.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{size}_{\mathrm{network}}(Q)=O(|V|+|A|),\qquad \operatorname{storage}(B)=O(n|A|)\ \text{for a dense explicit decoder}.

notation.meaning: numbers of explicit network vertices and arcs

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Size of a Layered-Network Lifting

children.title: Flow-to-Path Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between aggregate flow representations and path-based alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-to-Path Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite nonnegative flow decomposition specialized to unit source-to-sink flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in\mathbb{R}_+^A\) satisfy flow conservation at every vertex in \(V\setminus\{s,r\}\) and have value \(|y|=1\). Then there exist directed \(s\)-\(r\) paths \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\), coefficients \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\geq0\), and a nonnegative circulation \(z\) such that \(y=\sum_{k=1}^m\lambda_k\chi^{P_k}+z\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^m\lambda_k=1\). If \(G\) is acyclic, then \(z=0\), so every unit flow is a convex combination of \(s\)-\(r\) path-incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative unit source-to-sink flow is a convex combination of source-to-sink paths plus a nonnegative circulation; the circulation vanishes in an acyclic graph.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with source \(s\) and sink \(r\).
\(y\in\mathbb{R}_+^A\) satisfies flow conservation on \(V\setminus\{s,r\}\), and its net outflow from \(s\) is \(|y|=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are \(s\)-\(r\) paths \(P_k\), coefficients \(\lambda_k\geq0\) with \(\sum_k\lambda_k=1\), and a nonnegative circulation \(z\) such that \(y=\sum_k\lambda_k\chi^{P_k}+z\); if \(G\) is acyclic, then \(z=0\).

notation.meaning: net flow value from the source

source_refs.locator: 3.7 Two Harder Network Flow Problems* p. 57

source_witnesses.locator: 3.7 Two Harder Network Flow Problems* p. 57

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite extraction algorithm for a nonnegative source-to-sink flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonnegative \(s\)-\(r\) flow \(y\), repeatedly choose an \(s\)-\(r\) path in its positive-support graph, subtract the minimum residual flow on that path, and record the path and coefficient. Once the residual flow has value zero, repeatedly extract a directed positive-support cycle and subtract its minimum residual flow. Every extraction makes at least one positive residual arc zero, so at most \(|\{a:y_a>0\}|\) paths and cycles are extracted. With linear-time support searches, the running time is \(O(|A|(|V|+|A|))\). In an acyclic graph the cycle phase is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bottleneck path and cycle extraction constructs the decomposition using at most one extraction per initially positive arc.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(y\geq0\) satisfies flow conservation away from source \(s\) and sink \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y=\sum_{k=1}^{p}\lambda_k\chi^{P_k}+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\mu_j\chi^{C_j},\qquad p+q\leq |\{a:y_a>0\}|.
knowledge_statements.title: Constructive Flow Decomposition

children.title: State-Space Liftings
children.top_down_role: Lifted models organized around feasible states plus transitions.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon state-transition lifting with additive decoding into original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Add a supersink \(r\) and an arc from every state in \(F\) to \(r\). Let \(D\) be the resulting layered transition graph, let \(N\) be its node-arc incidence matrix, and let \(b_{s_0}=1\), \(b_r=-1\), with all other components of \(b\) equal to zero. Define \(Y=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^{A(D)}:Ny=b\}\) and \(Q=\{(x,y):y\in Y,\ x=\sum_{t=1}^T\sum_{a\in A_t}d_a y_a\}\). Then \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}\{\sum_{a\in P}d_a:P\text{ is an admissible complete state trajectory from }s_0\text{ to }F\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit flow through the finite state-transition network projects to the convex hull of the additive vectors encoded by complete admissible trajectories.
assumptions_latex: For each \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\), \(S_t\) is a finite set of reachable states, with initial state \(s_0\in S_0\) and acceptable terminal-state set \(F\subseteq S_T\).
For each \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\), \(A_t\subseteq S_{t-1}\times S_t\) is the set of admissible transitions, and every \(a\in A_t\) has a contribution \(d_a\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}\{\sum_{a\in P}d_a:P\text{ is an admissible complete state trajectory from }s_0\text{ to }F\}\).

notation.meaning: reachable state set at stage t
admissible transitions from stage t-1 to stage t

children.title: Dynamic-Programming Liftings
children.top_down_role: Lifted models derived from staged recursive decompositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Programming Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-state, finite-horizon dynamic-programming extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be the unit-flow polytope from \(s_0\) to the terminal set \(F\) in the layered transition graph, and define \(Q=\{(x,y):y\in Y,\ x=\sum_a d_a y_a\}\). Every vertex of \(Y\) is the incidence vector of a complete admissible trajectory. Consequently, every vertex of \(Q\) has an integral transition vector \(y\), and \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact finite dynamic program gives a network-flow extended formulation whose transition-flow vertices are integral and whose projection is the convex hull of the feasible object vectors.
assumptions_latex: A finite-horizon dynamic program has finite state sets \(S_t\), admissible transitions \(A_t\), initial state \(s_0\), and terminal set \(F\subseteq S_T\).
The set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) consists exactly of the vectors \(\sum_{a\in P}d_a\) obtained from complete admissible trajectories \(P\) from \(s_0\) to \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every vertex of \(Y\) is a trajectory-incidence vector, every vertex of \(Q\) has integral \(y\), and \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(X)\).

notation.meaning: set of feasible original object vectors
unit-flow polytope of the layered transition graph

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Dynamic Programming p. 79

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-objective correspondence induced by an exact additive dynamic-programming lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the exact decoding \(x=\sum_ad_ay_a\), assign arc \(a\) the cost \(\ell_a=c^\top d_a\). Then \[\min_{x\in X}c^\top x=\min_{P:s_0\leadsto F}\sum_{a\in P}\ell_a=\min\{\sum_a\ell_ay_a:y\in Y\}.\] Since the layered graph is finite and acyclic, a forward dynamic-programming or shortest-path pass returns an optimal path and hence an optimal integral transition vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear objective becomes additive arc cost, so an acyclic shortest-path pass optimizes the exact lifting and returns an integral trajectory.
assumptions_latex: Complete admissible trajectories represent X exactly.
The decoding is additive: \(x(P)=\sum_{a\in P}d_a\).
The transition graph is finite and layered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in X}c^\top x=\min_{y\in Y}\sum_a(c^\top d_a)y_a\text{, attained by a path.}
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Optimization by Dynamic-Programming Paths

knowledge_statements.statement_title: State-Graph Size Bound for Dynamic-Programming Liftings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation and optimization size measured by reachable states and transitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the layered transition graph have \(N\) reachable state vertices and \(M\) admissible arcs, and let the decoded vector have dimension \(n\). The unit-flow lifting uses \(M\) nonnegative arc variables, \(O(N)\) flow-balance rows, and \(n\) decoding equalities. Explicitly forming all arc costs and decoding data takes \(O(Mn)\) arithmetic operations, and the subsequent acyclic shortest-path pass takes \(O(N+M)\). The formulation is polynomial in the explicit state graph but may be exponential or pseudopolynomial in the compact input encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lifting is linear in its explicit state graph, but that graph may be exponential or pseudopolynomial in the original compact input.
assumptions_latex: Only reachable states and admissible transitions are retained.
Transition vectors are explicitly represented in \(\mathbb R^n\).
The graph is finite and acyclic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \#\mathrm{variables}=M,\quad\#\mathrm{rows}=O(N+n),\quad T_{\mathrm{path}}=O(N+M).
knowledge_statements.title: State-Graph Size Bound for Dynamic-Programming Liftings

children.title: Transition-Network Representations
children.top_down_role: Network encodings that connect state transitions across stages.

knowledge_statements.title: Transition-Network Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network representation of finite-stage state transitions and complete trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\bigcup_{t=0}^T S_t\) and \(A=\bigcup_{t=1}^T A_t\). Add a supersink \(r\) and an arc from each state in \(F\) to \(r\). If \(N\) is the node-arc incidence matrix of this augmented network and \(b_{s_0}=1\), \(b_r=-1\), with every other component of \(b\) equal to zero, define \(Y=\{y\in\mathbb{R}_+^{A(D)}:Ny=b\}\). The binary feasible points of \(Y\) are exactly the incidence vectors of admissible complete trajectories from \(s_0\) to \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The layered transition network represents complete admissible state trajectories as binary unit flows from the initial state to an acceptable terminal state.
assumptions_latex: For each \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\), \(S_t\) is a finite state layer, and \(s_0\in S_0\).
For each \(t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}\), \(A_t\subseteq S_{t-1}\times S_t\) is the set of admissible transitions, and \(F\subseteq S_T\) is the acceptable terminal-state set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The binary feasible points of \(Y\) are exactly the incidence vectors of admissible complete trajectories from \(s_0\) to \(F\).

notation.meaning: layered state-transition network before adding the supersink
flow on transition or terminal arc a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous unit-flow relaxation of a finite layered state-transition network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be the augmented layered transition network of the seed and \(Y=\{y\in\mathbb R_+^{A(D)}:Ny=b\}\), where \(N\) is its node-arc incidence matrix and \(b\) has unit supply at \(s_0\) and unit demand at the supersink. Then \(Y=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^P:P\text{ is an admissible complete }s_0\text{-to-supersink trajectory}\}\), so every vertex of \(Y\) is binary. Binary declarations are therefore unnecessary when this transition-flow system is not modified by additional integrality-destroying constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The continuous unit-flow polytope of a layered transition network is the convex hull of complete trajectory incidence vectors.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a finite layered directed network augmented by a supersink.
\(N\) is its node-arc incidence matrix and \(b\) is the integral unit source-to-sink balance vector.
No additional side constraints alter the isolated transition-flow polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Y=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^P:P\text{ is an admissible complete trajectory}\},\qquad \operatorname{vert}(Y)\subseteq\{0,1\}^{A(D)}.

notation.meaning: arc-incidence vector of a complete trajectory
