children.title: Extension-Complexity Lower-Bound Methods
children.top_down_role: Classical combinatorial, algebraic, and communication-based routes to lower bounds.

children.title: Rectangle-Covering Methods
children.top_down_role: Covering and support-structure methods for slack matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangle-Covering Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-based lower bound for nonnegative rank and polyhedral extension complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(S\in\mathbb R_+^{p\times q}\), define its support matrix by \(M_{ij}=1\) if and only if \(S_{ij}>0\). A one-rectangle is a set \(I\times J\subseteq[p]\times[q]\) on which every entry of \(M\) is one. Let \(\operatorname{rc}(M)\) be the minimum number of one-rectangles whose union contains every one-entry of \(M\). Each nonnegative rank-one summand has rectangular support, so
\[
\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\ge\operatorname{rc}(M).
\]
Consequently, when \(S\) is a slack matrix of a polytope \(P\), the slack-factorization characterization gives
\[
\operatorname{xc}(P)\ge\operatorname{rc}(M).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative rank-one factor has rectangular support, so the minimum rectangle cover of a slack matrix's positive entries lower-bounds nonnegative rank and extension complexity.
assumptions_latex: The nonnegative matrix satisfies \(S\in\mathbb R_+^{p\times q}\), and \(M_{ij}=1\) exactly when \(S_{ij}>0\).
A one-rectangle is a product \(I\times J\) containing only one-entries of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(M\) requires \(r\) one-rectangles to cover its one-entries, then \(\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\ge r\), and hence \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\ge r\) when \(S\) is a slack matrix of \(P\).

notation.meaning: A nonnegative matrix and its binary support matrix.

source_refs.locator: 6.6 The Complexity of Extended Formulations p. 105

source_witnesses.locator: 6.6 The Complexity of Extended Formulations p. 105

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary of rectangle-cover lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The value \(\operatorname{rc}(\operatorname{supp}S)\) depends only on the zero pattern of \(S\). Hence, if nonnegative matrices \(S,S'\) have identical support, rectangle-cover methods assign them the same bound even when their numerical nonnegative ranks differ. These methods cannot use positive-entry magnitudes or algebraic relations among them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rectangle-cover methods see only the zero pattern and cannot distinguish equal-support matrices through their positive values.
assumptions_latex: \(S,S'\ge0\) and \(\operatorname{supp}(S)=\operatorname{supp}(S')\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rc}(\operatorname{supp}S)=\operatorname{rc}(\operatorname{supp}S').
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Only Limitation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite optimization representation of the minimum one-rectangle cover.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be the family of maximal one-rectangles of a finite binary matrix \(M\), with \(z_R\in\{0,1\}\) for \(R\in\mathcal R\). Then \[\operatorname{rc}(M)=\min\left\{\sum_{R\in\mathcal R}z_R:\sum_{R\ni(i,j)}z_R\ge1\ \text{for every }M_{ij}=1\right\}.\] Restricting to maximal one-rectangles is without loss because every one-rectangle is contained in a maximal one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rectangle-cover number is exactly a set-cover optimum over maximal one-rectangles.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a finite binary matrix.
\(\mathcal R\) contains every maximal all-one Cartesian submatrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rc}(M)\text{ equals the displayed set-cover optimum}.
knowledge_statements.title: Rectangle Cover as Set Cover

children.title: Fooling-Set Methods
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial obstruction methods based on incompatible slack entries.

assumptions_latex: The matrix \(M\in\{0,1\}^{p\times q}\) is the support matrix of a nonnegative matrix \(S\).
A fooling set \(F\) consists of one-entries with pairwise incompatible cross entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every one-rectangle contains at most one member of \(F\), so \(\operatorname{rc}(M)\ge|F|\), \(\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\ge|F|\), and for a slack matrix \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\ge|F|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise cross-zero certificate for a rectangle-cover and extension-complexity lower bound.

source_refs.locator: 6.6 The Complexity of Extended Formulations p. 105

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\in\{0,1\}^{p\times q}\). A fooling set is a collection
\[
F=\{(i_k,j_k):k=1,\ldots,t\}
\]
such that \(M_{i_kj_k}=1\) for every \(k\), and for distinct \(k,\ell\), at least one cross entry satisfies
\[
M_{i_kj_\ell}=0\quad\text{or}\quad M_{i_\ell j_k}=0.
\]
No one-rectangle can contain two positions from \(F\). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{rc}(M)\ge |F|.
\]
If \(M\) is the support of a nonnegative matrix \(S\), then \(\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\ge|F|\); if \(S\) is a slack matrix of \(P\), this certifies \(\operatorname{xc}(P)\ge|F|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fooling set is a collection of positive positions with incompatible cross positions; its cardinality certifies lower bounds on rectangle covers, nonnegative rank, and extension complexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Fooling-Set Methods

source_witnesses.locator: 6.6 The Complexity of Extended Formulations p. 105

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic limitation of fooling-set certificates for low-rank matrices and polytope slack matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a matrix over a field and let \(F=\{(i_k,j_k):k=1,\ldots,t\}\) satisfy \(S_{i_kj_k}\ne0\) and \(S_{i_kj_\ell}S_{i_\ell j_k}=0\) for all distinct \(k,\ell\). Then \[t\le \operatorname{rank}(S)^2.\] A complete slack matrix of a \(d\)-dimensional polytope has ordinary rank \(d+1\), so every fooling set in it has size at most \((d+1)^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fooling set has at most the square of the matrix's ordinary rank, so this method gives at most a quadratic-in-dimension bound for polytope slack matrices.
assumptions_latex: Every selected diagonal position is nonzero.
For each distinct selected pair, at least one of the two cross entries is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |F|\le\operatorname{rank}(S)^2;\qquad S\text{ a complete slack matrix of a }d\text{-polytope}\Longrightarrow |F|\le(d+1)^2.

notation.meaning: Fooling set of nonzero matrix positions.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Squared Ceiling for Fooling Sets

children.title: Nonnegative-Rank Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Algebraic and information-theoretic lower bounds on nonnegative factorization size.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary algebraic bounds on nonnegative factorization size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(S\in\mathbb R_+^{p\times q}\), \[\operatorname{rank}(S)\le\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\le\min\{p,q\}.\] For a complete slack matrix of a \(d\)-dimensional polytope, the ordinary-rank lower bound is only \(d+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary rank lower-bounds nonnegative rank, but for a polytope slack matrix this elementary bound is only dimension plus one.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is entrywise nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rank}(S)\le\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\le\min\{p,q\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary-Rank Bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity Under Submatrices and Nonnegative Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction rules permitting hard submatrices or nonnegative images to transfer lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S'\) is a submatrix of \(S\), then \(\operatorname{rank}_+(S')\le\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\). More generally, for entrywise nonnegative matrices \(A,B\) of compatible dimensions, \[\operatorname{rank}_+(ASB)\le\operatorname{rank}_+(S).\] Therefore a certified lower bound for a submatrix or nonnegative image transfers to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting rows or columns and applying nonnegative linear maps cannot increase nonnegative rank, enabling lower-bound reductions.
assumptions_latex: All displayed products are dimensionally compatible.
\(A,S,B\) are entrywise nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rank}_+(S')\le\operatorname{rank}_+(S),\qquad \operatorname{rank}_+(ASB)\le\operatorname{rank}_+(S).
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Under Submatrices and Nonnegative Maps

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Invariance Under Positive Rescaling and Relabeling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix normalizations preserving nonnegative factorization size and its lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\in\mathbb R_+^{p\times q}\), let \(D_1\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\) and \(D_2\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}\) be positive diagonal matrices, and let \(P_1,P_2\) be permutation matrices. Then \[\operatorname{rank}_+(D_1P_1SP_2D_2)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S).\] Thus positive row or column scaling and row or column relabeling preserve every nonnegative-rank lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative rank is invariant under positive row or column scaling and under row or column permutations.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is entrywise nonnegative.
Every diagonal entry of \(D_1\) and \(D_2\) is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rank}_+(D_1P_1SP_2D_2)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S).

notation.meaning: Positive diagonal row- and column-scaling matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Invariance Under Positive Rescaling and Relabeling

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a nonempty polytope with facet description \(Ax\le b\) and vertex set \(V\).
\(S\in\mathbb{R}_+^{m\times |V|}\) is its slack matrix, \(S_{iv}=b_i-A_i v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\), so every lower bound on \(\operatorname{rank}_+(S)\) is a lower bound on the number of inequalities in every linear extended formulation of \(P\).

notation.meaning: minimum number of inequalities in a linear extended formulation of the polytope
least \(r\) for which the matrix factors as \(TU\) with \(T,U\) entrywise nonnegative and inner dimension \(r\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Yannakakis factorization theorem for linear extensions of polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty polytope \(P\), let \(S\) be any slack matrix whose rows index a facet description and whose columns index the vertices. The linear extension complexity of \(P\) equals the nonnegative rank of \(S\): \[\operatorname{xc}(P)=\operatorname{rank}_+(S).\] Consequently, if every factorization \(S=TU\) with entrywise nonnegative matrices \(T\in\mathbb{R}_+^{m\times r}\) and \(U\in\mathbb{R}_+^{r\times |V|}\) requires \(r\ge L\), then every polyhedron projecting linearly onto \(P\) requires at least \(L\) inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polytope's linear extension complexity equals the nonnegative rank of its slack matrix; therefore any nonnegative-rank lower bound also lower-bounds extended-formulation size.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegative-Rank Lower Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The factorization theorem fits this leaf and is mathematically standard, but the record supplies no authoritative citation or inspectable theorem locator. The convention for counting inequalities and treatment of non-full-dimensional polytopes should be confirmed by that source.

children.title: Classical Hard Polytope Families
children.top_down_role: Matching, cut, stable-set, and traveling-salesperson families used as extension-complexity obstructions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating hard sequences from easy members of the same named combinatorial family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bipartite graph \(G=(U,V,E)\), the perfect-matching polytope satisfies \[P_{\mathrm{PM}}(G)=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^E:x(\delta(w))=1\ \text{for every }w\in U\cup V\}.\] Consequently it has a polynomial-size direct formulation. Thus the existence of extension-complexity-hard matching polytopes does not imply that every matching polytope is hard; any lower-bound theorem must identify the graph sequence and indexing parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extension-complexity hardness belongs to specified sequences, not every member of a named family; bipartite perfect-matching polytopes have polynomial-size direct formulations.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(U,V,E)\) is bipartite and has a perfect matching.
Extension size counts inequalities, with equations either free or represented by two inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{xc}(P_{\mathrm{PM}}(G))\le |E|+O(|U|+|V|).

notation.meaning: Perfect-matching polytope of the bipartite graph.
Set of edges incident to vertex \(w\).

knowledge_statements.title: Hardness Is Sequence-Specific

assumptions_latex: Each family is indexed by its natural combinatorial size, such as vertices of the underlying graph.
Extension complexity counts inequalities in exact linear extended formulations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: These classical families contain sequences whose extension complexities grow superpolynomially; several standard sequences admit exponential lower bounds in their natural parameters.

notation.meaning: minimum number of inequalities in an exact linear extended formulation of \(P\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative obstruction property; precise rates depend on the chosen family and indexing convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist sequences of matching, cut, stable-set, and traveling-salesperson polytopes for which no polynomial-size exact linear extended formulation exists. Equivalently, for suitable sequences \((P_n)_{n\ge1}\) drawn from each of these classes and indexed by a natural combinatorial parameter \(n\), the function \(\operatorname{xc}(P_n)\) is superpolynomial in \(n\); for standard matching, cut, and traveling-salesperson sequences, stronger exponential lower bounds are known. Such conclusions are obtained by proving large nonnegative rank, or a subordinate communication or rectangle-covering lower bound, for an associated slack matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Classical matching, cut, stable-set, and traveling-salesperson polytope families contain sequences with superpolynomial exact linear extension complexity, with exponential bounds known for standard examples.
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Hard Polytope Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the hard-polytope-family container, but the simultaneous claims for matching, cut, stable-set, and traveling-salesperson families require family-specific sources and explicit parameter conventions.

children.title: Extension Model Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Extension-complexity variants obtained by restricting symmetry or changing the representing cone or integrality class.

children.title: Symmetric Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extensions constrained to preserve specified symmetries.

assumptions_latex: A finite group \(G\) acts affinely on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) and preserves \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\).
\(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^k\) is a polyhedron and \(\pi:Q\to P\) is an affine surjection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((Q,\pi)\) is a \(G\)-symmetric extension exactly when the action on \(P\) lifts to an action on \(Q\) commuting with \(\pi\).

notation.meaning: affine projection from the extension onto the represented polytope

review_flags: choice of affine versus coordinate-permutation symmetry needs source confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine group-equivariant linear extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extension \((Q,\pi)\) is \(G\)-symmetric if there exists an affine action \((g,y)\mapsto \widetilde g(y)\) of \(G\) on \(Q\) such that every \(\widetilde g\) preserves \(Q\) and \[\pi(\widetilde g(y))=g(\pi(y))\qquad\text{for every }g\in G\text{ and }y\in Q.\] Thus each prescribed symmetry of \(P\) has a lift to the auxiliary space, and projection intertwines the lifted and original actions. The symmetric extension complexity is the minimum number of inequalities among extensions satisfying this equivariance condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric extension is an extended formulation whose auxiliary polyhedron carries the prescribed group action and whose projection commutes with that action.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Extensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a coherent definition of a group-equivariant extension, but no source establishes that the intended local convention requires a coherent affine group action rather than individual symmetry lifts or coordinate-permutation symmetries.

children.title: Approximate Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extensions representing controlled outer or inner approximations.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is the target convex set and \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a comparison body containing the origin.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\), and approximation is measured by set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An outer \(\varepsilon\)-extension projects to a convex set \(K\) satisfying \(P\subseteq K\subseteq P+\varepsilon C\); an inner one satisfies \(P\mathbin{\dotminus}\varepsilon C\subseteq K\subseteq P\).

notation.meaning: projection of the lifted feasible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-inclusion approximation relative to a specified comparison body.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be a convex lifted feasible set and let \(K=\pi(Q)\). It is an outer \(\varepsilon\)-extension of \(P\) relative to \(C\) when \[P\subseteq K\subseteq P+\varepsilon C.\] It is an inner \(\varepsilon\)-extension when \[P\mathbin{\dotminus}\varepsilon C\subseteq K\subseteq P,\qquad P\mathbin{\dotminus}\varepsilon C:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:x+\varepsilon C\subseteq P\}.\] The formulation size is measured in the chosen lifted model, while the displayed inclusions specify the approximation guarantee; multiplicative or objective-wise conventions require separate normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate extension projects to a controlled outer enlargement or inner restriction of the target, with error measured relative to a declared comparison body.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Extensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent, but approximate-extension conventions are not canonical. An authoritative source is required for this comparison-body, Minkowski-enlargement, and erosion convention and any needed assumptions on the comparison body.

children.title: Semidefinite Extensions
children.top_down_role: Lifted representations using spectrahedral cones.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is convex.
\(\mathbb{S}_+^k\) denotes the cone of real positive-semidefinite \(k\times k\) matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) has a size-\(k\) semidefinite extension when it is the affine image of an affine slice of \(\mathbb{S}_+^k\).

notation.meaning: cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices of order \(k\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectrahedral lifts of convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A size-\(k\) semidefinite extension of \(P\) consists of symmetric matrices \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb{S}^k\), scalars \(b_1,\ldots,b_m\), and an affine map \(\pi:\mathbb{S}^k\to\mathbb{R}^d\) such that \[P=\pi\!\left(\left\{X\in\mathbb{S}_+^k:\langle A_i,X\rangle=b_i\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m\right\}\right).\] Thus \(P\) is represented as an affine image of a spectrahedron. Its semidefinite extension complexity is the least matrix order \(k\) admitting such a representation, under this size convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semidefinite extension represents a convex set as the affine image of an affine slice of a positive-semidefinite matrix cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Extensions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spectrahedral-lift definition and content kind fit the leaf, but the record has no citation. A source must confirm the affine-slice representation and the convention that size is the PSD matrix order.

children.title: Mixed-Integer Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extensions whose descriptive resources include auxiliary integer variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact mixed-integer linear lifts with auxiliary integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m,p,q\in\mathbb{Z}_+\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}\), \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}\), \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times q}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). A mixed-integer linear extension of \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is the system \[Q:=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{Z}^q:Ax+By+Cz\le b\}\] satisfying \[S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^p,\ \exists z\in\mathbb{Z}^q\text{ such that }(x,y,z)\in Q\}.\] Because the lifted feasible set includes integrality restrictions, its projection can be nonconvex. Any stated complexity measure must specify whether it counts inequalities, continuous auxiliary variables, integer auxiliary variables, coefficient encoding, or a combination of these resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-integer linear extension projects a finite linear system with explicitly declared continuous and integer auxiliary variables exactly onto the represented, possibly nonconvex, set.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is the set to be represented.
\(m,p,q\in\mathbb{Z}_+\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}\), \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p}\), \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times q}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection of \(Q\) onto the \(x\)-space is exactly \(S\).

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

review_flags: size convention may count inequalities, integer variables, or both

children.title: Finite Unions of Polyhedra
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral alternatives expressed in a common ambient space.

assumptions_latex: \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:A_i x\le b_i\}\) is a polyhedron for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\).
All alternatives use the same ambient \(x\)-space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The disjunctive feasible set is \(S=\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i=\{x:\bigvee_{i=1}^k(A_i x\le b_i)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite polyhedral disjunctions in a common Euclidean space.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finitely many polyhedra \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:A_i x\le b_i\}\), their disjunctive union is \[S:=\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^d:\bigvee_{i=1}^k(A_i x\le b_i)\right\}.\] Membership in \(S\) requires satisfaction of every inequality defining at least one alternative \(P_i\), but not simultaneous satisfaction of all alternatives. The set \(S\) is generally nonconvex even though every constituent \(P_i\) is convex; disjunctive formulations commonly introduce selector variables to encode the active alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite union of polyhedra contains exactly the points satisfying all inequalities of at least one polyhedral alternative in a common space.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Unions of Polyhedra

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Geometry of a Finite Polyhedral Union
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological and geometric properties of the union before convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_1,\ldots,P_k\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be polyhedra and \(S=\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\). Then \(S\) is closed. It is generally nonconvex and therefore generally not a polyhedron. If \(S\) is convex, then it is a polyhedron; equivalently, a finite union of polyhedra is itself polyhedral exactly when that union is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite polyhedral union is closed and generally nonconvex; it is itself a polyhedron exactly when it is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(k<\infty\).
Every \(P_i\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is a polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is closed},\qquad S\text{ is a polyhedron}\Longleftrightarrow S\text{ is convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Basic Geometry of a Finite Polyhedral Union

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generator representation of the closed convex hull of a finite polyhedral union
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex-hull formula for finitely many possibly unbounded, nonempty polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P_1,\ldots,P_k\subseteq\mathbb R^n be nonempty polyhedra, and for each i let V^i,R^i\subset\mathbb R^n be finite sets such that P_i=\operatorname{conv}(V^i)+\operatorname{cone}(R^i). Then \overline{\operatorname{conv}}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\right)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kV^i\right)+\operatorname{cone}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kR^i\right).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex hull of finitely many nonempty polyhedra equals the convex hull of all their point generators plus the cone generated by all their ray generators.
assumptions_latex: P_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a nonempty polyhedron},\quad i=1,\ldots,k
P_i=\operatorname{conv}(V^i)+\operatorname{cone}(R^i),\quad V^i,R^i\text{ finite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline{\operatorname{conv}}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\right)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kV^i\right)+\operatorname{cone}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kR^i\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection formula for the Balas lifted system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection onto a generator-plus-recession-ray aggregate. This result alone does not identify that aggregate with the closed convex hull of the union; that requires an additional recession-cone condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\le b^i\} and C_i=\{x:A_i x\le0\}=\operatorname{cone}(R^i) for i=1,\ldots,k, where each R^i is finite. For every nonempty P_i, suppose P_i=\operatorname{conv}(V^i)+\operatorname{cone}(R^i) with V^i finite. Define P=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i:P_i\ne\varnothing}V^i\right)+\operatorname{cone}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kR^i\right), and let Y consist of (x,x^1,\ldots,x^k,\delta) satisfying A_i x^i\le\delta_i b^i, \sum_{i=1}^k x^i=x, \sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i=1, and \delta_i\ge0. Then P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Y).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projection of the lifted system formed from scaled copies of the disjuncts equals the convex hull of the point generators of the nonempty disjuncts plus the cone generated by all listed recession rays.
assumptions_latex: k\ge1
P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\le b^i\},\quad i=1,\ldots,k
C_i=\{x:A_i x\le0\}=\operatorname{cone}(R^i),\quad R^i\text{ finite}
P_i\ne\varnothing\implies P_i=\operatorname{conv}(V^i)+\operatorname{cone}(R^i),\quad V^i\text{ finite}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-cone criterion for exact Balas projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient condition for the standard lifted system to project to the closed convex hull when some disjuncts may be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\le b^i\}, with \bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\ne\varnothing, and let C_i=\{x:A_i x\le0\}=\operatorname{cone}(R^i), where R^i is finite. Let Y be defined by A_i x^i\le\delta_i b^i, \sum_{i=1}^k x^i=x, \sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i=1, and \delta_i\ge0. Then \operatorname{proj}_x(Y)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\right) if and only if C_j\subseteq\operatorname{cone}\!\left(\bigcup_{i:P_i\ne\varnothing}R^i\right) for every j=1,\ldots,k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Balas lifted system represents the closed convex hull exactly if and only if every disjunct's homogeneous recession cone is contained in the cone generated by the recession rays associated with the nonempty disjuncts.
assumptions_latex: P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\le b^i\},\quad i=1,\ldots,k
\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\ne\varnothing
C_i=\{x:A_i x\le0\}=\operatorname{cone}(R^i),\quad R^i\text{ finite}
Y=\{(x,x^1,\ldots,x^k,\delta):A_i x^i\le\delta_i b^i,\ \sum_i x^i=x,\ \sum_i\delta_i=1,\ \delta_i\ge0\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_x(Y)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\right)\iff \forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\},\ C_j\subseteq\operatorname{cone}\!\left(\bigcup_{i:P_i\ne\varnothing}R^i\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended Formulation for the Convex Hull of Two Bounded Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull representation for a union of two bounded, nonempty polyhedra; the auxiliary variables are existentially quantified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If P^i=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A^ix\leq b^i\} for i=1,2 are bounded and nonempty, then
\[\operatorname{conv}(P^1\cup P^2)=\left\{x:\exists y^1,y^2,z^1,z^2\text{ such that }x=y^1+y^2,\ A^iy^i\leq b^iz^i\ (i=1,2),\ z^1+z^2=1,\ z^1,z^2\geq0\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of two bounded nonempty polyhedra has an extended formulation using scaled copies of their defining systems and nonnegative weights that sum to one.
assumptions_latex: P^i=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A^ix\leq b^i\}\quad(i=1,2)
P^1\text{ and }P^2\text{ are bounded and nonempty}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(P^1\cup P^2)=\{x:\exists y^1,y^2,z^1,z^2,\ x=y^1+y^2,\ A^iy^i\leq b^iz^i\ (i=1,2),\ z^1+z^2=1,\ z^1,z^2\geq0\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplier Characterization of Valid Inequalities for a Two-Polyhedron Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An if-and-only-if certificate for inequalities valid on the convex hull of two nonempty polyhedra in the nonnegative orthant; coefficient inequalities are componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P^i=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:A^ix\leq b^i\} for i=1,2 be nonempty. The inequality \gamma x\leq\gamma_0 is valid for \operatorname{conv}(P^1\cup P^2) if and only if there exist u^1,u^2\geq0 such that \gamma\leq u^iA^i and \gamma_0\geq u^ib^i for i=1,2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inequality is valid for the convex hull of two nonempty polyhedra in the nonnegative orthant exactly when each polyhedron admits a nonnegative multiplier certificate with aggregated coefficients dominating the proposed coefficients and aggregated right-hand side no greater than the proposed right-hand side.
assumptions_latex: P^i=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_+^n:A^ix\leq b^i\}\quad(i=1,2)
P^1\text{ and }P^2\text{ are nonempty}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \gamma x\leq\gamma_0\text{ is valid for }\operatorname{conv}(P^1\cup P^2)\iff\exists u^1,u^2\geq0:\ \gamma\leq u^iA^i,\ \gamma_0\geq u^ib^i\quad(i=1,2).

children.title: Finite Unions of Convex Sets
children.top_down_role: Convex alternatives requiring nonlinear or conic hull representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite convex alternatives in a common ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty convex sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), the finite convex disjunction represents \(S=\bigcup_{i=1}^kC_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\bigvee_{i=1}^k(x\in C_i)\}\). Thus membership requires membership in at least one alternative. Although each \(C_i\) is convex, \(S\) need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite union of convex sets contains points belonging to at least one convex alternative and is generally nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(k<\infty\).
Each \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and convex.
All alternatives use the same ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=\bigcup_{i=1}^kC_i=\{x:\bigvee_{i=1}^k(x\in C_i)\},\quad S\text{ need not be convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Unions of Convex Sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic topology of finite convex unions before specialized hull reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) are closed, their finite union \(S\) is closed. If they are also bounded, then \(S\) is compact and \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is compact and closed. Without boundedness, closedness of the alternatives does not guarantee closedness of \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite closed convex unions are closed, and bounded alternatives have a compact closed hull; unbounded alternatives may have a nonclosed hull.
assumptions_latex: \(k<\infty\).
Every \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is closed};\quad (\forall i,\ C_i\text{ bounded})\Rightarrow\operatorname{conv}(S)\text{ is compact and closed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness and Compact-Hull Boundary

children.title: Conjunctive Normal Forms
children.top_down_role: Logical representations organized as conjunctions of clause-like components.

assumptions_latex: \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\) are Boolean atoms.
A literal is an atom \(p_j\) or its negation \(\neg p_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A formula is in conjunctive normal form exactly when it is a finite conjunction of clauses, each clause being a finite disjunction of literals.

notation.meaning: Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propositional CNF used to express conjunctions of disjunctive constraints.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Boolean formula \(\Phi\) is in conjunctive normal form if it has the structure \[\Phi=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{m}\left(\bigvee_{j=1}^{r_i}\ell_{ij}\right),\] where every \(\ell_{ij}\) is a literal, hence either an atom \(p_s\) or its negation \(\neg p_s\). Each inner disjunction is a clause, and an assignment satisfies \(\Phi\) exactly when it satisfies at least one literal in every clause. In disjunctive modeling, atoms may encode algebraic predicates or activated constraint systems rather than free Boolean variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjunctive normal form is an AND of clauses, where each clause is an OR of Boolean literals.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjunctive Normal Forms

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

children.title: Disjunctive Normal Forms
children.top_down_role: Logical representations organized as unions of conjunction-defined alternatives.

assumptions_latex: \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\) are Boolean atoms.
A literal is an atom \(p_j\) or its negation \(\neg p_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A formula is in disjunctive normal form exactly when it is a finite disjunction of terms, each term being a finite conjunction of literals.

notation.meaning: Boolean formula in disjunctive normal form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propositional DNF used to enumerate alternative conjunctions of constraints.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Boolean formula \(\Phi\) is in disjunctive normal form if it has the structure \[\Phi=\bigvee_{i=1}^{m}\left(\bigwedge_{j=1}^{r_i}\ell_{ij}\right),\] where every \(\ell_{ij}\) is a literal, hence either an atom \(p_s\) or its negation \(\neg p_s\). Each inner conjunction is a term, and an assignment satisfies \(\Phi\) exactly when it satisfies every literal in at least one term. In disjunctive modeling, each consistent term can identify one algebraic alternative in a finite union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjunctive normal form is an OR of terms, where each term is an AND of Boolean literals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility Equivalence of a Tighter Disjunctive Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the previously defined formulations \((P)\) and \(\mathcal P\), index set \(M\), and sets \(Q_m^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector \(t\) is feasible for \((P)\) if and only if there exist vectors \(t^k\), scalars \(\lambda_k^m\) indexed by \(m\in M\) and \(k\in Q_m^*\), and a vector \(y\) such that \(t,t^k,\lambda_k^m,y\) satisfy the constraints of \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is feasible for the original problem exactly when it can be extended by the specified auxiliary vectors, scalars, and vector y to satisfy the tighter disjunctive formulation.
assumptions_latex: (P),\ \mathcal P,\ M,\text{ and }Q_m^*\text{ are as previously defined.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t\in\operatorname{Feas}(P)\iff \exists\,(t^k),(\lambda_k^m),y\;\text{such that}\;(t,(t^k),(\lambda_k^m),y)\in\operatorname{Feas}(\mathcal P).

children.title: Normal-Form Conversion
children.top_down_role: Structural changes arising when logical representations move between normal forms.

assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is a finite propositional formula over finitely many atoms.
Equivalence means equality of truth values under every Boolean assignment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeated use of negation laws and distributivity produces equivalent CNF and DNF formulas, although their explicit sizes may grow exponentially.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truth-preserving syntactic conversion without auxiliary atoms.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite propositional formula \(\Phi\). First eliminate implications and biconditionals. Push every negation to the atoms using De Morgan laws and double-negation elimination. For CNF, repeatedly distribute disjunction over conjunction using \[A\vee(B\wedge C)\equiv(A\vee B)\wedge(A\vee C).\] For DNF, repeatedly distribute conjunction over disjunction using \[A\wedge(B\vee C)\equiv(A\wedge B)\vee(A\wedge C).\] Remove duplicate literals, contradictory terms, tautological clauses, and absorbed components. Stop when the required normal-form grammar holds, and output the resulting formula, which is logically equivalent to \(\Phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminate derived connectives, push negations to atoms, and apply distributive laws until an equivalent CNF or DNF expression is obtained.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Form Conversion

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-size conversion with auxiliary atoms that preserves satisfiability and recovers the original formula by existential projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite propositional formula \(\Phi\), introduce a fresh atom \(q_\psi\) for each nonliteral subformula \(\psi\). Add constant-size CNF clauses encoding the equivalence between \(q_\psi\) and the connective defining \(\psi\), and impose \(q_\Phi\). The resulting CNF \(T(\Phi)\) satisfies
\[\Phi(p)\iff \exists q\;T(\Phi)(p,q),\]
has size \(O(|\Phi|)\), and permits every satisfying assignment of \(\Phi\) to be extended to a satisfying assignment of \(T(\Phi)\). In general, \(T(\Phi)\) is not equivalent to \(\Phi\) over the original atoms without existentially eliminating the fresh atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tseitin conversion produces a linear-size CNF with auxiliary atoms that is existentially equivalent to the input and equisatisfiable with it.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is represented as a finite formula tree or acyclic Boolean circuit.
The introduced atoms are fresh.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(p)\iff\exists q\,T(\Phi)(p,q)\) and \(|T(\Phi)|=O(|\Phi|)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Tseitin Definitional CNF Conversion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Truth-Table Construction of Canonical Normal Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic conversion of a finite Boolean function into full DNF or full CNF without auxiliary atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\). For each assignment \(a\in\{0,1\}^n\), define
\[T_a:=\bigwedge_{j=1}^n\begin{cases}p_j,&a_j=1,\\ \neg p_j,&a_j=0,\end{cases}\qquad C_a:=\bigvee_{j=1}^n\begin{cases}\neg p_j,&a_j=1,\\ p_j,&a_j=0.\end{cases}\]
Then
\[f\equiv\bigvee_{a:f(a)=1}T_a\qquad\text{and}\qquad f\equiv\bigwedge_{a:f(a)=0}C_a.\]
The empty disjunction denotes false and the empty conjunction denotes true.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerating satisfying assignments gives a canonical full DNF, while enumerating falsifying assignments gives a canonical full CNF.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a Boolean function of the finite atom set \(p_1,\ldots,p_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite Boolean function has an equivalent full DNF and an equivalent full CNF over the same atoms.

notation.meaning: minterm true only at assignment a
maxterm false only at assignment a

knowledge_statements.title: Truth-Table Construction of Canonical Normal Forms

children.title: Normal-Form Size Growth
children.top_down_role: Representation expansion associated with normal-form transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Form Size Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case explicit conversion without auxiliary variables or circuit sharing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When formula size is the number of literal occurrences in an explicit tree-form representation and neither auxiliary atoms nor shared subexpressions are allowed, conversion between CNF and DNF can require exponential size. The CNF family \[\Phi_n:=\bigwedge_{i=1}^{n}(x_i\vee y_i)\] has \(O(n)\) literal occurrences, but every DNF equivalent to \(\Phi_n\) has at least \(2^n\) terms and therefore at least \(n2^n\) literal occurrences after redundant literals are removed. Dually, the DNF family \[\Psi_n:=\bigvee_{i=1}^{n}(x_i\wedge y_i)\] has \(O(n)\) literal occurrences, while every equivalent CNF has at least \(2^n\) clauses and at least \(n2^n\) literal occurrences. Thus the minimum explicit output size in the opposite normal form is \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) in the worst case under this representation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without auxiliary atoms or shared subexpressions, some linear-size CNF formulas require exponentially large equivalent DNF formulas, and conversely some linear-size DNF formulas require exponentially large equivalent CNF formulas.
assumptions_latex: Formula size is the number of literal occurrences in an explicit tree-form representation.
Conversion introduces no auxiliary atoms or shared subexpressions.
\(x_1,y_1,\ldots,x_n,y_n\) are distinct Boolean atoms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There are size-\(O(n)\) formulas whose smallest equivalent formula in the opposite normal form has \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) literal occurrences.

notation.meaning: number of independent pairs of Boolean atoms in the example families

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Moving Between Conjunctive and Disjunctive Normal Forms p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Universal Exponential Upper Bounds for Full Normal Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case output bounds over a fixed set of n Boolean atoms without auxiliary atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every Boolean function on \(n\) atoms has a DNF containing at most \(2^n\) terms and a CNF containing at most \(2^n\) clauses. Full minterms and maxterms contain \(n\) literal occurrences each, so either representation has at most \(n2^n\) literal occurrences before simplification. Thus auxiliary-free conversion to either explicit normal form has output size \(O(n2^n)\); together with the exponential lower-bound families, the exponential order is worst-case tight up to polynomial factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full truth-table forms give an O(n2^n) universal upper bound, matching the exponential character of the seed's lower-bound families.
assumptions_latex: The function uses \(n\) Boolean atoms.
Size counts literal occurrences in an explicit formula without auxiliary atoms or shared subexpressions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{size}_{\mathrm{CNF}}(f),\operatorname{size}_{\mathrm{DNF}}(f)\le n2^n\) for the full normal-form constructions.
knowledge_statements.title: Universal Exponential Upper Bounds for Full Normal Forms

children.top_down_role: Dependence of formulation strength or size on the selected logical normal form.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Sensitivity to Normal Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-set counterexample showing that convexification need not preserve equivalence between Boolean normal forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S_1=\{(1,0),(-1/2,\sqrt{3}/2),(-1/2,-\sqrt{3}/2)\}\), let \(S_2=-S_1\), and let \(S_3=\{(0,0)\}\). The Boolean identity \((S_1\cap S_2)\cup S_3=(S_1\cup S_3)\cap(S_2\cup S_3)\) holds, and both sides equal \(S_3\). Nevertheless,
\[\operatorname{conv}((S_1\cap S_2)\cup S_3)=S_3\subsetneq \operatorname{conv}(S_1\cup S_3)\cap\operatorname{conv}(S_2\cup S_3).\]
Thus logically identical sets obtained from distributively equivalent normal forms can yield different relaxations when their constituent sets are convexified separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This example shows that logically equivalent disjunctive and conjunctive normal forms can produce different relaxations when their constituent sets are convexified separately.
assumptions_latex: \(S_1,S_2,S_3\subset\mathbb R^2\) are the finite sets displayed in the statement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}((S_1\cap S_2)\cup S_3)\subsetneq\operatorname{conv}(S_1\cup S_3)\cap\operatorname{conv}(S_2\cup S_3)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General containment governing the strength difference between distributively equivalent set expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For arbitrary sets \(A,B,C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\),
\[\operatorname{conv}((A\cap B)\cup C)\subseteq \operatorname{conv}(A\cup C)\cap\operatorname{conv}(B\cup C).\]
The containment can be strict even though
\[(A\cap B)\cup C=(A\cup C)\cap(B\cup C).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexifying the undistributed union is contained in the intersection obtained by separately convexifying the distributed clauses, and the containment can be strict.
assumptions_latex: \(A,B,C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) are arbitrary sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}((A\cap B)\cup C)\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(A\cup C)\cap\operatorname{conv}(B\cup C)\), with equality not guaranteed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary-bound disjunction regrouping does not strengthen the hull relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies a normal-form transformation that is strength-neutral unless additional constraints participate in the basic step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:0\le x_j\le1,\ j=1,\ldots,n\},\qquad
S_j=\{x\in K:x_j\le0\ \vee\ x_j\ge1\},\quad j=1,\ldots,n.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcap_{j=1}^nS_j\right)=\bigcap_{j=1}^n\operatorname{conv}(S_j).
\]
Consequently, replacing a set of disjunctions \(x_j\le0\vee x_j\ge1\), \(j\in T\), by
\[
\bigvee_{S\subseteq T}\left(x_j\le0\ (j\in S),\ x_j\ge1\ (j\in T\setminus S)\right)
\]
before taking the hull relaxation produces the same relaxation. A stronger hull relaxation requires the basic step to involve other constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within the unit cube, convexifying the conjunction of all binary-bound disjunctions gives the same set as intersecting their individual convex hulls. Regrouping such disjunctions alone therefore cannot strengthen the hull relaxation; additional constraints must participate for strengthening to occur.
assumptions_latex: K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:0\le x_j\le1,\ j=1,\ldots,n\}
S_j=\{x\in K:x_j\le0\vee x_j\ge1\},\quad j=1,\ldots,n
T\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcap_{j=1}^nS_j\right)=\bigcap_{j=1}^n\operatorname{conv}(S_j),\quad\text{and regrouping only these binary-bound disjunctions before hull convexification yields no stronger relaxation.}

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Disjunctive Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional GDP with algebraic constraints, Boolean propositions, and nested logical structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A generalized disjunctive program has continuous variables \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), Boolean variables \(Y\), global constraints \(g(x)\leq0\), a Boolean formula \(\Omega(Y)=\mathrm{True}\), and indexed disjunctions
\[\bigvee_{i\in D_k}\bigl[Y_{ki}\ \wedge\ r_{ki}(x)\leq0\bigr],\qquad k\in K.\]
Its feasible set consists of assignments \((x,Y)\) satisfying the global constraints, \(\Omega\), and every disjunction, meaning that at least one selected alternative in each \(D_k\) has both a true indicator and satisfied associated constraints. Nested logic is represented within \(\Omega\) or by linked propositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: GDP combines continuous constraints, Boolean logic, and indexed algebraic alternatives in one model, with each disjunction requiring at least one active feasible alternative.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) and every \(D_k\) are finite.
Each \(r_{ki}\) has a specified domain containing \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{(x,Y):x\in X,\ g(x)\leq0,\ \Omega(Y),\ \bigwedge_{k\in K}\bigvee_{i\in D_k}(Y_{ki}\wedge r_{ki}(x)\leq0)\}\).

notation.meaning: constraints of alternative i in disjunction k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: General GDP representation using global algebraic constraints, Boolean-indexed disjunctive terms, term-dependent costs, and propositional restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A generalized disjunctive program has the form
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{x,c,Y}\quad & f(x)+\sum_{k\in K}c_k\\
\text{s.t.}\quad & g(x)\le 0,\\
&\bigvee_{i\in D_k}\left[\begin{array}{c}Y_{ik}\\ r_{ik}(x)\le 0\\ c_k=\gamma_{ik}\end{array}\right],\qquad k\in K,\\
&\Omega(Y)=\mathrm{True},\\
&x^{\mathrm{lo}}\le x\le x^{\mathrm{up}},
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(c_k\in\mathbb R\), and \(Y_{ik}\in\{\mathrm{True},\mathrm{False}\}\). If \(Y_{ik}\) is true, then \(r_{ik}(x)\le0\) and \(c_k=\gamma_{ik}\) are enforced; otherwise those conditions are ignored. The Boolean restrictions may be expressed in conjunctive normal form as
\[
\Omega(Y)=\bigwedge_{t=1}^{T}\left[\left(\bigvee_{Y_{ik}\in R_t}Y_{ik}\right)\vee\left(\bigvee_{Y_{ik}\in Q_t}\neg Y_{ik}\right)\right],
\]
and are assumed to contain \(\bigvee_{i\in D_k}Y_{ik}\) for every \(k\in K\). The functions \(f\), \(g\), and \(r_{ik}\) may define linear, convex nonlinear, or nonconvex GDP regimes, which call for different solution methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized disjunctive program minimizes a continuous objective plus disjunction-specific costs subject to global algebraic constraints, bounds on the continuous variables, Boolean-indexed disjunctions, and propositional restrictions. A true Boolean variable activates its term's inequalities and assigned cost; otherwise those conditions are ignored. The Boolean restrictions may be written in conjunctive normal form and are assumed to include an OR condition for each disjunction. Linear, convex nonlinear, and nonconvex functions define distinct GDP regimes requiring different solution methods.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R
g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^l
r_{ik}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m
x\in\mathbb R^n,\quad c_k\in\mathbb R,\quad Y_{ik}\in\{\mathrm{True},\mathrm{False}\}
i\in D_k,\quad k\in K
\Omega(Y)\text{ contains }\bigvee_{i\in D_k}Y_{ik}\text{ for every }k\in K
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Y_{ik}=\mathrm{True}\implies\bigl(r_{ik}(x)\le0\land c_k=\gamma_{ik}\bigr),\qquad Y_{ik}=\mathrm{False}\implies\text{the corresponding term conditions are ignored}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational semantics for disjunctive programming and the representation of a binary restriction as a two-term disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conjunctive constraint set requires every member to be satisfied. A disjunctive constraint set requires at least one member to be satisfied, but does not require all members. A disjunctive program combines conjunctive constraints with one or more disjunctions. In particular, \[x_{jk}\in\{0,1\}\iff (x_{jk}=0)\lor(x_{jk}=1).\] Consequently, a mixed-integer formulation whose binary variables encode alternatives can be represented as a disjunctive program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjunctive constraints must all hold, whereas a disjunction requires at least one alternative. A disjunctive program combines ordinary constraints with one or more such alternatives. A binary restriction is equivalently the disjunction that the variable equals zero or one.
assumptions_latex: x_{jk}\text{ is intended to be binary}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines finite disjunctive constraints and records equivalent disjunctive representations of conditional expressions and piecewise-function inequalities on the covered branch domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\ge 1\) and \(G_j\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). A disjunctive constraint has the form \(x\in\bigcup_{j=1}^pG_j\), equivalently \(\bigvee_{j=1}^p(x\in G_j)\). The conditional expression \(\operatorname{if}(x\in G_1)\operatorname{then}(x\in G_2)\operatorname{else}(x\in G_3)\) is equivalently \((x\in G_1\land x\in G_2)\lor(x\notin G_1\land x\in G_3)\). If \(f(x)=f_k(x)\) on \(G_k\), then, for \(x\in\bigcup_{k=1}^pG_k\), the constraint \(f(x)\le 0\) is equivalently \(\bigvee_{k=1}^p(x\in G_k\land f_k(x)\le 0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite disjunctive constraint requires membership in at least one of several subsets of Euclidean space. If-then-else expressions and inequalities for piecewise-defined functions can be expressed as disjunctions of their branch conditions and branch constraints; the piecewise equivalence applies on the domain covered by the branches.

G_j\subseteq\mathbb R^n\quad(j=1,\ldots,p)
f(x)=f_k(x)\quad\text{for }x\in G_k,\ k=1,\ldots,p
x\in\bigcup_{k=1}^pG_k\quad\text{for the piecewise-function reformulation}

knowledge_statements.title: Trigger-Variable Disjunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-hot Boolean triggers controlling finite algebraic alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given sets \(P_i\subseteq X\) for \(i\in D\), a trigger-variable disjunction introduces \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) and imposes
\[\sum_{i\in D}y_i=1,\qquad y_i=1\ \Longrightarrow\ x\in P_i\quad(i\in D).\]
Consequently its projection onto the original variables is \(\bigcup_{i\in D}P_i\). If simultaneous alternatives are permitted, the equality may be replaced by \(\sum_i y_i\geq1\); the projected set remains the union when every active trigger enforces its associated membership and at least one trigger must be active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary trigger variables select algebraic alternatives; under one-hot selection, projecting out the triggers recovers exactly the union of the alternative feasible sets.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is finite and nonempty.
\(P_i\subseteq X\) is specified for every \(i\in D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,y):\sum_i y_i=1,\ y_i\in\{0,1\},\ y_i=1\Rightarrow x\in P_i\}=\bigcup_{i\in D}P_i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Disaggregated Convex-Combination Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted hull representation for a finite union of nonempty polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\leq b_i\}\) be a nonempty polytope for each \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Define
\[Q=\left\{(x,x^1,\ldots,x^m,\lambda):x=\sum_{i=1}^m x^i,\ A_i x^i\leq b_i\lambda_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\},\]
where \(x,x^i\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^m\). Then \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i)\). Adding \(\lambda_i\in\{0,1\}\) for every \(i\) instead yields an extended formulation whose projection is \(\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each alternative receives its own scaled variable copy. Linking these copies with convex weights gives an extended formulation whose projection is the convex hull of the union; binary weights recover the union itself.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) is finite and positive.
\(P_i\) is a nonempty polytope for every \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
All alternatives lie in the common ambient space \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i)\).

notation.meaning: variable copy assigned to alternative i

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Polyhedral Unions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-based hull formulation for a finite union of polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(P_i=\operatorname{conv}(V_i)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), where \(V_i\) is finite and nonempty. Then
\[\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i\right)=\left\{x:\ x=\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{v\in V_i}\mu_{iv}v,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{v\in V_i}\mu_{iv}=1,\ \mu_{iv}\geq0\right\}.\]
Defining \(\lambda_i=\sum_{v\in V_i}\mu_{iv}\) provides alternative weights. If the \(\lambda_i\) are binary, exactly one polytope contributes and the projected set is the original union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of finitely many polytopes consists exactly of convex combinations of all their vertices; binary alternative weights recover the unconvexified union.
assumptions_latex: \(m<\infty\).
Every \(V_i\subset\mathbb R^n\) is finite and nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\) equals the displayed vertex-weight projection.

notation.meaning: finite vertex set generating polytope i
weight assigned to vertex v of alternative i

knowledge_statements.title: Unions with Common Recession Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogenized hull formulation for polyhedra sharing one recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\leq b_i\}\) be nonempty polyhedra with the common recession cone \(C=\{d:A_i d\leq0\}\) for every \(i\). Define
\[Q=\left\{(x,x^1,\ldots,x^m,\lambda):x=\sum_i x^i,\ A_i x^i\leq b_i\lambda_i,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\}.\]
Then \(\operatorname{proj}_x Q=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\), and this convex hull is closed. The common-cone hypothesis ensures that zero-weight copies contribute only recession directions already shared by every alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For polyhedra with a common recession cone, the usual homogenized disaggregated formulation projects exactly onto the closed convex hull of their union.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P_i\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
\(\operatorname{rec}(P_i)=C\) for all \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
\(m<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\), and this set is closed.

knowledge_statements.title: Unions in Different or Partially Shared Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedded hull representation for bounded alternatives with distinct native variable spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(E_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to\mathbb R^n\) be a specified affine embedding. Define
\[Q=\left\{(x,z_1,\ldots,z_m,\lambda):z_i\in S_i,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1,\ x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iE_i(z_i)\right\}.\]
Then \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i=1}^mE_i(S_i))\). Equivalently, one may use vectors \(w_i\in\lambda_iE_i(S_i)\) and impose \(x=\sum_iw_i\). Shared and absent coordinates are determined by the specified embeddings \(E_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternatives in distinct native spaces can be embedded into common coordinates and combined with convex weights; projecting the resulting lifted set gives the convex hull of the embedded union.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) is finite and positive.
Each \(S_i\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
Each \(E_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to\mathbb R^n\) is an explicitly specified affine embedding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{i=1}^mE_i(S_i))\).

notation.meaning: embedding of alternative i into common coordinates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex hull and facets for a union of block-cardinality polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specific hull description for two unit-cube alternatives imposing lower-cardinality constraints on distinct block families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite index sets $M_i$ $(i=1,\ldots,r)$ and $N_j$ $(j=1,\ldots,s)$, let $x^i(S)=\sum_{k\in S}x_k^i$ and $y^j(T)=\sum_{k\in T}y_k^j$, and define
\[
P^1=\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^n:x^i(M_i)\ge p_i\ \text{for all }i\},\qquad
P^2=\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^n:y^j(N_j)\ge \ell_j\ \text{for all }j\}.
\]
Then $\operatorname{conv}(P^1\cup P^2)$ is defined by the unit-cube bounds and the inequalities
\[
\frac{x^i(S_i)}{|S_i|+p_i-|M_i|}+\frac{y^j(T_j)}{|T_j|+\ell_j-|N_j|}\ge1
\]
for every $i,j$, every $S_i\subseteq M_i$ with $|M_i|-p_i+1\le |S_i|\le |M_i|$, and every $T_j\subseteq N_j$ with $|N_j|-\ell_j+1\le |T_j|\le |N_j|$. For a fixed indexed inequality, it defines a facet whenever $1\le p_i\le |M_i|-1$ and $1\le \ell_j\le |N_j|-1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of the two unit-cube alternatives is described by the cube bounds and normalized subset-sum inequalities coupling each x block with each y block. An indexed inequality is facet-defining when both corresponding cardinality thresholds are strictly between zero and their block sizes.
assumptions_latex: M_i\text{ and }N_j\text{ are finite index sets}
P^1=\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^n:x^i(M_i)\ge p_i\ \forall i\}
P^2=\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^n:y^j(N_j)\ge \ell_j\ \forall j\}
S_i\subseteq M_i,\quad |M_i|-p_i+1\le |S_i|\le |M_i|
T_j\subseteq N_j,\quad |N_j|-\ell_j+1\le |T_j|\le |N_j|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lifted union-hull representation for partially shared variable spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The intact product-space representation for two row-covering-form polytopes embedded into the union of their coordinate sets; the corrupted explicit inequality display is excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=\{y\in[0,1]^M:Ay\geq\mathbf 1\}\), \(Q=\{w\in[0,1]^N:Bw\geq\mathbf 1\}\), and
\[
Z=(P\times[0,1]^N)\cup([0,1]^M\times Q).
\]
Define
\[
\widetilde P=\{(y^{M\cap N},y^{M\setminus N},0^{N\setminus M}):y\in P\},
\quad
\widetilde Q=\{(w^{M\cap N},0^{M\setminus N},w^{N\setminus M}):w\in Q\}.
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{conv}(\widetilde P\cup\widetilde Q)=\left\{x\in[0,1]^{M\cup N}:x=(y^{M\cap N},y^{M\setminus N},0^{N\setminus M})+(w^{M\cap N},0^{M\setminus N},w^{N\setminus M}),\ (y,w)\in\operatorname{conv}(Z)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Embed each polytope into the union of the two coordinate sets by setting its absent coordinates to zero. The convex hull of the embedded union is represented through the corresponding product-space union hull, adding the two values on shared coordinates and retaining the appropriate value on each unshared coordinate.

P=\{y\in[0,1]^M:Ay\geq\mathbf 1\}

children.title: Unions with Incompatible Recession Structure
children.top_down_role: Union regimes requiring additional closure or representation care.

knowledge_statements.title: Unions with Incompatible Recession Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict closure gap caused by incompatible recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_1=\{(0,t):t\geq0\}\) and \(P_2=\{(1,t):t\leq0\}\). Their recession cones differ. For \(H=\operatorname{conv}(P_1\cup P_2)\), the set \(H\) is not closed: \((0,-1)\notin H\), whereas \((0,-1)\in\operatorname{cl}H\). Consequently,
\[H\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}H.\]
In this example the standard closed homogenized disaggregation represents \(\operatorname{cl}H\), not \(H\). Thus an exact claim for the nonclosed convex hull requires additional recession hypotheses or explicit closure handling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This pair of rays has incompatible recession directions and a nonclosed convex hull. The standard closed homogenized representation yields its closure rather than the hull itself.
assumptions_latex: \(P_1,P_2\subset\mathbb R^2\) are the rays displayed in the statement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(P_1\cup P_2)\subsetneq\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(P_1\cup P_2)\).

notation.meaning: convex hull of the displayed union

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-Hull Homogenization for Arbitrary Polyhedral Alternatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Target of the standard homogenized formulation without a common-recession hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_ix\leq b_i\}\) be nonempty polyhedra and define \[Q=\left\{(x,x^1,\ldots,x^m,\lambda):x=\sum_i x^i,\ A_ix^i\leq b_i\lambda_i,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1,\ \lambda_i\geq0\right\}.\] Without assuming common recession cones, \[\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i\right).\] Hence this formulation represents the ordinary convex hull exactly if and only if that hull is closed. Equality of recession cones is sufficient, but not necessary, for this closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For arbitrary polyhedral alternatives, standard homogenized disaggregation gives the closed union hull and gives the ordinary hull exactly when that hull is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(m<\infty\).
Each \(P_i\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_xQ=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i).

children.title: Traditional Big-M Formulations

knowledge_statements.title: Traditional Big-M Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected one-hot formulation using finite deactivation constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(P_i=\{x\in X:A_i x\leq b_i\}\), where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and choose a finite vector \(M_i\) satisfying \(A_i x-b_i\leq M_i\) componentwise for every \(x\in X\). Define
\[Q=\left\{(x,y):x\in X,\ A_i x\leq b_i+M_i(1-y_i)\ \text{for all }i,\ \sum_{i=1}^m y_i=1,\ y_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\]
Then \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i\). Replacing \(y_i\in\{0,1\}\) by \(0\leq y_i\leq1\) gives a valid relaxation whose strength depends on the selected constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite big-M constants deactivate every unselected alternative over the domain X. Binary one-hot triggers model the union exactly, while continuous triggers generally give a relaxation whose strength depends on those constants.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) is finite and positive.
\(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the common domain.
Every component of \(M_i\) is a finite valid upper bound on \(A_i x-b_i\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i\).

notation.meaning: vector of finite deactivation constants for alternative i

knowledge_statements.title: Row-Wise Big-M Calibration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent calibration of each disjunctive inequality over the inactive domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a domain \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and alternative rows \(a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_{ij}\). For every pair \((i,j)\), solve or bound
\[M_{ij}^{\star}=\sup_{x\in X}\bigl(a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}x-b_{ij}\bigr).\]
If every value is finite, output the constraints \(a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_{ij}+M_{ij}^{\star}(1-y_i)\). If any supremum is infinite, report that the corresponding finite big-M row is unavailable on \(X\). Optimization may stop early only when a certified upper bound is accepted, in which case that bound replaces \(M_{ij}^{\star}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calibrate each big-M row by maximizing its violation over the inactive domain; an unbounded maximum means no finite valid constant exists for that row.
assumptions_latex: The domain \(X\) contains every point allowed while alternative \(i\) is inactive.
Each row \((a_{ij},b_{ij})\) is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_{ij}^{\star}=\sup_{x\in X}(a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}x-b_{ij})\), or finite big-M calibration fails when this value is infinite.

notation.meaning: smallest valid nonnegative-free deactivation constant for row j of alternative i
domain possible when the row is inactive

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LP-Dual Certificate for a Calibrated Row
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation and certificate for row-wise calibration over a polyhedral inactive domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Cx\le d\}\ne\varnothing\) and \(M^{\star}=\sup\{a^{\mathsf T}x-b:Cx\le d\}\). The linear-programming dual is \[\inf\{d^{\mathsf T}\lambda-b:C^{\mathsf T}\lambda=a,\ \lambda\ge0\}.\] Every dual-feasible \(\lambda\) certifies that \(M=d^{\mathsf T}\lambda-b\) is a valid deactivation coefficient. If the primal optimum is finite, LP strong duality gives an optimal dual multiplier with value \(M^{\star}\); if the primal is unbounded above, no finite valid coefficient exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a polyhedral inactive domain, any feasible LP-dual multiplier certifies a valid row constant, and an optimal multiplier certifies the tight constant when the violation maximum is finite.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\{x:Cx\le d\}\ne\varnothing\).
\(C,d,a,b\) are finite-dimensional linear-programming data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M^{\star}=\inf\{d^{\mathsf T}\lambda-b:C^{\mathsf T}\lambda=a,\lambda\ge0\}\) when \(M^{\star}<\infty\), and every dual-feasible \(\lambda\) certifies a valid coefficient.

notation.meaning: polyhedral description of the inactive domain

children.title: Disaggregated Big-M Formulations
children.top_down_role: Big-M representations that separate logical rows or alternative-specific variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Disaggregated Big-M Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Big-M representation with constants separated by alternative and constraint row.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(P_i=\{x\in X:a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_{ij},\ j\in J_i\}\). Choose finite constants \(M_{ij}\) satisfying
\[M_{ij}\geq\sup_{x\in X}(a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}x-b_{ij})\qquad(i=1,\ldots,m,\ j\in J_i),\]
and define
\[Q=\left\{(x,y):x\in X,\ a_{ij}^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_{ij}+M_{ij}(1-y_i)\ \text{for all }i,j,\ \sum_{i=1}^m y_i=1,\ y_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\]
Then \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i\). After relaxing the selectors to \(0\leq y_i\leq1\), this formulation dominates any otherwise identical formulation whose deactivation constants are componentwise no smaller.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disaggregated big-M formulation assigns a separate valid constant to each row. Binary selectors preserve the union, and row-wise constants strengthen the continuous relaxation relative to componentwise larger shared constants.
assumptions_latex: \(m\) and every \(J_i\) are finite.
\(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the common domain.
Every \(M_{ij}\) is finite and valid over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i\), and its continuous relaxation is contained in every corresponding relaxation using componentwise larger constants.

children.title: Local Constant Tightness
children.top_down_role: Relaxation effects of locally calibrated Big-M constants.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Constant Tightness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal validity and monotonic relaxation strength of a single big-M constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the implication row \(y=1\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b\) on an inactive domain \(X
eq\varnothing\). A finite constant \(M\) makes
\[a^{\mathsf T}x\leq b+M(1-y)\]
valid for every \(x\in X\) when \(y=0\) if and only if \(M\geq M^{\star}:=\sup_{x\in X}(a^{\mathsf T}x-b)\). Hence \(M^{\star}\) is the smallest valid constant. Among otherwise identical continuous relaxations, replacing \(M>M^{\star}\) by \(M^{\star}\) cannot enlarge the feasible region and may strictly reduce it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tight local big-M value is the maximum possible row violation while inactive. Any smaller value is invalid, and any larger value cannot strengthen the relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\).
\(M^{\star}=\sup_{x\in X}(a^{\mathsf T}x-b)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is valid}\iff M\geq M^{\star}\), and the relaxation with \(M^{\star}\) dominates those with larger constants.

notation.meaning: row-wise supremal violation on the inactive domain
domain feasible while the implication is inactive

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tight Constant Under a Nonnegative Big-M Convention
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local constant tightness when modeling conventions require a nonnegative deactivation coefficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the implication \(y=1\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) over a nonempty inactive domain \(X\), let \(v:=\sup_{x\in X}(a^{\mathsf T}x-b)<\infty\). Under the convention \(M\ge0\), the smallest valid coefficient is \[M_+^{\star}=\max\{0,v\}.\] Thus the tight nonnegative coefficient is zero when the guarded inequality already holds throughout \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When big-M coefficients must be nonnegative, the tight value is the positive part of the largest inactive-state violation and is zero if the guarded row already holds throughout the inactive domain.
assumptions_latex: \(X\ne\varnothing\).
\(v=\sup_{x\in X}(a^{\mathsf T}x-b)<\infty\).
The formulation convention requires \(M\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is valid and nonnegative}\iff M\ge M_+^{\star}:=\max\{0,v\}.\)

notation.meaning: smallest valid coefficient under the nonnegative convention

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_k=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_kx\le b_k\}\) for \(k=1,\ldots,K\), and assume every \(P_k\) is nonempty and bounded. The disaggregated formulation uses \(x=\sum_{k=1}^Kx^k\), \(A_kx^k\le b_k\lambda_k\), \(\lambda_k\ge0\) for every \(k\), and \(\sum_{k=1}^K\lambda_k=1\). knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Big-M Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines formulations mixing disaggregated hull components with compact big-M implications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a union \(S=\bigcup_{k=1}^K P_k\), a hybrid big-M formulation is an extended mixed-integer system that partitions its alternative-specific conditions into sets \(H\) and \(B\). Conditions indexed by \(H\) are imposed through alternative copies \(x_H^k\) and aggregation equations \(x_H=\sum_kx_H^k\); conditions indexed by \(B\) retain shared variables and are imposed as \(a_{kr}^{\mathsf T}x\le b_{kr}+M_{kr}(1-z_k)\). It also requires \(z\in\{0,1\}^K\) and \(\sum_kz_k=1\). Validity requires every inactive alternative to be relaxed without deleting any point of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hybrid formulation disaggregates selected structure while encoding the remaining alternative-specific constraints with valid big-M implications and shared variables.
assumptions_latex: \(S=\bigcup_{k=1}^K P_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(H\) and \(B\) partition the modeled alternative-specific conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every integer-feasible projected point belongs to \(S\), and every point of \(S\) has an integer-feasible lift, provided all \(M_{kr}\) are valid.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-interface representation of a linear binary-triggered implication, separated from implementation-specific reformulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\) and \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). A solver-native indicator constraint submitted as \(z=1\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) represents the integer feasible set \[\{(x,0):x\in X\}\cup\{(x,1):x\in X,\ a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\}.\] The interface does not require the modeler to supply an explicit deactivation coefficient \(M\). The interface semantics alone make no solver-independent claim about the internal reformulation, root relaxation, branching, separation, or ideality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A native indicator directly submits a binary-triggered inequality without a user-selected big-M. Its logical integer semantics are fixed, but its internal implementation and relaxation strength are solver-dependent.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the declared base domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) be required exactly when \(z=1\). children.title: Sequentially Convexifiable Systems

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a polyhedron, let \(D_i=\bigcup_{j\in J_i}H_{ij}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and set \(S=P\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^mD_i\). For a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\), define \(Q_0=P\) and \(Q_t=\operatorname{conv}(Q_{t-1}\cap D_{\pi(t)})\). children.title: Faciality Conditions
children.top_down_role: Facial structure used to recognize valid sequential convexification regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Faciality Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stagewise faciality predicate used to assess whether local convexifications can preserve exact hull structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an order \(\pi\), let \(Q_{t-1}\) be the relaxation before processing \(D_{\pi(t)}=\bigcup_{j\in J_{\pi(t)}}H_{\pi(t)j}\). The stagewise faciality condition holds at stage \(t\) when every nonempty set \(F_{tj}=Q_{t-1}\cap H_{\pi(t)j}\) is a face of \(Q_{t-1}\). Equivalently, for each such \(j\), there exist \(c_{tj}\) and \(\beta_{tj}\) with \(Q_{t-1}\subseteq\{x:c_{tj}^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta_{tj}\}\) and \(F_{tj}=\{x\in Q_{t-1}:c_{tj}^{\mathsf T}x=\beta_{tj}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each stage, every surviving branch must be an exposed face of the current relaxation; this facial structure is checkable by supporting hyperplanes.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_{t-1}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a polyhedron.
\(D_{\pi(t)}\) has finitely many polyhedral branches.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonempty \(Q_{t-1}\cap H_{\pi(t)j}\) is exposed by a supporting equality of \(Q_{t-1}\).
