knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines faciality for a disjunctive program expressed in conjunctive normal form and states its equivalent containment criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F_0=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge b,\ x\ge0\}, and suppose the disjunctive program is expressed in conjunctive normal form with clause indices j\in S and alternatives i\in Q_j. The program is facial if, for every j\in S and i\in Q_j, F_0\cap\{x:d^ix\ge d_{i0}\} is a face of F_0. Equivalently, it is facial if and only if F_0\subseteq\{x:d^ix\le d_{i0}\} for every such j and i.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disjunctive program is facial when every inequality appearing in its disjunctions defines a face of the base polyhedron. Equivalently, the base polyhedron lies in the oppositely oriented halfspace for each inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Faciality suffices for exact sequential convexification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes order-independent exact recovery of the disjunctive hull by sequentially convexifying the clauses of a facial disjunctive set.

children.title: Convexification-Order Effects
children.top_down_role: Dependence of intermediate strength on the selected convexification order.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexification-Order Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records how staged relaxations can depend on the permutation of local convexification operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each permutation \(\pi\), define \(Q_0^\pi=P\) and \(Q_t^\pi=\operatorname{conv}(Q_{t-1}^\pi\cap D_{\pi(t)})\). At every stage, \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq Q_t^\pi\subseteq P\). Because intersection with a disjunction and convexification do not generally commute across distinct disjunctions, two orders \(\pi\) and \(\sigma\) can produce different, even incomparable, intermediate relaxations and can satisfy \(Q_m^\pi\ne Q_m^\sigma\). Thus an order may recover \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) while another leaves a strict relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing the order of local convexifications can change intermediate and final relaxation strength; one order may recover the hull while another does not.
assumptions_latex: \(S=P\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^mD_i\).
\(\pi\) and \(\sigma\) are permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq Q_t^\pi\subseteq P\), but equality between relaxations generated by different orders is not guaranteed.

notation.meaning: stage-t relaxation generated in order pi

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient operator condition ensuring that staged convexification is independent of processing order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For disjunctions \(D_1,\ldots,D_m\), define \(T_i(C):=\operatorname{conv}(C\cap D_i)\). Suppose that for every pair \(i,j\) and every set \(C\) reachable from \(P\) by a sequence of distinct operators not containing \(T_i\) or \(T_j\), \[T_i(T_j(C))=T_j(T_i(C)).\] Then every permutation \(\pi\) produces the same final relaxation \(T_{\pi(m)}\circ\cdots\circ T_{\pi(1)}(P)\). Consequently, differing final relaxations imply failure of this commutativity condition on some reachable intermediate set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every pair of unused local convexification operators commutes on every reachable intermediate set, all processing orders have the same final relaxation. Different final outcomes therefore witness failed commutativity somewhere in the process.
assumptions_latex: \(m<\infty\).
\(T_i(C)=\operatorname{conv}(C\cap D_i)\).
The stated pairwise commutativity holds on every applicable reachable intermediate set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\pi(m)}\circ\cdots\circ T_{\pi(1)}(P)=T_{\sigma(m)}\circ\cdots\circ T_{\sigma(1)}(P)\) for all permutations \(\pi,\sigma\).

knowledge_statements.title: Commutativity Criterion for Order Independence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite union-of-polyhedra example in which one processing order recovers the full hull and the reverse order leaves a strict relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=(0,0)\), \(B=(2,0)\), \(M=(1,0)\), \(U=(-1,1)\), \(V=(-1,-1)\), \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{A,B,U,V\}\), \(D_1=\{A\}\cup\{B\}\), and \(D_2=\{A\}\cup\{M\}\cup\{U\}\cup\{V\}\). With \(T_i(C)=\operatorname{conv}(C\cap D_i)\), \[T_2(T_1(P))=\operatorname{conv}\{A,M\},\qquad T_1(T_2(P))=\{A\}.\] Since \(P\cap D_1\cap D_2=\{A\}\), the order \((2,1)\) recovers the full hull whereas \((1,2)\) leaves a strict relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two finite polyhedral disjunctions can give different final staged relaxations: one order returns the exact singleton hull, while the reverse order leaves a nontrivial segment.
assumptions_latex: Singletons are regarded as polyhedra, so each \(D_i\) is a finite polyhedral union.
Convexification uses \(T_i(C)=\operatorname{conv}(C\cap D_i)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_1(T_2(P))=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap D_1\cap D_2)=\{A\}\subsetneq\operatorname{conv}\{A,M\}=T_2(T_1(P)).\)

children.title: Failure of Sequential Convexifiability
children.top_down_role: Systems for which local convexifications do not recover the complete hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Sequential Convexifiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes failure when no ordering of local convexifications recovers the complete disjunctive hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=P\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^mD_i\), and for every permutation \(\pi\) define \(Q_0^\pi=P\) and \(Q_t^\pi=\operatorname{conv}(Q_{t-1}^\pi\cap D_{\pi(t)})\). Sequential convexifiability fails precisely when, for every permutation \(\pi\), the final relaxation strictly contains the desired hull: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subsetneq Q_m^\pi\). Equivalently, each order admits a witness \(x^\pi\in Q_m^\pi\setminus\operatorname{conv}(S)\). Such witnesses show that local hull operations cannot reproduce the global interaction among the disjunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential convexifiability fails if every possible processing order leaves points outside the convex hull of the complete feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(S=P\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^mD_i\).
\(m<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall\pi,\ \exists x^\pi\in Q_m^\pi\setminus\operatorname{conv}(S)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separating-objective certificate for failure under a fixed convexification order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an order \(\pi\), let \(H=\operatorname{conv}(S)\), and suppose \(H\) is nonempty and closed. Then \(H\subsetneq Q_m^\pi\) if and only if there exists \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \[\sup_{x\in Q_m^\pi}c^\top x>\sup_{x\in H}c^\top x.\] Consequently, sequential convexifiability fails exactly when every permutation admits such an objective-gap certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed order fails exactly when a linear objective separates its final relaxation from the complete hull; universal failure requires such a gap for every order.
assumptions_latex: \(S=P\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^mD_i\).
\(H=\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is nonempty and closed.
\(Q_m^\pi\) is the final convex relaxation for order \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\subsetneq Q_m^\pi\iff\exists c\in\mathbb R^n:\ \sup_{x\in Q_m^\pi}c^\top x>\sup_{x\in H}c^\top x.

children.title: Invalid Small-M Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of intended feasible alternatives from insufficient bounding constants.

knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Small-M Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded one-variable example showing that an insufficient big-M deletes intended feasible points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<U<\infty\), \(x\in[0,U]\), and \(z\in\{0,1\}\). The implication \(z=0\Rightarrow x\le0\) has intended set \(S=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,1):0\le x\le U\}\). Its big-M inequality is \(x\le Mz\). If \(M<U\), the intended point \((U,1)\in S\) violates \(x\le Mz\), so the formulation is invalid. More generally, validity requires \(M\ge\sup\{x:x\in[0,U]\}=U\) for this implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the implication that x must vanish when z is zero, choosing M below x's upper bound wrongly removes feasible points with z equal to one.
assumptions_latex: \(0<U<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M<U\Rightarrow (U,1)\in S\setminus\{(x,z):x\le Mz\}\).

children.title: Weak Large-M Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxation degradation caused by excessively loose bounding constants.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Large-M Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-variable family quantifying relaxation weakness when a valid big-M exceeds the tight bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,1):0\le x\le U\}\) with \(U>0\). Its convex hull is described by \(0\le z\le1\) and \(0\le x\le Uz\). A valid big-M formulation with \(M>U\) instead relaxes to \(0\le x\le U\), \(0\le z\le1\), and \(x\le Mz\). The point \((U,U/M)\) belongs to this relaxation but not to \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\). As \(M/U\) grows, its selector coordinate approaches zero, quantifying the loss of relaxation strength.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid but oversized M admits fractional points excluded by the union hull, and the discrepancy grows as M increases relative to the tight bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((U,U/M)\in R_M\setminus\operatorname{conv}(S)\), where \(R_M=\{(x,z):0\le x\le U,\ 0\le z\le1,\ x\le Mz\}\).

children.title: Big-M Numerical Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Scaling, conditioning, and tolerance problems caused by large coefficients.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tolerance Amplification in a Big-M Row
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional numerical bound under an explicitly stated acceptance convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b+Mz\), whose intended active state is \(z=0\). Suppose a numerical acceptance rule permits \(0\le z\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\) while treating \(z\) as zero and permits absolute row residual at most \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{row}}\). Then an accepted point can satisfy \(a^{\mathsf T}x-b\le M\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{row}}\). Thus this convention guarantees logical violation at most \(\delta\) only if \(M\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{row}}\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under an explicit tolerance convention, selector error is amplified by M and combines with the permitted row residual.
assumptions_latex: The stated absolute integrality and row-residual acceptance convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a^{\mathsf T}x-b\le M\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{row}}.
knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance Amplification in a Big-M Row

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Solver-independent row-scaling diagnostic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the row \(a^{\mathsf T}x-Mz\le b\), assume \(a\) has a nonzero coefficient and define \(\rho\) as the largest divided by the smallest nonzero absolute coefficient among \(a\) and \(-M\). If \(M\ge\max_j|a_j|\), then \(\rho=M/\min_{j:a_j\ne0}|a_j|\). Hence, with \(a\) fixed, this coefficient-range diagnostic grows linearly with \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once M dominates the ordinary row coefficients, the row’s coefficient range grows linearly with M.
assumptions_latex: At least one coefficient of \(a\) is nonzero.
\(M\ge\max_j|a_j|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho=\frac{M}{\min_{j:a_j\ne0}|a_j|}.
knowledge_statements.title: Big-M Coefficient-Range Growth
Big-M Numerical Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies feasibility and integrality-tolerance amplification caused by a large big-M coefficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b+Mz\), encoding an implication active at \(z=0\). If a solver accepts \(0\le z\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\) as numerically integral at zero, the row permits \(a^{\mathsf T}x-b\le M\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\), even though the intended active inequality permits no positive violation. Hence ensuring implication error at most \(\delta\) requires \(M\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\le\delta\), in addition to ordinary row-feasibility tolerances. Large \(M\) also increases coefficient range relative to the nonzero coefficients of \(a\), worsening scaling and conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrality tolerance can turn a tiny selector error into an M-times-larger logical violation; large M also creates adverse coefficient scaling.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}<1\).
\(z\) is treated as zero whenever \(0\le z\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^{\mathsf T}x-b\le M\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\); therefore logical error bounded by \(\delta\) requires \(M\varepsilon_{\mathrm{int}}\le\delta\).

children.title: Nonclosed Union Hulls

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonclosed Hull of Two Closed Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional example exhibiting an excluded hull limit point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_0=\{(0,0)\}\) and \(C_1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:xy\ge1\}\cap\mathbb R_+^2\). Both sets are closed and convex, and \(\operatorname{conv}(C_0\cup C_1)=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0\}\). For every \(a>0\), the point \((a,0)\) is excluded although \((a,1/n)\) belongs to the hull for all sufficiently large \(n\) and converges to \((a,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The origin and the positive hyperbola epigraph are closed convex sets whose convex hull is not closed.
assumptions_latex: The ambient space is \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(C_0\cup C_1)\text{ is not closed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Hull of Two Closed Convex Sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundedness regime in which the pathology is impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) are nonempty compact sets and \(k<\infty\), then \(\bigcup_{i=1}^kC_i\) is compact and its convex hull is compact, hence closed. Therefore a nonclosed convex hull of finitely many closed alternatives cannot occur when every alternative is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite union of compact alternatives has a compact, closed convex hull, so this pathology requires an unbounded alternative.
assumptions_latex: \(k<\infty\).
Every \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^kC_i\right)\text{ is compact and closed}.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Alternatives Exclude Nonclosed-Hull Failure

assumptions_latex: The ambient space is \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convex hull of a finite union of closed convex sets need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-set counterexample in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_0=\{(0,0)\}\) and \(C_1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:x>0,\ y>0,\ xy\ge 1\}\). Both sets are closed and convex. Their union hull satisfies \[\operatorname{conv}(C_0\cup C_1)=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,y):x>0,\ y>0\}.\] This hull is not closed: every point \((a,0)\) with \(a>0\) is excluded, although \((a,1/n)\) belongs to the hull for every sufficiently large integer \(n\) and converges to \((a,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two closed convex sets can have a nonclosed convex hull: the positive-quadrant hyperbola epigraph together with the origin generates the open positive quadrant plus the origin.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Union Hulls

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically correct and fits the failure-boundary container, but it has no citation with an inspectable locator.

children.top_down_role: Encodings using a distinct selector coordinate for each alternative.

children.title: Unary Selector Encodings
children.top_down_role: Selector representations using one coordinate per alternative.

assumptions_latex: There are \(k\ge 2\) mutually exclusive alternatives indexed by \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Alternative \(i\) is represented by the unary code \(e^i\), using one binary selector per alternative.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard unary representation of a finite exclusive choice.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Integer Programming Models p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A unary selector encoding introduces \(z\in\{0,1\}^k\) and imposes \(\sum_{i=1}^k z_i=1\). The selected alternative is \(i\) exactly when \(z_i=1\). Equivalently, the feasible code set is \[\{z\in\{0,1\}^k:\sum_{i=1}^k z_i=1\}=\{e^1,\ldots,e^k\}.\] Thus every alternative has a distinct length-\(k\) code containing one unit entry and \(k-1\) zero entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unary encoding assigns one binary variable to each alternative and requires exactly one variable to equal one.
knowledge_statements.title: Unary Selector Encodings

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Integer Programming Models p. 45

children.title: One-Hot Feasibility Structure
children.top_down_role: Feasible selector geometry restricted to a single active alternative.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Hot Feasibility Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility predicate for a one-hot binary selector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\ge 2\) be an integer and let \(z\in\{0,1\}^k\). The one-hot feasibility condition is \[\sum_{i=1}^k z_i=1.\] It holds if and only if there is a unique index \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\) such that \(z_i=1\) and \(z_j=0\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\setminus\{i\}\). Consequently, it excludes the all-zero assignment and every assignment selecting two or more alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integer k of at least two, a binary vector is one-hot precisely when its entries sum to one, giving a unique selected alternative.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(k\ge 2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condition \(\sum_{i=1}^k z_i=1\) is equivalent to selecting exactly one alternative.

notation.meaning: an index distinct from the selected index

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Integer Programming Models p. 45

children.title: Selector-Simplex Geometry
children.top_down_role: Continuous relaxation geometry associated with one-coordinate-per-alternative selectors.

knowledge_statements.title: Selector-Simplex Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of the continuous one-hot relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\ge 2\) be an integer. The continuous selector set is \[\Delta_k=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}_+^k:\sum_{i=1}^k z_i=1\right\}=\operatorname{conv}\{e^1,\ldots,e^k\}.\] It is a \((k-1)\)-dimensional simplex in \(\mathbb{R}^k\), and its extreme points are precisely \(e^1,\ldots,e^k\). Thus every extreme point of the selector relaxation is integral, although nonextreme points can represent convex mixtures of alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an integer k of at least two, relaxing one-hot selectors gives the standard simplex, whose only vertices are the integral unit vectors.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(k\ge 2\).
The continuous relaxation uses \(z\in\mathbb{R}_+^k\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^k z_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxed selector set \(\Delta_k\) is a \((k-1)\)-dimensional simplex whose vertices are exactly \(e^1,\ldots,e^k\).

children.title: Unary Encoding Size
children.top_down_role: Variable and constraint burdens associated with unary selector representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Unary Encoding Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts only the selector code and its one-hot equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer \(k\ge 2\), a unary selector uses a vector \(z\in\{0,1\}^k\), so the number of selector variables is \(N_{\mathrm{var}}=k\). Its code-defining system contains the equality \(\sum_{i=1}^k z_i=1\) and \(k\) binary declarations. In the continuous relaxation, the binary declarations can be replaced by the \(k\) inequalities \(z_i\ge 0\), because the equality then implies \(z_i\le 1\). Hence both the selector-coordinate count and the number of coordinate declarations or relaxation inequalities are \(\Theta(k)\). This count excludes constraints linking selectors to alternative-specific variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unary code uses one selector coordinate per alternative, so its selector representation has linear size in the number of alternatives.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(k\ge 2\).
The model distinguishes the alternatives using a unary selector \(z\in\{0,1\}^k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unary selector has \(N_{\mathrm{var}}=k\) coordinates and selector-encoding size \(\Theta(k)\).

source_refs.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

children.title: Binary Encodings
children.top_down_role: Compact encodings using binary codes for alternatives.

assumptions_latex: There are \(k\ge 2\) alternatives.
The code length is \(r=\lceil\log_2 k\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An injective map into \(\{0,1\}^r\) represents all alternatives using the minimum possible binary code length.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic representation of finite alternatives by binary codewords.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary encoding of \(k\) alternatives is an injection \(h:\{1,\ldots,k\}\to\{0,1\}^r\). The selected alternative \(i\) is represented by \(y=h(i)\). Since \(r\) bits provide at most \(2^r\) distinct words, every such encoding satisfies \(r\ge\lceil\log_2 k\rceil\); enumerating any \(k\) distinct words of length \(\lceil\log_2 k\rceil\) attains this bound. Formulation constraints must additionally exclude unused words when \(k<2^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinct alternatives receive distinct bit strings; exactly ceiling log base two of the alternative count bits suffice, with unused codes excluded.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Encodings

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

children.title: Adjacency-Preserving Code Family
children.top_down_role: Encodings designed to preserve adjacency relationships among alternatives.

children.title: Gray-Code Encodings
children.top_down_role: Alternative encodings using codewords with controlled bit transitions.

assumptions_latex: The alternatives are ordered as \(1,\ldots,k\).
The code length satisfies \(r\ge\lceil\log_2 k\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consecutive alternatives receive binary words at Hamming distance one.

notation.meaning: Gray code assigned to alternative i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reflected Gray coding for a linearly ordered alternative set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Gray-code encoding is an injection \(g:\{1,\ldots,k\}\to\{0,1\}^r\) satisfying \[d_H(g(i),g(i+1))=1\qquad(i=1,\ldots,k-1).\] One construction takes the first \(k\) words of the binary-reflected Gray sequence, whose zero-based word is \(g(i)=(i-1)\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}\lfloor(i-1)/2\rfloor\), expressed in \(r\) bits. Thus moving between consecutive alternatives changes exactly one code coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gray code assigns ordered alternatives distinct bit strings so each consecutive pair differs in exactly one bit.
knowledge_statements.title: Gray-Code Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reflected Gray-code construction is mathematically coherent and fits the representation leaf, but no source or inspectable locator supports the construction and formula.

children.title: Adjacency-Aware Encodings
children.top_down_role: Encodings designed around neighborhood relations among alternatives.

assumptions_latex: Alternatives are vertices of an adjacency graph \(G=(V,E)\).
Each alternative receives a distinct binary codeword.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The encoding is adjacency-aware exactly when every designated adjacent pair has Hamming distance one.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-based definition of adjacency preservation by binary codes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an injective code map \(h:V\to\{0,1\}^r\), adjacency awareness with respect to \(G\) means \[d_H(h(u),h(v))=1\quad\text{for every }\{u,v\}\in E.\] Equivalently, \(h\) embeds every edge of \(G\) as an edge of the \(r\)-dimensional hypercube. The condition constrains designated adjacent alternatives but does not, unless separately required, forbid nonadjacent alternatives from also receiving codewords at Hamming distance one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An encoding is adjacency-aware when every edge of the alternative graph maps to a one-bit transition in the code hypercube.
knowledge_statements.title: Adjacency-Aware Encodings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated edge-preservation condition is precise, but “adjacency-aware” is terminology whose intended one-way meaning requires a source; no citation is supplied.

children.title: Codeword Transition Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometric effects of codeword changes between neighboring alternatives.

assumptions_latex: Codewords \(u,v\) lie in \(\{0,1\}^r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The segment joining adjacent codewords is a hypercube edge exactly when their Hamming distance is one.

notation.meaning: line segment joining u and v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypercube geometry of transitions between binary codewords.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For distinct \(u,v\in\{0,1\}^r\), the segment \([u,v]\) is a one-dimensional face of the binary hypercube \([0,1]^r\) if and only if \(d_H(u,v)=1\). In that case there is a unique coordinate \(j\) with \(u_j\ne v_j\); every other coordinate remains fixed along the segment, while coordinate \(j\) ranges over \([0,1]\). If \(d_H(u,v)>1\), their segment is a diagonal rather than a hypercube edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-bit code transition traces a hypercube edge; a transition changing multiple bits traces a diagonal.
knowledge_statements.title: Codeword Transition Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hypercube-edge characterization is correct and the property kind fits, but the record has no cited source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Adjacency Preservation Failures
children.top_down_role: Encoding regimes where code geometry does not retain the intended alternative adjacency.

assumptions_latex: Four alternatives are ordered as \(1,2,3,4\).
They receive ordinary two-bit binary codes in numerical order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compact distinct coding alone does not preserve adjacency of ordered alternatives.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smallest ordinary-binary example exhibiting a multi-bit adjacent transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assign \(h(1)=00\), \(h(2)=01\), \(h(3)=10\), and \(h(4)=11\). These codewords are distinct and use the minimum length \(r=2\). Nevertheless, alternatives \(2\) and \(3\) are consecutive while \[d_H(h(2),h(3))=d_H(01,10)=2.\] Their transition changes both coordinates and is a diagonal of \([0,1]^2\). Hence minimum-length binary coding does not by itself preserve the path adjacency of an ordered alternative set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ordinary codes 00, 01, 10, 11 are compact, but the consecutive transition from 01 to 10 changes two bits.
knowledge_statements.title: Adjacency Preservation Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-bit counterexample is correct and fits the adjacency-failure leaf, but it lacks the required cited evidence.

children.title: General-Integer Encodings
children.top_down_role: Alternative encodings using bounded nonbinary integer coordinates.

assumptions_latex: There are \(k\ge 2\) alternatives.
An integer radix \(b\ge 2\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Base-\(b\) digits encode all alternatives using \(\lceil\log_b k\rceil\) bounded integer coordinates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positional bounded-integer encoding of a finite alternative set.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=\lceil\log_b k\rceil\). Represent alternative \(i\) by the unique digit vector \(y\in\{0,\ldots,b-1\}^r\) satisfying \[i-1=\sum_{j=1}^r y_j b^{j-1}.\] The map is injective because positional representations are unique, and \(b^r\ge k\) supplies enough codewords. When \(k<b^r\), code vectors representing integers \(k,\ldots,b^r-1\) must be excluded by the formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternatives can be encoded as base-b digit vectors, using ceiling log base b bounded integer coordinates and excluding unused digit patterns.
knowledge_statements.title: General-Integer Encodings

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

children.title: Ordered-Union Incremental Models
children.top_down_role: Incremental formulations for consecutively ordered alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordered-Union Incremental Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental representation of a continuous ordered piecewise-linear union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\ge 1\) be an integer, let \(a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_m\) be real breakpoints, and let \(f_0,ldots,f_m\in\mathbb{R}\). For \(j=1,\ldots,m\), set \(L_j=a_j-a_{j-1}\) and \(s_j=(f_j-f_{j-1})/L_j\). Introduce \(0\le\delta_j\le L_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\) and \(z_j\in\{0,1\}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m-1\), subject to \[\delta_j\ge L_jz_j,\qquad \delta_{j+1}\le L_{j+1}z_j\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m-1).\] Define \[x=a_0+\sum_{j=1}^m\delta_j,\qquad t=f_0+\sum_{j=1}^m s_j\delta_j.\] The projection of this system onto \((x,t)\) is exactly the union of the consecutive line segments joining \((a_{j-1},f_{j-1})\) to \((a_j,f_j)\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For at least one consecutively ordered segment, bounded increments and ordered binary indicators represent exactly the union of the line segments of the continuous piecewise-linear graph.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb{Z}\) and \(m\ge 1\).
\(a_0,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(a_0<a_1<\cdots<a_m\).
\(f_0,\ldots,f_m\in\mathbb{R}\) specify the values of a continuous piecewise-linear graph at the breakpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection onto \((x,t)\) equals \(\bigcup_{j=1}^m[(a_{j-1},f_{j-1}),(a_j,f_j)]\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Integer Programming Models p. 45

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 2. Integer Programming Models p. 45

children.title: Piecewise-Linear Incremental Models
children.top_down_role: Incremental formulations for ordered univariate segments.

assumptions_latex: Breakpoints satisfy \(t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\), with \(d_i=t_i-t_{i-1}\).
The continuous piecewise-linear function has value \(f_0\) at \(t_0\) and slope \(s_i\) on \([t_{i-1},t_i]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,v)\) lies on the specified piecewise-linear graph over \([t_0,t_m]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous univariate piecewise-linear graph with ordered breakpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(z_0=1\), \(z_m=0\), and impose \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m-1\). The incremental representation is
\[
x=t_0+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_i,\qquad v=f_0+\sum_{i=1}^{m}s_i\delta_i,
\]
with
\[
d_i z_i\leq \delta_i\leq d_i z_{i-1}\qquad(i=1,\ldots,m).
\]
The constraints fill earlier segments before later segments are used, so at most one increment is strictly between its bounds. The resulting \((x,v)\) represents the graph over \([t_0,t_m]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Segment increments are used in order: all preceding segments are full, at most one segment is partial, and all following segments are unused.
knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Linear Incremental Models

children.title: Incremental Branching Structure
children.top_down_role: Branching behavior induced by cumulative alternative activation.

assumptions_latex: The incremental variables satisfy \(d_i z_i\leq\delta_i\leq d_i z_{i-1}\), with \(z_0=1\), \(z_m=0\), and positive \(d_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Branching on \(z_k\) partitions the domain at breakpoint \(t_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable branching in the standard incremental formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(k\in\{1,\ldots,m-1\}\), the branch \(z_k=0\) implies \(\delta_i=0\) for every \(i>k\), hence \(x\leq t_k\). The branch \(z_k=1\) implies \(z_i=1\) and \(\delta_i=d_i\) for every \(i\leq k\), hence \(x\geq t_k\). Thus branching on a cumulative activation variable produces the ordered interval disjunction
\[
x\in[t_0,t_k]\quad\text{or}\quad x\in[t_k,t_m].
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branching on a cumulative activation variable splits the modeled interval at the corresponding breakpoint into a left and a right subinterval.
knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Branching Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The branching property and content kind fit the terminal container, and the stated implications are mathematically consistent with the incremental constraints. No citation or inspectable locator is supplied, however, and the statement includes derivational proof text; authoritative formulation-specific support is required.

children.title: Embedding Formulations
children.top_down_role: Geometric embeddings that combine alternatives with selected integer codes.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Mixed Integer Linear Programming Formulation Techniques
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Vielma, Section 9 and related embedding framework
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Mixed Integer Linear Programming Formulation Techniques

children.title: Cayley-Embedding Formulations
children.top_down_role: Lifted formulations obtained by embedding alternatives at distinct code points.

assumptions_latex: Each \(P_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty polytope.
The vectors \(e^1,\ldots,e^m\) are the unit vectors of \(\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x\bigl(Q\cap(\mathbb{R}^n\times\{e^1,\ldots,e^m\})\bigr)=\bigcup_{i=1}^mP_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical unit-vector Cayley embedding of a finite polyhedral union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Cayley embedding of the alternatives is
\[
Q=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}P_i\times\{e^i\}\right)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}.
\]
A point \((x,y)\in Q\) with \(y=e^i\) necessarily has \(x\in P_i\), because a unit vector cannot be expressed as a nontrivial convex combination of the other unit vectors. Therefore imposing \(y\in\{e^1,\ldots,e^m\}\), equivalently \(y\in\{0,1\}^m\) and \(\sum_i y_i=1\), yields an exact lifted formulation of \(\bigcup_iP_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each alternative is placed at a distinct unit-vector code; restricting the lifted selector to those codes recovers exactly the original union.
knowledge_statements.title: Cayley-Embedding Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Cayley embedding and selector restriction match the node and are mathematically plausible, but the record supplies no source or locator and includes an argument for exactness. A source specifically supporting the embedded-union formulation is required.

children.title: Logarithmic Formulations
children.top_down_role: Embedding formulations using logarithmically many selector coordinates.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\geq2\) alternatives \(P_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
Distinct codes \(h^i\in\{0,1\}^r\) are assigned with \(r=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact embedded-union model uses \(r=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) binary selector coordinates.

notation.meaning: binary code assigned to alternative i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary embedding with the minimum selector dimension for arbitrary finite alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
Q_H=\operatorname{conv}\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}P_i\times\{h^i\}\right).
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{proj}_x\left(Q_H\cap(\mathbb{R}^n\times\{0,1\}^r)\right)=\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}P_i.
\]
Indeed, if a convex combination of binary codewords is itself binary, every positively weighted codeword agrees in every coordinate, and injectivity therefore identifies one alternative. Thus any linear description of \(Q_H\), together with \(y\in\{0,1\}^r\), is an exact logarithmic-selector formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning distinct binary codes to alternatives gives an exact embedding using the minimum possible logarithmic number of binary selector coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Logarithmic Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary embedding is an appropriate representation for this leaf. Exactness and the minimum-selector claim are plausible under injective binary coding, but neither has cited support, and the statement contains proof text. A specialized source must establish the formulation and clarify that minimality concerns binary selector dimension only.

children.title: Branching-Compatible Embeddings
children.top_down_role: Embeddings selected to support useful partitions under branching.

assumptions_latex: Distinct codewords \(h^1,\ldots,h^m\in\{0,1\}^r\) index alternatives.
Branching is performed on individual selector coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each selector branch induces the alternative partition \((I_{k,0},I_{k,1})\).

notation.meaning: alternatives having bit b in coordinate k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-branching compatibility for a prescribed family of alternative partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(k\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\) and \(b\in\{0,1\}\), define
\[
I_{k,b}=\{i:h_k^i=b\}.
\]
An embedding is branching-compatible with a prescribed collection \(\mathcal{P}\) of binary partitions of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) if every \((S,\bar S)\in\mathcal{P}\) equals \((I_{k,0},I_{k,1})\), up to exchanging sides, for some coordinate \(k\). In the embedded formulation, the branches \(y_k=0\) and \(y_k=1\) then retain precisely the alternatives indexed by \(I_{k,0}\) and \(I_{k,1}\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An embedding is compatible with desired branching when each desired alternative partition is realized by fixing one code coordinate to zero or one.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Compatible Embeddings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is an appropriate content kind, and the coordinate-induced partitions are internally coherent. The proposed meaning of 'branching-compatible' is specialized and context dependent, so it cannot be accepted without an authoritative source or an explicitly governed project definition.

children.title: Embedding-Code Complexity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs among integer dimension, formulation size, ideality, and code geometry.

children.title: Encoding Dimension
children.top_down_role: Integer-coordinate burden associated with representing alternatives.

assumptions_latex: An injective binary encoding assigns one vector in \(\{0,1\}^r\) to each of \(m\geq1\) alternatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\geq\lceil\log_2m\rceil\), and equality is attainable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic dimension bound for injective binary alternative codes.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an injective assignment of binary codewords in \(\{0,1\}^r\) to \(m\) alternatives, the selector dimension satisfies
\[
r\geq\lceil\log_2m\rceil.
\]
This bound is attainable for every \(m\geq1\) by selecting \(m\) distinct codewords of length \(\lceil\log_2m\rceil\). Thus \(\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) is the minimum binary selector dimension when no additional geometric or branching restrictions are imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distinguishing m alternatives requires at least the ceiling of log base two of m binary coordinates, and that number suffices when no further restrictions are imposed.
knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Dimension

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.1 Problems, Instances, Encoding Size p. 17

children.title: Embedding Formulation Size
children.top_down_role: Row, column, or auxiliary-variable burden of embedding-based representations.

assumptions_latex: A specified rational mixed-integer extended-formulation presentation consists of scalar linear constraints, auxiliary continuous variables, integer variables, and rational coefficients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The presentation-specific formulation-size profile is \((p,q,r,L)\).

notation.meaning: number of scalar linear constraints, with each equality counted as two inequalities
numbers of auxiliary continuous and integer variables
total binary encoding length of the rational data in the specified presentation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A presentation-specific multidimensional size convention for rational embedding formulations.

source_refs.locator: 6.6 The Complexity of Extended Formulations p. 105
Chapter 10. Sizes and the theoretical complexity of linear inequalities and linear programming p. 120
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a specified rational embedding-formulation presentation, define its size profile as \((p,q,r,L)\). Here \(p\) is the number of scalar linear constraints, counting each equality as two inequalities; \(q\) is the number of auxiliary continuous variables; \(r\) is the number of integer variables; and \(L\) is the total binary encoding length of all rational coefficients and right-hand sides in that presentation. The profile is presentation dependent, so transformations such as equation elimination require recomputation of all four components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a specified presentation, embedding size records scalar constraints, auxiliary continuous variables, integer variables, and the binary encoding length of its rational data.
knowledge_statements.title: Embedding Formulation Size

children.title: Code Geometry Complexity
children.top_down_role: Structural complexity arising from the placement and adjacency of encoding vectors.

assumptions_latex: The code set \(H=\{h^1,\ldots,h^m\}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}^r\) is finite.
An irredundant rational inequality description of \(\operatorname{conv}(H)\) is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa(H)=(f(H),L(H))\) quantifies the descriptive complexity of the code geometry.

notation.meaning: number of facets of the code polytope
minimum coefficient encoding length of an irredundant description

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One precise complexity measure for rational code polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(H)\) be the number of facets of \(\operatorname{conv}(H)\). Among irredundant rational systems \(Ay\leq b\) describing \(\operatorname{conv}(H)\), let \(L(H)\) be the minimum total binary encoding length after every inequality is scaled to primitive integer coefficients. Define the code-geometry complexity by
\[
\kappa(H)=(f(H),L(H)).
\]
This measure distinguishes code sets having the same cardinality and ambient dimension but requiring different numbers or arithmetic sizes of inequalities to describe their convex hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Code geometry complexity records both the facet count and the smallest rational coefficient length needed to describe the code polytope.
knowledge_statements.title: Code Geometry Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition could fit this leaf, but the proposed measure is not established by a source and is ambiguous for code polytopes that are not full dimensional, where affine-hull equations and relative facets must be treated explicitly. The minimization and coefficient-normalization convention also needs authoritative or project-governed support.

children.title: Ideality–Complexity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Relationships between exact relaxation behavior and representation burden.

assumptions_latex: For nonempty polytopes \(P_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and distinct codes \(h^i\), the lifted integer-feasible set is exactly \(F_H=\bigcup_i P_i\times\{h^i\}\).
The continuous relaxation \(R\) is expressed in the same \((x,y)\)-space and contains \(F_H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the hull-exact convention, ideality is \(R=\operatorname{conv}(F_H)=Q_H\), while formulation compactness is measured separately.

notation.meaning: continuous relaxation in the lifted space
convex hull of the encoded alternatives

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of hull-exact relaxation ideality from syntactic formulation compactness.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Convex Hulls and Perfect Formulations p. 20
5.1 Comparing the Strength of Different Formulations p. 70

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
F_H=\bigcup_i P_i\times\{h^i\},\qquad Q_H=\operatorname{conv}(F_H).
\]
Under the hull-exact convention, a relaxation \(R\) in the same \((x,y)\)-space is ideal when
\[
R=Q_H.
\]
Ideality concerns relaxation strength, whereas compactness concerns the numbers of constraints, auxiliary variables, selector coordinates, and coefficient bits. A selector dimension of \(r=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) alone gives no bound on the number or encoding length of inequalities in a hull-exact description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the hull-exact convention, ideality means that the lifted relaxation equals the convex hull of the encoded alternatives; logarithmically many selector bits alone do not bound the size of that hull description.
knowledge_statements.title: Ideality–Complexity Tradeoffs

children.title: Branching-Compatible Complexity
children.top_down_role: Representation burdens associated with encodings designed for effective branching.

assumptions_latex: A binary decision tree isolates each of \(m\) alternatives.
Every internal node branches on one binary selector coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case branching depth satisfies \(D\geq\lceil\log_2m\rceil\), with equality attainable by a balanced code tree.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-tree depth for isolating alternatives by coordinate branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A binary tree of worst-case depth \(D\) has at most \(2^D\) leaves. If every one of \(m\) alternatives must occupy a distinct leaf, then
\[
D\geq\lceil\log_2m\rceil.
\]
This bound is attained when alternatives receive distinct length-\(r\) binary codes with \(r=\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) and the used coordinate branches form a balanced separating tree. Additional requirements that branches induce prescribed ordered or geometric partitions can force either greater selector dimension or an unbalanced tree and hence larger worst-case depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate branching needs logarithmic depth to isolate m alternatives in the best case; prescribed geometric partitions may require more depth or more coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching-Compatible Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logarithmic decision-tree depth bound is plausible and the complexity-bound kind fits the leaf, but no source supports the coordinate-branching model, attainability claim, or the effect of prescribed partitions. The statement also contains proof text. A specialized locator is required.

children.title: Convex-Combination Models
children.top_down_role: Vertex-weight formulations for piecewise graphs and epigraphs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjacency Is Essential for Nonconvex Piecewise Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection obtained after removing segment-selection or adjacent-support restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the breakpoint equations \(x=\sum_jt_j\lambda_j\), \(v=\sum_jf_j\lambda_j\), \(\lambda\ge0\), and \(\sum_j\lambda_j=1\), removing segment-selection constraints projects to \[\operatorname{conv}\{(t_j,f_j):j=0,\ldots,m\},\] not generally to the piecewise-linear graph. For the vertices \((0,0),(1,1),(2,0)\), the weights \(\lambda_0=\lambda_2=1/2\) produce \((x,v)=(1,0)\), although the graph value at \(x=1\) is \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without adjacency enforcement, breakpoint weights describe the convex hull of all graph vertices and can create points outside the piecewise-linear graph.
assumptions_latex: The graph is specified by finitely many ordered breakpoint vertices.
Adjacency or segment-selection constraints are omitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_{x,v}\{\lambda\ge0:\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1\}=\operatorname{conv}\{(t_j,f_j)\}_j.

notation.meaning: unrestricted convex weight of breakpoint j

knowledge_statements.title: Adjacency Is Essential for Nonconvex Piecewise Graphs

assumptions_latex: Breakpoints satisfy \(t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\), with graph values \(f_j\) at \(t_j\).
Variables \(z_i\) select one segment and variables \(\lambda_j\) are nonnegative vertex weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation represents exactly the union of the line segments joining consecutive graph vertices.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disaggregated segment-selection model for a univariate piecewise-linear graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Impose
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{m}\lambda_j=1,\qquad
x=\sum_{j=0}^{m}t_j\lambda_j,\qquad
v=\sum_{j=0}^{m}f_j\lambda_j,\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_i=1,
\]
where \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and \(\lambda_j\geq0\) for \(j=0,\ldots,m\). Couple the vertex weights to the selected segments by
\[
\lambda_0\leq z_1,\qquad
\lambda_m\leq z_m,\qquad
\lambda_j\leq z_j+z_{j+1}\quad(j=1,\ldots,m-1).
\]
The feasible \((x,v)\) are exactly the points on the union of the consecutive graph segments joining \((t_{i-1},f_{i-1})\) and \((t_i,f_i)\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary variable selects one segment, and convex weights interpolate between that segment's two endpoint vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Combination Models

children.title: SOS2 Formulations
children.top_down_role: Adjacency-constrained convex-combination formulations for ordered breakpoints.

assumptions_latex: The index set \(\{0,1,\ldots,m\}\) is ordered.
Weights satisfy \(\lambda_j\geq0\) for \(j=0,\ldots,m\) and \(\sum_{j=0}^{m}\lambda_j=1\).
Breakpoints satisfy \(t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\), with graph values \(f_j\) at \(t_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The SOS2 constraint restricts \(\lambda\) to the union of adjacent edges of the simplex and yields the consecutive piecewise-linear graph.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard ordered SOS2 semantics for piecewise-linear interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The vector \(\lambda=(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_m)\) satisfies an SOS2 constraint when there exists \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) such that
\[
\operatorname{supp}(\lambda)\subseteq\{i-1,i\}.
\]
Equivalently, at most two weights are positive and, if two are positive, their indices are consecutive. With the simplex constraints, the equations
\[
x=\sum_{j=0}^{m}t_j\lambda_j,\qquad
v=\sum_{j=0}^{m}f_j\lambda_j
\]
represent exactly the piecewise-linear graph formed by the consecutive vertices \((t_j,f_j)\), \(j=0,\ldots,m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOS2 weight vector has positive entries only at one breakpoint or two consecutive breakpoints, thereby enforcing interpolation along a single adjacent segment.
knowledge_statements.title: SOS2 Formulations

children.title: Logarithmic Piecewise Models
children.top_down_role: Compact encoded formulations for piecewise-linear alternatives.

assumptions_latex: There are \(m\ge 2\) ordered affine pieces with breakpoints \(t_1<\cdots<t_{m+1}\).
A distinct code \(h^i\in\{0,1\}^k\), where \(k=\lceil\log_2 m\rceil\), is assigned to each piece \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation uses \(k\) binary variables while selecting exactly one piece or two adjacent breakpoints.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: logarithmic encodings of an ordered piecewise-linear disjunction use binary codes for its intervals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedding representation for a univariate ordered piecewise-linear graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let piece \(i\) join breakpoints \(t_i\) and \(t_{i+1}\), and assign it a distinct code \(h^i\in\{0,1\}^k\), where \(k=\lceil\log_2 m\rceil\). A logarithmic piecewise model is an extended mixed-integer representation whose integer points satisfy \(y=h^i\) for some \(i\), \(\lambda\ge0\), \(\sum_{j=1}^{m+1}\lambda_j=1\), and \(\lambda_j=0\) whenever \(j\notin\{i,i+1\}\). The represented point is \(x=\sum_j t_j\lambda_j\), with the function value obtained by the same convex combination of breakpoint values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary code identifies an active interval, while convex-combination weights are restricted to that interval's two endpoints, requiring only logarithmically many binary variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Logarithmic Piecewise Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logarithmic binary count and interval-support idea are plausible, but distinct codes alone do not specify the embedding inequalities linking y and lambda. An authoritative formulation-level source is needed to determine the precise hypotheses and representation.

children.title: Multivariate Triangulation Models
children.top_down_role: Disjunctive formulations based on cells, simplices, and compatible triangulations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition for simplex-wise affine rules to define one continuous piecewise-affine function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let affine functions \(f_i\) and \(f_j\) be assigned to simplices \(T_i\) and \(T_j\) of a compatible triangulation. They define a single-valued continuous function on \(T_i\cup T_j\) if and only if \[f_i(v)=f_j(v)\qquad\text{for every vertex }v\text{ of }T_i\cap T_j.\] Since the intersection is a common face and both restrictions are affine, vertex agreement is equivalent to agreement everywhere on that face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine simplex pieces join continuously exactly when their values agree at every vertex of each shared face.
assumptions_latex: \(T_i\cap T_j\) is empty or a common face of both simplices.
Each local rule is affine on its simplex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_i|_{T_i\cap T_j}=f_j|_{T_i\cap T_j}\iff f_i(v)=f_j(v)\ \forall v\in\operatorname{vert}(T_i\cap T_j).

notation.meaning: affine function assigned to simplex i

knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Face Compatibility of Simplex Pieces

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous Relaxation Projects to the Lifted-Vertex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection obtained by relaxing the selectors in the stated barycentric simplex-selection formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the formulation with \(z_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i z_i=1\), \(\lambda_v\ge0\), \(\sum_v\lambda_v=1\), and \(\lambda_v\le\sum_{i:v\in T_i}z_i\), relaxing selector integrality yields \[\operatorname{proj}_{x,w}=\operatorname{conv}\{(v,f(v)):v\in V\}.\] Consequently, the relaxation equals the graph only when the triangulated graph itself equals this convex hull; otherwise it contains convex combinations spanning different simplices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxed simplex selectors project to the convex hull of all lifted triangulation vertices, not generally to the piecewise-affine graph.
assumptions_latex: Every triangulation vertex belongs to at least one simplex.
Shared vertex values consistently define the lifted vertices \((v,f(v))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_{x,w}(Q_{\mathrm{relax}})=\operatorname{conv}\{(v,f(v)):v\in V\}.

notation.meaning: barycentric simplex-selection formulation with relaxed selectors

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Relaxation Projects to the Lifted-Vertex Hull

assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) is triangulated by finitely many simplices \(T_1,\ldots,T_m\) with compatible intersections.
The target function is affine on every simplex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selecting one simplex and taking barycentric coordinates represents exactly the triangulated piecewise-affine graph.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: simplex selection with barycentric coordinates is the standard disjunctive model of a triangulated piecewise-affine graph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite compatible triangulation of a bounded multivariate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be the vertices of a compatible triangulation \(\{T_i\}_{i=1}^m\) of \(D\), and let \(f\) be affine on each \(T_i\). The graph of \(f\) is represented by \(z\in\{0,1\}^m\), \(\sum_i z_i=1\), \(\lambda_v\ge0\), \(\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_v=1\), and \(\lambda_v\le\sum_{i:v\in T_i}z_i\). Then \(x=\sum_{v\in V}v\lambda_v\) and \(w=\sum_{v\in V}f(v)\lambda_v\). Thus positive barycentric weights belong only to the selected simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary variable selects one simplex, and barycentric weights over its vertices represent the point and its piecewise-affine function value.
knowledge_statements.title: Multivariate Triangulation Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simplex-selection and barycentric representation is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordering facet-adjacent simplices and their vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive ordering procedure for a facet-adjacent triangulation in dimension at least three.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a facet-adjacent triangulation \(\mathcal S\) of \(d\)-simplices with \(d\ge3\), choose adjacent \(S_1,S_2\) sharing \(d\) vertices, label their extreme vertices so that \(\bar x_d^{S_1}=\bar x_0^{S_2}\) and \(\bar x_0^{S_1}=\bar x_d^{S_2}\), and initialize \(\mathcal S'=(S_1,S_2)\). While \(|\mathcal S'|\ne n\), choose \(S\notin\mathcal S'\) adjacent to some \(S_i\in\mathcal S'\), select \(w\in(\mathcal V(S)\cap\mathcal V(S_i))\setminus\{\bar x_0^{S_i},\bar x_d^{S_i}\}\), and insert \(S\) immediately before or after \(S_i\), updating the endpoint labels according to whether \(\bar x_0^{S_i}\in\mathcal V(S)\). Return \(\mathcal S'\), whose simplex and vertex ordering satisfies \(\mathrm{(O1)}\) and \(\mathrm{(O2)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with two facet-adjacent simplices and compatible endpoint labels. Repeatedly select an unordered simplex sharing a facet with an ordered simplex, choose a shared non-endpoint vertex, update the endpoint labels, and insert the simplex on the prescribed side. Return the resulting ordering satisfying (O1) and (O2).
assumptions_latex: d\ge3
\mathcal S\text{ is a facet-adjacent triangulation of }d\text{-simplices}
n=|\mathcal S|
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal S'\text{ orders all simplices and labels their vertices so that }\mathrm{(O1)}\text{ and }\mathrm{(O2)}\text{ hold}

children.title: Inactive-Point Geometry

\(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) is the prescribed inactive point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inactive regime is the singleton \(\{(\bar x,0)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singleton inactive regime in an on-off convex disjunction.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.2 From the Convex Hull to the Union Itself p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary activation variable \(z\in\{0,1\}\), the inactive-point geometry associated with the prescribed point \(\bar x\) is the singleton set \(S_0:=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R^n\times\{0,1\}:x=\bar x,\ z=0\}=\{(\bar x,0)\}\). It fixes every continuous component at \(\bar x\) whenever the modeled object is inactive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the indicator is zero, every continuous variable is fixed at the prescribed inactive point.

\(z\in\{0,1\}\) is the activation indicator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active regime is \(C\times\{1\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The active convex region determined by \(C\) is \(S_1:=\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R^n\times\{0,1\}:x\in C,\ z=1\}=C\times\{1\}\). Thus activation fixes the indicator at one and leaves the continuous vector constrained precisely by \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the indicator is one, the continuous vector must lie in the designated convex feasible region.

children.title: Two-Regime Union Geometry
children.top_down_role: Union structure combining an inactive state with an active convex regime.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex.
\(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(z\) is binary in the original union.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The convex hull consists exactly of \((x,z)\) with \(0\le z\le1\) and \(x=(1-z)\bar x+zu\) for some \(u\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull representation of a singleton and a convex active regime.

source_refs.locator: 2.1.2 From the Convex Hull to the Union Itself p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(S:=\{(\bar x,0)\}\cup(C\times\{1\})\). Its convex hull is \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,z):0\le z\le1,\ \exists u\in C\text{ such that }x=(1-z)\bar x+zu\}.\] At \(z=0\) this gives \(x=\bar x\); at \(z=1\) it gives \(x\in C\); and intermediate values interpolate between the two regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relaxation interpolates between the inactive point and an arbitrary active point using the activation coordinate as the mixing weight.
knowledge_statements.title: Two-Regime Union Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1.2 From the Convex Hull to the Union Itself p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded Active Set Can Produce a Nonclosed Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp closure failure for an unbounded active interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take \(C=[1,\infty)\subseteq\mathbb R\) and \(\bar x=0\). Then \[\operatorname{conv}\bigl(\{(0,0)\}\cup(C\times\{1\})\bigr)=\{(x,z):0<z\le1,\ x\ge z\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] The sequence \((1,1/k)\) belongs to this hull and converges to \((1,0)\), which does not; the closure has zero-activation ray \(\{(x,0):x\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed unbounded active interval yields a nonclosed hull through recession limits at zero activation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(\{(0,0)\}\cup(C\times\{1\}))\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Active Set Can Produce a Nonclosed Hull

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of the singleton–convex-set hull for a closed, possibly unbounded active set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\), and set \(S=\{(\bar x,0)\}\cup(C\times\{1\})\). Then \[\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,z):0<z\le1,\ x\in(1-z)\bar x+zC\}\cup\{(\bar x+d,0):d\in\operatorname{rec}(C)\}.\] The ordinary hull has zero-activation slice \(\{(\bar x,0)\}\), so it is closed exactly when \(\operatorname{rec}(C)=\{0\}\), equivalently when the closed convex set \(C\) is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing the two-regime hull adds the inactive point translated by every recession direction; for a closed convex active set, the ordinary hull is closed exactly in the bounded case.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S)\cap\{z=0\}=(\bar x+\operatorname{rec}(C))\times\{0\}\), and \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\) is closed iff \(C\) is bounded.

notation.meaning: recession cone of the active convex set

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Hull and Recession Boundary

children.title: Inactive-Point Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of the designated inactive value with the active-domain closure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition indicated by the leaf scope for a possibly nonclosed active convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex and let \(\bar x\) be the prescribed inactive point. Inactive-point compatibility with the active-domain closure holds exactly when \(\bar x\in\operatorname{cl}C\). If \(C\) is closed, this is equivalent to \(\bar x\in C\). Under closure compatibility, \(\operatorname{cl}(C\cup\{\bar x\})=\operatorname{cl}C\); the unclosed projection equals \(C\) only when \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inactive point is closure-compatible precisely when it belongs to the closure of the active domain; actual membership is additionally needed for the unclosed projection to remain C.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and convex.
\(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) is the prescribed inactive point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\text{ is closure-compatible}\iff\bar x\in\operatorname{cl}C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Compatibility with the Active-Domain Closure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Compatibility Need Not Imply Active Membership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal nonclosed-domain boundary separating membership in C from membership in its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=(0,\infty)\subseteq\mathbb R\) and \(\bar x=0\), one has \(\bar x\in\operatorname{cl}C\setminus C\). Thus the inactive point is compatible with the active-domain closure, but the projection \(C\cup\{\bar x\}=[0,\infty)\) is not equal to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inactive point can lie in the closure of a nonclosed active domain without being an active-domain member.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\in\operatorname{cl}C\) but \(\bar x\notin C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Compatibility Need Not Imply Active Membership

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) is the prescribed inactive point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Inactive-point compatibility holds exactly when \(\bar x\in C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: compatibility means the inactive point is also admissible in the continuous active geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility convention for a common-domain on-off convex model.

children.title: Semicontinuous Activation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ideal Convex-Hull Formulation of a Semicontinuous Variable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact binary formulation and continuous hull for a bounded nonnegative semicontinuous variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<\ell\le u<\infty\) and \(S=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(x,1):\ell\le x\le u\}\). Then \[S=\{(x,z):z\in\{0,1\},\ \ell z\le x\le uz\}\] and \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,z):0\le z\le1,\ \ell z\le x\le uz\}.\] Thus the standard activation links are exact for binary z and ideal in the displayed variables after relaxing z.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower and upper activation links exactly model a zero-or-positive-interval variable, and their continuous relaxation is its convex hull.
assumptions_latex: The inactive value is zero.
\(0<\ell\le u<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,z):0\le z\le1,\ell z\le x\le uz\}\).

notation.meaning: positive active lower and upper bounds

assumptions_latex: The inactive value is zero.
The active bounds satisfy \(0<\ell\le u<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The linear constraints \(\ell z\le x\le uz\), \(z\in\{0,1\}\), represent \(x\in\{0\}\cup[\ell,u]\).

notation.meaning: positive active lower and upper bounds

Introducing \(z\in\{0,1\}\), this set is represented exactly by \[\ell z\le x\le uz.\] If \(z=0\), these inequalities force \(x=0\); if \(z=1\), they impose the active interval \(\ell\le x\le u\).

children.title: Fixed-Charge Activation
children.top_down_role: Setup decisions coupled with continuous operating activity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes permission to operate from equivalence between setup and positive use.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The link \(0\le x\le Uz\) permits \((x,z)=(0,1)\), so it does not imply \(z=1\Rightarrow x>0\). If \(F>0\), changing an idle state from \((0,1)\) to \((0,0)\) excludes idle activation at a minimization optimum only when that change preserves every other constraint and leaves all other objective terms unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacity link permits an idle activated setup; a positive fixed charge removes it at optimality only when deactivation has no other consequence.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le x\le Uz\) with \(U\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (0,1)\text{ is feasible under the link; if }F>0\text{ and idle deactivation preserves all other model data, an optimum with }x=0\text{ has }z=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Idle-Setup Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical bounded nonnegative activity formulation with a setup charge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a nonnegative activity with valid finite capacity \(U\), let \(z\in\{0,1\}\), and impose \[0\le x\le Uz.\] Then \(z=0\) forces \(x=0\), while \(x>0\) forces \(z=1\). Adding \(Fz+cx\), with \(F\ge0\), to a minimization objective charges the fixed amount \(F\) whenever positive activity occurs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid capacity link shuts activity off when the setup binary is zero and makes positive activity trigger the fixed charge.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le x\le U\) is valid for active operation.
\(U<\infty\).
The minimized objective contains \(Fz\) with \(F\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x>0\Rightarrow z=1,\qquad z=0\Rightarrow x=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Linked Fixed-Charge Formulation

assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) contains the inactive point \(0\).
Operating activity satisfies \(x=0\) when \(z=0\), and a setup cost \(F\ge0\) is charged when \(z=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The activated objective contribution is \(Fz+c(x)\) over the on-off feasible set.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed-charge models couple a binary setup decision to continuous activity and add a fixed cost
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed setup charge coupled to an on-off operating decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A fixed-charge activation model consists of \(z\in\{0,1\}\), an operating vector \(x\), and the disjunction \((x,z)=(0,0)\) or \(x\in X\) and \(z=1\). If \(F\ge0\) is the setup charge and \(c:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is the operating cost, its objective contribution is \(Fz+c(x)\), with the convention that \(c(0)=0\) in the inactive regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary setup decision permits continuous operation and adds a fixed charge whenever operation is active.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Charge Activation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly couples a setup indicator, an on-off operating set, and a fixed objective charge, but it lacks an inspectable citation with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) index a group of bounded continuous variables satisfying \(|x_i|\le M_i\). Group activation introduces one indicator \(z_G\in\{0,1\}\) and imposes \[-M_i z_G\le x_i\le M_i z_G\qquad(i\in G).\] Thus \(z_G=0\) forces \(x_i=0\) for every \(i\in G\), whereas \(z_G=1\) permits all group members within their valid bounds.

children.title: Multi-Level Activation
children.top_down_role: Activation structures with several permitted operating levels.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Disaggregated Convex-Hull Formulation for Finite Activation Levels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ideal continuous formulation of a finite union of compact convex activation-level regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_0,\ldots,C_L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty compact convex sets, with \(C_0=\{0\}\), and let \(S=\bigcup_{r=0}^L(C_r\times\{e_r\})\). Then \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\left\{(x,y):\begin{array}{l}\text{there exist }x^0,\ldots,x^L\text{ with }x=\sum_{r=0}^Lx^r,\\\sum_{r=0}^Ly_r=1,\quad y\ge0,\quad x^r\in y_rC_r\quad(r=0,\ldots,L)\end{array}\right\}.\] Requiring \(y\in\{0,1\}^{L+1}\) recovers the one-hot multi-level union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disaggregating the operating vector by level and scaling each level region by its simplex weight gives the convex hull of a finite multi-level activation union.
assumptions_latex: Each \(C_r\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(C_0=\{0\}\) is the inactive level.
\(e_r\) is the \(r\)-th unit vector in the level-indicator space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,y):\exists(x^r)_r,\ x=\sum_r x^r,\ \sum_r y_r=1,\ y\ge0,\ x^r\in y_rC_r\ \forall r\}.

notation.meaning: Unit vector encoding selection of level \(r\).

knowledge_statements.title: Disaggregated Convex-Hull Formulation for Finite Activation Levels

assumptions_latex: There are ordered operating levels \(r=0,1,\ldots,L\), with level \(0\) inactive.
Each active level \(r\) has feasible region \(C_r\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exactly one level is selected, and \(x\) belongs to its associated feasible region.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a finite multi-level activation is a disjunction represented by one-hot level indicators
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite one-hot representation of several activation intensities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_0:=\{0\}\) and let \(C_r\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) describe operating level \(r\) for \(r=1,\ldots,L\). A multi-level activation model uses \(y_r\in\{0,1\}\), \(\sum_{r=0}^L y_r=1\), and enforces the disjunction \[y_r=1\ \Longrightarrow\ x\in C_r\qquad(r=0,\ldots,L).\] Hence exactly one activation level is chosen, with level zero forcing inactivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One-hot indicators choose exactly one operating level, each of which has its own feasible region; level zero is inactive.
knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Level Activation
