children.title: Disjunction Grouping
children.top_down_role: Aggregation of selected disjunctions into jointly represented groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunction Grouping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint convexification of selected logical components according to a partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For logical components \(j\in J\), let \(D_j=\bigcup_{k\in K_j}S_{jk}\), and let \(\Pi\) be a partition of \(J\). For each group \(G\in\Pi\), define the grouped disjunction \[D_G=\bigcup_{\kappa\in\prod_{j\in G}K_j}\ \bigcap_{j\in G}S_{j,\kappa_j}.\] By distributivity, \(D_G=\bigcap_{j\in G}D_j\). The grouped convexification relaxation is \(R_\Pi=\bigcap_{G\in\Pi}\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(D_G)\); it preserves joint disjunctive information within each group while composing different groups by intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disjunction grouping jointly enumerates and convexifies logical alternatives within each block of a partition.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and every alternative set \(K_j\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_G=\bigcap_{j\in G}D_j\) and \(R_\Pi=\bigcap_{G\in\Pi}\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(D_G)\).

children.title: Grouping Granularity
children.top_down_role: Choice of group size for balancing joint convexification against representation burden.

knowledge_statements.title: Grouping Granularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonic strengthening obtained by merging disjunction groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi\) and \(\Gamma\) be partitions of the same component index set, with \(\Pi\) refining \(\Gamma\), and define \(R_\Pi\) and \(R_\Gamma\) by groupwise closed convexification. Every group of \(\Gamma\) is a union of groups of \(\Pi\). Since the closed convex hull of a joint intersection is contained in the intersection of the corresponding closed convex hulls, \[R_\Gamma\subseteq R_\Pi.\] Thus coarser partitions, which create larger groups, yield relaxations at least as strong as finer partitions; equality may hold when no cross-group convex-hull inequalities are generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger disjunction groups give at least as strong a relaxation because they retain more joint convex-hull information.
assumptions_latex: \(\Pi\) refines \(\Gamma\).
Both relaxations use the same component sets and closure convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_\Gamma\subseteq R_\Pi\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Strength Gain from Merging Groups
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonempty example showing strictness of the granularity-containment relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[D_1=\{(0,0),(2,0),(0,2)\},\qquad D_2=\{(0,0),(2,2)\}.\] Then \(D_1\cap D_2=\{(0,0)\}\), so joint grouping gives \(\operatorname{conv}(D_1\cap D_2)=\{(0,0)\}\). Singleton grouping gives \[\operatorname{conv}(D_1)\cap\operatorname{conv}(D_2)=\{(t,t):0\le t\le1\}.\] Hence merging the two groups yields a strict strengthening even though the joint feasible set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separately convexifying two finite disjunctions can retain a fractional segment that disappears when the disjunctions are grouped jointly.
assumptions_latex: Both component disjunctions use the same two-dimensional variable space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(D_1\cap D_2)\subsetneq\operatorname{conv}(D_1)\cap\operatorname{conv}(D_2)\).

children.title: Linkage–Grouping Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Interactions between linkage coverage, disjunction grouping, formulation size, and relaxation strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Linkage–Grouping Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength-size tradeoff between independent linkage and joint disjunction enumeration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a finite component set \(J\) is given, component \(j\in J\) has \(q_j=|K_j|\ge1\) alternatives, and a partition \(\Pi\) of \(J\) is represented by explicitly enumerating the joint alternatives within every group. The number of enumerated grouped alternatives is \[N(\Pi)=\sum_{G\in\Pi}\prod_{j\in G}q_j.\] Merging groups cannot weaken the associated groupwise convexification, but it replaces separate enumeration by Cartesian-product enumeration. Singleton grouping uses \(\sum_{j\in J}q_j\) alternatives, whereas one joint group uses \(\prod_{j\in J}q_j\). Partial linkage may reduce formulation size by retaining only selected compatibility equations, but its strength relative to a particular grouping depends on those equations; no universal ordering follows from \(N(\Pi)\) alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger explicitly enumerated groups retain at least as much joint convex-hull information but may require many more alternatives; partial linkage can reduce size, although its relative strength depends on which compatibility equations are retained.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) and every \(K_j\) are finite and nonempty.
Each group is represented by explicit enumeration of all Cartesian-product alternatives within that group.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\Pi)=\sum_{G\in\Pi}\prod_{j\in G}q_j\), and merging groups yields an equally strong or stronger groupwise convexification.

notation.meaning: number of alternatives in component j
number of explicitly enumerated grouped alternatives

children.title: Strength Loss under Composition
children.top_down_role: Loss of joint hull information when component formulations are intersected independently.

knowledge_statements.title: Strength Loss under Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General convex-hull loss caused by independently composing component relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For feasible component sets \(S_1,\ldots,S_m\) in a common finite-dimensional space, independently convexifying and composing them gives \(R=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S_i)\). The exact closed convex relaxation of the composed model is \(H=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\bigcap_{i=1}^mS_i)\). Always \(H\subseteq R\), but equality is not guaranteed. A point in \(R\setminus H\) can use a different convex decomposition for each component, with no single decomposition supported on jointly feasible points; inequalities excluding such points encode information lost under composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent component relaxations may use incompatible convex decompositions, producing a relaxation strictly larger than the joint convex hull.
assumptions_latex: All component sets lie in the same finite-dimensional space.
Closed convex hulls are used to cover nonclosed convexifications.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\bigcap_iS_i)\subseteq\bigcap_i\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(S_i)\), possibly strictly.

children.title: Bounded-Integer-Auxiliary Representability
children.top_down_role: Representability regimes using bounded auxiliary integer variables.

assumptions_latex: The formulation data are rational.
The auxiliary integer vector is componentwise bounded by finite integral vectors \(\ell\) and \(u\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear mixed-integer representability with every auxiliary integer coordinate bounded.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is bounded-integer-auxiliary MILP representable if there exist rational matrices \(A,B,C\), a rational vector \(d\), dimensions \(p,q\geq 0\), and finite vectors \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z^q\) with \(\ell\leq u\), such that
\[
S=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^p,\ \exists z\in\mathbb Z^q,\ Ax+By+Cz\leq d,\ \ell\leq z\leq u\right\}.
\]
The bounds apply to the auxiliary integer variables; the original variables and continuous auxiliaries need not be bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set has bounded-integer-auxiliary representation when it is the projection of a rational linear system whose auxiliary integer variables range over a finite box.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Integer-Auxiliary Representability

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary geometric structure induced by bounded auxiliary integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has a rational bounded-integer-auxiliary representation, then there exist finitely many rational polyhedra \(P_1,\ldots,P_t\) such that
\[
S=\bigcup_{k=1}^tP_k
\]
and every nonempty \(P_k\) has the same recession cone. The finitely many admissible integer vectors index the polyhedra obtained by fixing the integer auxiliaries and projecting the continuous auxiliaries; the homogeneous projected system, and hence its recession cone, is independent of the fixed integer value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded integer auxiliaries induce a finite union of rational polyhedra sharing one recession cone.
assumptions_latex: The formulation data are rational.
Every auxiliary integer coordinate ranges over a finite set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is a finite union of rational polyhedra whose nonempty members have a common recession cone.

notation.meaning: Projected polyhedra indexed by feasible bounded-integer assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Common-Recession Decomposition

children.title: Projected Mixed-Integer Representability
children.top_down_role: Representability obtained after projecting auxiliary continuous and integer variables.

assumptions_latex: All matrices and right-hand sides are rational.
Integrality is imposed only on the designated coordinates \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q\cap(\mathbb R^{n+p}\times\mathbb Z^q))\).

notation.meaning: rational polyhedron in the extended space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard rational linear mixed-integer projection definition.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is projected mixed-integer linear representable if there exist integers \(p,q\geq0\), rational matrices \(A,B,C\), and a rational vector \(d\) for which
\[
S=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^p,\ \exists z\in\mathbb Z^q,\ Ax+By+Cz\leq d\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, with \(Q=\{(x,y,z):Ax+By+Cz\leq d\}\), the represented set is the projection onto the original coordinates of \(Q\cap(\mathbb R^{n+p}\times\mathbb Z^q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected mixed-integer set consists exactly of original-variable points admitting continuous and integer auxiliaries satisfying one rational linear system.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Mixed-Integer Representability

children.title: Common-Recession Representability
children.top_down_role: Finite-union representations organized by compatible recession cones.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Heterogeneous Recession Can Invalidate the Standard Homogenized Union Formulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure boundary for the standard disaggregated selector construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For general nonempty polyhedra \(P_i=\{x:A_ix\leq b_i\}\), a zero selector permits any \(x^i\in\operatorname{rec}(P_i)\) because \(A_ix^i\leq0\). If recession cones differ, the formulation
\[
x=\sum_i x^i,\qquad A_ix^i\leq b_i\lambda_i,
\qquad \sum_i\lambda_i=1,
\qquad \lambda\in\{0,1\}^t
\]
can therefore add directions from an unselected alternative. For example, let
\[
P_1=\{(s,0):s\geq0\},\qquad P_2=\{(0,1)\}.
\]
Selecting \(P_2\) while taking the zero-selector copy \(x^1=(1,0)\in\operatorname{rec}(P_1)\) produces \((1,1)\), which is not in \(P_1\cup P_2\). Thus the common-recession hypothesis cannot simply be removed from this formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different recession cones let zero-selector copies contribute foreign directions; a two-dimensional rational example makes the standard homogenized binary formulation strictly larger than the union.
assumptions_latex: The standard homogenized disaggregated selector formulation is used without additional recession restrictions.
The alternatives need not share a recession cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard formulation can strictly contain \(\bigcup_iP_i\); common recession is a validity boundary for this construction.

notation.meaning: Disaggregated copy and selector for alternative \(i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Heterogeneous Recession Can Invalidate the Standard Homogenized Union Formulation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Homogenized Binary Formulation for a Common-Recession Union
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit exact union formulation and its continuous hull relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_ix\leq b_i\}\) be nonempty rational polyhedra satisfying \(\operatorname{rec}(P_i)=R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,t\). Then \(\bigcup_{i=1}^tP_i\) is the \(x\)-projection of
\[
x=\sum_{i=1}^t x^i,
\qquad A_ix^i\leq b_i\lambda_i\quad(i=1,\ldots,t),
\]
\[
\sum_{i=1}^t\lambda_i=1,

yqquad \lambda_i\in\{0,1\}\quad(i=1,\ldots,t).
\]
Replacing binary selectors by \(\lambda_i\geq0\) projects onto \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\), which is a closed rational polyhedron under the common-recession hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disaggregated homogenized copies and binary selectors exactly represent a finite common-recession union; relaxing the selectors gives its convex hull.
assumptions_latex: Each \(P_i\) is a nonempty rational polyhedron.
All \(P_i\) have the same recession cone \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The binary formulation projects to \(\bigcup_iP_i\), and its continuous-selector relaxation projects to \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_iP_i)\).

notation.meaning: Selector or convex-combination weight for alternative \(i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Homogenized Binary Formulation for a Common-Recession Union

assumptions_latex: Each \(P_i\) is a nonempty rational polyhedron.
All members of the finite family have the same recession cone \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The union \(S=\bigcup_{i=1}^tP_i\) admits a bounded-selector mixed-integer linear representation.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the common-recession formulation theorem.
Exact rational extended-formulation hypotheses require source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite rational-polyhedral unions encoded by bounded disjunct selectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:A_i x\leq b_i\}\) be nonempty rational polyhedra for \(i=1,\ldots,t\). The common-recession condition is
\[
\operatorname{rec}(P_i)=\{r\in\mathbb R^n:A_i r\leq0\}=R\qquad(i=1,\ldots,t).
\]
Under this condition, the finite union \(S=\bigcup_{i=1}^tP_i\) can be represented by a rational mixed-integer linear extended formulation using bounded binary selector variables. Thus the disjunct index is finite while every unbounded direction belongs to the shared cone \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite family of rational polyhedra with one common recession cone can be represented using bounded binary variables selecting a member of the union.
knowledge_statements.title: Common-Recession Representability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The common-recession condition and bounded-selector representability claim fit the leaf and are plausibly stated, but the record supplies no citation for the nontrivial formulation theorem. A source must confirm the rational-polyhedral hypotheses and the exact binary extended-formulation conclusion.

children.title: Representability under Integer-Dimension Limits
children.top_down_role: Expressive consequences of restricting the number or type of auxiliary integer variables.

assumptions_latex: The formulation is rational and linear.
At most \(k\) auxiliary coordinates are constrained to be integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership in the restricted class is exactly the existence of such a projection with integer dimension at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of the hierarchy induced by bounding auxiliary integer dimension.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\), a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is MILP representable with auxiliary integer dimension at most \(k\) if there exist \(p\geq0\), \(q\leq k\), rational matrices \(A,B,C\), and a rational vector \(d\) such that
\[
S=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^p,\ \exists z\in\mathbb Z^q,\ Ax+By+Cz\leq d\right\}.
\]
The least feasible \(q\), when it exists, is the auxiliary integer dimension of \(S\) relative to rational linear extended formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integer-dimension-limited class contains sets obtainable by projecting rational linear formulations with no more than a prescribed number of auxiliary integer coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Representability under Integer-Dimension Limits

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integer-Dimension Hierarchy and Continuous Base Level
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nesting, base case, and exhaustion of the auxiliary-integer-dimension hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M_k\) be the class of sets representable by finite rational linear extended formulations with at most \(k\) auxiliary integer coordinates. Then \(\mathcal M_0\subseteq\mathcal M_1\subseteq\cdots\), \(\mathcal M_0\) is exactly the class of rational polyhedra, and every rational projected-MILP set belongs to \(\mathcal M_k\) for some finite \(k\). Hence \(\bigcup_{k\ge0}\mathcal M_k\) is the full rational projected-MILP class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dimension-limited classes are nested, level zero consists of rational polyhedra, and their union is ordinary finite-dimensional rational MILP representability.
assumptions_latex: Formulations have finitely many variables and rational linear data.
The number of continuous auxiliary variables is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal M_0=\{\text{rational polyhedra}\},\quad \mathcal M_k\subseteq\mathcal M_{k+1},\quad \bigcup_{k\ge0}\mathcal M_k=\mathcal M.

notation.meaning: Sets representable with at most k auxiliary integer coordinates.

review_flags: No strictness of successive inclusions is asserted.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Dimension Hierarchy and Continuous Base Level

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One Unrestricted Integer Strictly Exceeds Every Finite Binary Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expressive separation between unrestricted general-integer auxiliaries and every formulation using finitely many binary auxiliaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal B_{<\infty}\) be the class of projections of finite rational linear systems having finitely many binary auxiliary variables and arbitrarily many continuous auxiliaries. Every member of \(\mathcal B_{<\infty}\) is a finite union of rational polyhedra. The set \(\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R\) has the one-general-integer representation \(\{x\in\mathbb R:\exists z\in\mathbb Z,\ x=z\}\), but it is not a finite union of polyhedra. Consequently, \(\mathbb Z\in\mathcal M_1\setminus\mathcal B_{<\infty}\), and \(\mathcal M_0\subsetneq\mathcal M_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One unrestricted integer auxiliary represents the integer lattice, whereas no finite collection of binary auxiliaries does; in particular, the zero- and one-general-integer levels are distinct.
assumptions_latex: All formulations are finite, rational, and linear.
Binary auxiliary variables have domain \(\{0,1\}\).
Continuous auxiliary dimension is unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb Z\in\mathcal M_1\setminus\mathcal B_{<\infty},\qquad \mathcal M_0\subsetneq\mathcal M_1.

notation.meaning: Sets representable using finitely many binary auxiliaries and continuous auxiliaries.
Sets representable with at most k unrestricted integer auxiliary coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General-Integer and Binary Dimension Are Not Interchangeable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed encoding comparison is deferred because its canonical home is the separate integer-dimension tradeoff leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bounded integer variable \(z\in\{L,\ldots,U\}\) can be represented using \(k=\lceil\log_2(U-L+1)\rceil\) binary variables, an affine binary expansion, and constraints excluding unused codes. An unrestricted integer variable cannot be replaced by a fixed finite collection of binary variables because the latter has a finite joint domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded general integers admit finite binary encodings, whereas unrestricted integers do not admit fixed finite binary encodings.
assumptions_latex: L,U\in\mathbb Z,\quad L\le U.
Binary auxiliaries take values in \(\{0,1\}\).
The encodings are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\in\{L,\ldots,U\}\Rightarrow \lceil\log_2(U-L+1)\rceil\text{ binaries suffice, while an unrestricted }z\in\mathbb Z\text{ has no fixed finite binary encoding}.

The claim does not supply a strictness theorem for the hierarchy defined at this leaf.

children.title: Nonrepresentability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Set structures that fall outside a selected mixed-integer formulation class.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric and arithmetic witnesses for the bounded-set obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge2\), the Euclidean unit ball \(B_2^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\|x\|_2\le1\}\) is not rational MILP representable because it is not a finite union of polytopes. If \(\alpha\notin\mathbb Q\), the singleton \(\{\alpha\}\) is also not rational MILP representable because every zero-dimensional rational polytope has rational coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neither a Euclidean ball nor a singleton at an irrational coordinate has an exact finite rational MILP representation.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q\).
All formulation data are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B_2^n\text{ and }\{\alpha\}\text{ are not rational MILP representable}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary geometric condition for bounded rational MILP-representable sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a bounded set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the projection of a finite rational mixed-integer linear system, then \(S\) is a finite union of rational polytopes. Consequently, a bounded set that is not a finite union of rational polytopes is not rational MILP representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every bounded rational MILP-representable set is a finite union of rational polytopes; violating this condition proves nonrepresentability.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is bounded.
The formulation is finite, linear, and rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ rational MILP representable}\Longrightarrow S=\bigcup_{i=1}^tP_i\text{ for rational polytopes }P_i.

notation.meaning: Rational polytope in the original-variable space.

review_flags: A structural-characterization source would improve documentation.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Set Polyhedral-Union Obstruction

assumptions_latex: The selected formulation class uses bounded integer auxiliaries and has a common recession cone \(R\).
The candidate set \(S\) contains some \(x\) but omits \(x+r\) for some \(r\in R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is not representable in the selected common-recession, bounded-auxiliary class.
review_flags: No supplied locator establishes the stated nonrepresentability criterion.
Boundary is scoped only to the common-recession bounded-auxiliary class.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A necessary recession-closure test for one restricted representability regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the class of finite unions \(S=\bigcup_{i=1}^tP_i\) in which every nonempty polyhedron \(P_i\) has the same recession cone \(R\). Every member of this class satisfies
\[
S+R=S.
\]
Consequently, if a candidate set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) has points \(x\in S\) and \(r\in R\) such that \(x+r\notin S\), then \(S+R\nsubseteq S\) and no representation of the stipulated common-recession form exists. This criterion does not exclude unrestricted mixed-integer representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of closure under the required common recession cone rules out a bounded-selector common-recession representation, though it need not rule out broader formulations.

children.title: Relaxation-Strength Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Root-bound improvements compared with their modeling and solution costs.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Root Strength Does Not Determine Total Solution Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between static relaxation dominance and algorithm-dependent computational performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Projected containment orders linear relaxation bounds, but it does not by itself order formulation size, matrix density, numerical conditioning, per-node solution time, branch-and-bound node count, or total runtime. Any implication from a stronger root relaxation to lower total solution cost requires an explicitly fixed algorithmic and cost model together with additional assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stronger root relaxation does not, by itself, guarantee a cheaper overall solve.
assumptions_latex: The formulations represent the same integer-feasible problem.
One projected continuous relaxation is contained in the other.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_1\subseteq P_2\not\Rightarrow\text{lower total computational cost for formulation 1}.\)
review_flags: The nonimplication is conditional on the absence of a fixed algorithmic cost model; it does not claim that every stronger formulation is slower.
knowledge_statements.title: Root Strength Does Not Determine Total Solution Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise comparison of projected relaxation strength and explicitly selected formulation-cost coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For equivalent formulations \(F_1,F_2\), let \(P_i\) be their projected continuous relaxations and let \(K(F_i)\in\mathbb R^r\) be a fixed vector of costs for which smaller coordinates are preferred. Say that \(F_1\) strength–cost dominates \(F_2\) when \[P_1\subseteq P_2,\qquad K(F_1)\le K(F_2)\ \text{componentwise},\] with at least one strict comparison. If one formulation has the tighter relaxation but larger cost in at least one selected coordinate, the pair exhibits a Pareto tradeoff under \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formulation is unambiguously better under selected cost coordinates only when it is no weaker and no more costly componentwise; otherwise strength and cost may trade off.
assumptions_latex: The formulations have the same integer-feasible projection and objective semantics.
Relaxation strength is compared after projection to the same original-variable space.
The coordinates and direction of preference of \(K\) are fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_1\subseteq P_2\land K(F_1)\le K(F_2)\) defines componentwise strength–cost dominance; crossed comparisons are Pareto-incomparable.

notation.meaning: projected continuous relaxation of formulation i

knowledge_statements.title: Strength–Cost Pareto Comparison

assumptions_latex: Two formulations describe the same integer-feasible set and objective.
Their continuous relaxations have finite optimal values for the chosen minimization objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relaxation strength improves monotonically with the lower bound, while formulation cost must be compared separately.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly formalizes the multidimensional strength-cost comparison.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization convention; computational cost is treated as a separate resource vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For equivalent minimization formulations \(F_1\) and \(F_2\), let \(P_{F_i}\) denote their continuous relaxations and define \(L(F_i)=\inf\{c^Tx:x\in P_{F_i}\}\). If \(P_{F_1}\subseteq P_{F_2}\) after projection to common variables, then
\[
L(F_1)\geq L(F_2).
\]
Thus \(F_1\) supplies a bound at least as strong as \(F_2\). A formulation is unambiguously preferable under a resource vector \(K\) only when it has no weaker bound and no larger chosen costs; otherwise the pair exhibits a relaxation-strength tradeoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tighter relaxation gives at least as strong a minimization bound, but it is preferable only after accounting separately for its modeling and solution costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Strength Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relaxation inclusion implication for a common minimization objective is standard and correctly directed. The broader claim about when a formulation is unambiguously preferable depends on a componentwise ordering and interpretation of the resource vector K that are not fully formalized, and no source supports the combined strength-cost principle.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-independent characterization of containment between projected relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_1,P_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty closed convex sets. Then \[P_1\subseteq P_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \inf_{x\in P_1}c^\top x\ge \inf_{x\in P_2}c^\top x\quad\text{for every }c\in\mathbb R^n,\] with infima interpreted in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected containment is equivalent to dominance for every linear minimization objective.
assumptions_latex: \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are nonempty closed convex subsets of the same finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_1\subseteq P_2\iff[\forall c,\ \inf_{P_1}c^\top x\ge\inf_{P_2}c^\top x]\).
review_flags: This equivalence elaborates the general definition of formulation dominance rather than the local strength-cost tradeoff.
knowledge_statements.title: All-Objectives Characterization of Projected Strength

intermediate_metadata.reason: The locally owned inventory is the accepted componentwise strength–cost Pareto comparison and the failure boundary separating root strength from total computational cost. The proposed all-objectives characterization was deferred to the general formulation-dominance node. Representation size-density, integer dimension, branching-propagation behavior, reoptimization-degeneracy effects, and family-specific tradeoffs remain in their sibling or dedicated scopes.

children.title: Row Count Burden
children.top_down_role: Computational burden associated with the number of formulation constraints.

assumptions_latex: The linear formulation is written as \(Ax\leq b\) with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The row-count burden is \(m\), the number of scalar linear constraints.
review_flags: Locator supports matrix dimensions only provisionally, not solver-specific performance effects.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural row count, excluding presolve-dependent computational claims.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a linear or mixed-integer formulation whose scalar constraints are assembled as \(Ax\leq b\), with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), the row-count burden is
\[
R(A)=m.
\]
Equalities may be counted either as single stored rows or as two inequalities, but the convention must be fixed before comparing formulations. The metric measures the number of explicit scalar constraint rows before presolve; it does not by itself determine relaxation strength, factorization cost, or solution time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Row-count burden is the number of explicitly stored scalar constraint rows under a fixed equality-counting and presolve convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Row Count Burden

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4
source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundant row replication increases row burden arbitrarily without changing feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), and suppose \(a^\top x\le\beta\) is one row of the system. Repeating that row \(q\ge1\) additional times leaves \(F\) unchanged but increases the displayed row count by \(q\). Hence equivalent formulations can have arbitrarily different row counts, and row count alone orders neither relaxation strength nor solution time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicating an existing inequality preserves the feasible set while increasing the displayed row count arbitrarily.
assumptions_latex: \(a^\top x\le\beta\) is already a row of \(Ax\le b\).
Repeated stored rows are counted separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The repeated-row description has the same feasible set and \(q\) additional rows.

notation.meaning: number of additional stored row copies

knowledge_statements.title: Row Count Is Representation-Dependent

children.title: Column Count Burden
children.top_down_role: Computational burden associated with original plus auxiliary variables.

assumptions_latex: The formulation uses a variable vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), with designated coordinates possibly integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The column-count burden is \(n\), optionally decomposed by variable domain.

notation.meaning: numbers of continuous, general-integer, and binary columns

review_flags: Locator supports matrix dimensions only provisionally, not solver-specific performance effects.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural variable count with an optional domain decomposition.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a formulation with variable vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), the column-count burden is
\[
C=n.
\]
For mixed-integer formulations it may be refined as \(C=n_c+n_i+n_b\), where \(n_c\), \(n_i\), and \(n_b\) count continuous, general-integer, and binary columns under disjoint domain categories. Fixed or eliminated variables are included or excluded according to a declared preprocessing convention. Column count measures representation size but does not alone quantify branching difficulty or relaxation quality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Column-count burden is the number of formulation variables, optionally separated into continuous, general-integer, and binary columns under a fixed preprocessing convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Column Count Burden

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4
source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed dummy auxiliaries show that column count is not intrinsic to the represented set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) and any \(k\ge1\), the lifted system
\[
Ax\le b,\qquad z=0,\qquad z\in\mathbb R^k
\]
satisfies
\[
\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,z):Ax\le b,\ z=0\}=F,
\]
but has \(n+k\) columns when fixed auxiliaries are counted. Thus projection-equivalent formulations can have arbitrarily different column counts; column count alone orders neither relaxation strength nor computational difficulty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding fixed auxiliary variables preserves the represented set while increasing the displayed column count arbitrarily.
assumptions_latex: \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\).
Fixed auxiliary variables are counted under the declared column-count convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,z):Ax\le b,\ z=0\}=F\) although the lifted system has \(n+k\) columns.
knowledge_statements.title: Column Count Is Representation-Dependent

children.title: Matrix Nonzero Burden
children.top_down_role: Storage and linear-algebra burden associated with matrix nonzeros.

assumptions_latex: The coefficient matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\) is stored explicitly or in a sparse format.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matrix nonzero burden is \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)=|\{(i,j):a_{ij}\neq0\}|\).
review_flags: Locator is provisional for matrix notation and does not certify implementation-level storage costs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact structural count of nonzero constraint coefficients.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), define the support \(\operatorname{supp}(A)=\{(i,j):a_{ij}\neq0\}\). The matrix nonzero burden is
\[
N(A)=\operatorname{nnz}(A)=|\operatorname{supp}(A)|.
\]
Only coefficients in the declared constraint matrix are counted; objective coefficients, bounds, and generated rows require separate conventions. Unlike row or column count, \(N(A)\) distinguishes formulations having equal dimensions but substantially different coefficient sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix nonzero burden counts nonzero constraint coefficients and distinguishes equally sized formulations with different sparsity patterns.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Nonzero Burden

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4
source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Equality Systems Can Have Different Nonzero Burdens
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An invertible row transformation preserves an equality-system feasible set but can densify its matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A=I_n\), let \(b\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular with no zero entries. Then
\[
\{x:Ax=b\}=\{x:QAx=Qb\},
\]
but
\[
\operatorname{nnz}(A)=n,\qquad \operatorname{nnz}(QA)=\operatorname{nnz}(Q)=n^2.
\]
Thus nonzero burden is a property of the displayed representation rather than the feasible set alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense invertible row transformation can change an equivalent equality description from n to n-squared nonzeros.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is nonsingular and every entry of \(Q\) is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:Ax=b\}=\{x:QAx=Qb\}\) but \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)=n\) and \(\operatorname{nnz}(QA)=n^2\).

notation.meaning: number of nonzero entries of M

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Equality Systems Can Have Different Nonzero Burdens

children.title: Matrix Density Effects
children.top_down_role: Solver behavior associated with sparse versus dense formulation matrices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines coefficient density and states the precise sparse matrix-vector accounting boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m,n\ge1\),
\[
\rho(A)=\frac{\operatorname{nnz}(A)}{mn},\qquad 0\le\rho(A)\le1.
\]
In a sparse representation that visits each stored nonzero a constant number of times, coefficient processing for \(Av\) uses \(\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\) arithmetic operations and stored-coefficient accesses. If a complete length-\(m\) output must also be initialized or written, total work is \(\Theta(m+\operatorname{nnz}(A))\) in that model. These bounds do not determine factorization fill-in or solver runtime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Density is the occupied fraction of matrix positions; sparse matrix-vector coefficient work is proportional to nonzeros, with an additional row-output term when the full result is produced.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m,n\ge1\).
The sparse representation visits each stored nonzero a constant number of times.
A complete output vector contributes \(\Theta(m)\) initialization or writing work when that work is included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(A)=\operatorname{nnz}(A)/(mn)\), coefficient processing is \(\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\), and complete-output work is \(\Theta(m+\operatorname{nnz}(A))\).
review_flags: Corrects the deferred seed candidate by including the full-output term and separating coefficient processing from total output work.
knowledge_statements.title: Density and Sparse Matrix-Vector Work

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equal Density Does Not Determine Support Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A scalar density does not determine how nonzeros are distributed among rows and columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\ge2\), let \(A=I_n\), and let \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) have \(B_{1j}=1\) for every \(j\) and all other entries zero. Then
\[
\rho(A)=\rho(B)=\frac1n,
\]
yet every row and column of \(A\) contains one nonzero, whereas \(B\) has one row containing all \(n\) nonzeros and \(n-1\) zero rows. Equal dimensions and density therefore do not determine support distribution, rank, block structure, fill-in, or solver runtime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrices can have identical dimensions and density but radically different support distributions, so density alone cannot predict numerical behavior.
assumptions_latex: Density is \(\rho(M)=\operatorname{nnz}(M)/n^2\) for an \(n\times n\) matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(A)=\rho(B)=1/n\) although their row-support profiles and ranks differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Equal Density Does Not Determine Support Geometry

assumptions_latex: The matrix has positive dimensions \(m,n\geq1\).
Sparse multiplication visits each stored nonzero a constant number of times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(A)=\operatorname{nnz}(A)/(mn)\), and sparse matrix-vector multiplication costs \(\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\) arithmetic operations.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the sparse-operation complexity bound.
Factorization and solver-runtime effects are deliberately excluded.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density and sparse matrix-vector cost; no claim about factorization runtime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m,n\geq1\), its coefficient density is
\[
\rho(A)=\frac{\operatorname{nnz}(A)}{mn},\qquad 0\leq\rho(A)\leq1.
\]
In the sparse-arithmetic model where each stored nonzero is read and used a constant number of times, computing \(Av\) requires \(\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(A))=\Theta(\rho(A)mn)\) arithmetic operations and coefficient accesses. This bound concerns matrix-vector multiplication only; density can affect numerical factorization through fill-in, but density alone does not determine that fill-in.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Density is the fraction of nonzero coefficients; in the standard sparse model, a matrix-vector product costs time proportional to the nonzero count.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Density Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The density definition is standard, but the claimed Theta(nnz(A)) cost for computing a complete matrix-vector product requires a more precise model: producing or initializing an m-dimensional output generally contributes an m term, while Theta(nnz(A)) describes coefficient processing when output initialization is excluded or already provided. No citation is supplied to resolve the intended complexity model.

children.title: Size–Density Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Cases where reducing rows or columns increases matrix density or memory pressure.

assumptions_latex: Two matrices are compared under the same row, column, and zero-detection conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Size and density satisfy the exact identity \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)=\rho(A)mn\).
review_flags: Source support is provisional for matrix notation; the identity follows from the declared density definition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact accounting relation among dimensions, density, and nonzero count.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m,n\geq1\), row count, column count, density, and nonzero burden obey
\[
\operatorname{nnz}(A)=\rho(A)mn.
\]
Hence enlarging one or both dimensions need not increase the nonzero burden proportionally if density decreases. Conversely, a formulation with fewer rows or columns can still contain more coefficients if its density rises sufficiently. Therefore representation size should be compared through the tuple \((m,n,\operatorname{nnz}(A),\rho(A))\), rather than through either dimensions or density alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dimensions, density, and nonzero count are linked exactly, so a smaller matrix can still store more coefficients when it is sufficiently denser.
knowledge_statements.title: Size–Density Tradeoffs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Preliminaries from linear algebra, matrix theory, and Euclidean geometry p. 4
source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

children.title: Integer-Dimension Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs involving the number, domain, and encoding of auxiliary integer variables.

assumptions_latex: The integer variable satisfies \(0\leq z\leq U\) with integral \(U\geq1\).
The encoding variables are binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bounded integer coordinate can be replaced exactly by \(q=\lceil\log_2(U+1)\rceil\) binary coordinates and one range inequality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact binary encoding of one nonnegative bounded integer variable.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z\in\mathbb Z\) satisfy \(0\leq z\leq U\), where \(U\in\mathbb Z_+\), and set \(q=\lceil\log_2(U+1)\rceil\). The exact binary representation is
\[
z=\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}2^j b_j,\qquad \sum_{j=0}^{q-1}2^j b_j\leq U,\qquad b_j\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Every integer in \(\{0,\ldots,U\}\) has such an encoding, and every feasible encoding yields one of those integers. The substitution trades one general-integer coordinate for \(q\) binary coordinates and an additional range row.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded integer variable can be encoded exactly with logarithmically many binaries, trading one general-integer coordinate for additional binary columns and a range constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Dimension Tradeoffs

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Mixed Integer Formulations p. 9

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum binary dimension of an injective encoding of a bounded integer domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An injective encoding of the \(U+1\) values in \(\{0,1,\ldots,U\}\) by \(q\) binary coordinates requires \(2^q\ge U+1\). Consequently \[q\ge\left\lceil\log_2(U+1)\right\rceil.\] The positional encoding in the immutable seed attains this bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any injective binary encoding needs at least the ceiling of the base-two logarithm of the domain cardinality, and positional encoding attains that dimension.
assumptions_latex: Each integer value has a distinct binary code.
The code uses exactly \(q\) binary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\ge\lceil\log_2(U+1)\rceil\).

notation.meaning: upper endpoint of the integer domain

knowledge_statements.title: Binary-Coordinate Information Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integer Dimension Does Not Order Relaxation Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating exact discrete representability from projected continuous-relaxation performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replacing a bounded integer variable by an exact binary encoding preserves the integer-feasible projection, but integer dimension alone does not determine the continuous-relaxation projection. That projection also depends on the constraints imposed on the encoding variables and their interaction with the remaining formulation. Hence fewer integer coordinates imply neither a stronger nor a weaker projected continuous relaxation without additional structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-dimensional exact integer encoding is not automatically stronger or weaker after integrality is relaxed.
assumptions_latex: The compared formulations represent the same bounded integer values when their designated variables are integral.
Strength is compared after relaxing integrality and projecting to common original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{smaller integer dimension}\not\Rightarrow\text{an ordering of projected continuous relaxations}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Integer Dimension Does Not Order Relaxation Strength

children.title: Branching-Propagation Quality Coupling
children.top_down_role: How formulation variables and constraints support effective search partitions and domain reduction.

children.title: Branching Quality
children.top_down_role: Formulation features affecting variable selection, partition balance, and search discrimination.

assumptions_latex: The node relaxation is a minimization problem with finite lower-bound value \(\beta(R)\).
Branching produces nonempty child relaxations \(R_1,\ldots,R_k\subseteq R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{br}}(R;R_1,\ldots,R_k)=\min_{1\le j\le k}\{\beta(R_j)-\beta(R)\}\ge 0\).

notation.meaning: Lower bound obtained by solving relaxation R

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-child bound improvement for a minimization branch-and-bound node.

source_refs.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization node relaxation \(R\), let \(\beta(R)\) be its valid lower bound. If a branching disjunction yields nonempty children \(R_1,\ldots,R_k\subseteq R\), define its worst-child branching quality by \[Q_{\mathrm{br}}(R;R_1,\ldots,R_k):=\min_{1\le j\le k}\bigl(\beta(R_j)-\beta(R)\bigr).\] Because restriction cannot decrease the optimal value of a minimization relaxation, \(Q_{\mathrm{br}}\ge 0\). Larger values mean that every child improves the parent bound by at least that amount.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Branching quality is the smallest lower-bound improvement among all children of a minimization node; a larger score means uniformly stronger child bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching Quality

source_witnesses.locator: 2.2.1 Outline of the general branch-and-bound method p. 15

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited branch-and-bound outline does not establish this worst-child metric. Moreover, monotonicity requires β to be the relaxation optimal value or an explicitly monotone bound functional, and finite child values must be assumed; arbitrary valid lower bounds need not satisfy the claimed inequality.

children.title: Propagation Quality
children.top_down_role: Formulation features affecting domain reduction and inference strength during search.

assumptions_latex: The current finite domain is a box \(D=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\).
The propagator \(P\) is sound and contracting, producing \(P(D)=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i',u_i']\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{prop}}(D,P)=|I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I}\left(1-\frac{u_i'-\ell_i'}{u_i-\ell_i}\right)\in[0,1]\).

notation.meaning: Indices having positive initial domain width
Average normalized width removed by propagation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: normalized domain reduction is a conventional propagation-strength metric
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized bound-domain reduction by a sound propagator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I:=\{i:u_i>\ell_i\}\), and suppose \(I\ne\varnothing\). The propagation quality of \(P\) on \(D\) is \[Q_{\mathrm{prop}}(D,P):=\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{i\in I}\left(1-\frac{u_i'-\ell_i'}{u_i-\ell_i}\right).\] Soundness means every feasible point in \(D\) remains in \(P(D)\), while contraction gives \(0\le Q_{\mathrm{prop}}(D,P)\le1\). The endpoints represent no reduction and fixation of every initially nonfixed coordinate, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Propagation quality is the average fraction of each nonzero variable-domain width removed without deleting feasible points.
knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Quality

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalized-width formula is coherent, but it is one possible propagation-quality convention. A source is needed to support this exact averaging and normalization choice.

children.title: Branching–Propagation Interaction
children.top_down_role: Regimes where search partitions alter subsequent inference effectiveness.

assumptions_latex: A branching disjunction creates children \(D_1,\ldots,D_k\) from a parent domain \(D\).
The same sound propagator \(P\) is applied to parent and children, and all propagation scores are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{\mathrm{bp}}=\sum_{j=1}^k w_jQ_{\mathrm{prop}}(D_j,P)-Q_{\mathrm{prop}}(D,P)\), with synergy exactly when \(I_{\mathrm{bp}}>0\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative child weights summing to one

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: interaction is measured as propagation gain relative to the unbranched parent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incremental propagation strength exposed by branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For weights \(w_j\ge0\) satisfying \(\sum_{j=1}^k w_j=1\), define the branching-propagation interaction by \[I_{\mathrm{bp}}:=\sum_{j=1}^k w_jQ_{\mathrm{prop}}(D_j,P)-Q_{\mathrm{prop}}(D,P).\] Positive interaction means that propagation removes a larger weighted fraction of domain width after branching than at the parent. Zero interaction means no average incremental reduction, and negative interaction means the chosen normalized score records less average reduction in the children.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interaction score compares weighted propagation quality after branching with propagation quality at the parent; a positive value indicates synergy.
knowledge_statements.title: Branching–Propagation Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The score is a proposed convention whose value depends on child weights and separately normalized child domains. A source must justify the formula and its interpretation as branching–propagation synergy.

children.title: Reoptimization Behavior
children.top_down_role: Formulation behavior across repeated relaxation solves with related model states.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic safe protocol for re-solving related relaxations from reusable solver state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For related problems \(P^1,\ldots,P^T\), retain state \(s^{t-1}\) after solving \(P^{t-1}\). Before solving \(P^t\), check compatibility with all changed variables, rows, bounds, and the selected algorithm. If compatible, initialize from \(s^{t-1}\); otherwise use a valid default state. Repair lost primal or dual feasibility and continue until the ordinary optimality, infeasibility, unboundedness, or unresolved-status tests for \(P^t\) are met. Reused state alone never certifies the changed problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reuse compatible state when possible, fall back safely otherwise, and certify every changed problem with its normal status tests.
assumptions_latex: Each problem has a declared solver and status-certificate convention.
Compatibility is checked against all model changes.
A valid default initialization is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Every reported status for }P^t\text{ is justified by tests applied to }P^t.

notation.meaning: solver state retained from the preceding solve

knowledge_statements.title: Certified State-Reuse Reoptimization Protocol

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Warm Starts Have No Solver-Independent Work Dominance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on performance conclusions obtainable from compatible state reuse alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W_{\mathrm{warm}}(P,s)\) and \(W_{\mathrm{cold}}(P)\) denote work under fixed warm- and cold-start policies. Compatibility of \(s\) and correctness of both policies do not imply \(W_{\mathrm{warm}}(P,s)\le W_{\mathrm{cold}}(P)\). Such dominance requires additional assumptions on the algorithm, state quality, repair, presolve, tie-breaking, and work metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid warm start is not guaranteed to reduce work; comparisons require fixed policies and metrics.
assumptions_latex: Both policies apply valid status tests.
The work metric and implementation policies are fixed before comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{State compatibility alone}\not\Rightarrow W_{\mathrm{warm}}(P,s)\le W_{\mathrm{cold}}(P).

notation.meaning: work under specified warm- and cold-start policies

review_flags: This is a non-dominance boundary, not a claim that warm starts are typically slower.
knowledge_statements.title: Warm Starts Have No Solver-Independent Work Dominance

assumptions_latex: A fixed constraint matrix \(A\) defines a sequence of linear programs with data \((b^t,c^t)\).
Each solve after the first is initialized from the preceding basis \(B^{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{reopt}}(1,T)=\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=2}^T p_t\), where smaller values indicate better warm-start reoptimization behavior.

notation.meaning: Number of simplex pivots needed for solve t from the preceding basis

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pivot count measures computational work in simplex reoptimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Warm-start simplex effort across related linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(T\ge2\) linear programs \(\min\{(c^t)^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b^t,\ x\ge0\}\) with common matrix \(A\). After solving instance \(t-1\), initialize instance \(t\) from its final basis and let \(p_t\) be the pivots required by a fixed simplex variant, including any feasibility-restoration pivots. Define \[Q_{\mathrm{reopt}}(1,T):=\frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=2}^T p_t.\] This metric is meaningful only with the pivot rule, crash procedure, and presolve policy held fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reoptimization behavior is measured by the average simplex pivots needed when each related LP starts from the preceding solve's basis.
knowledge_statements.title: Reoptimization Behavior

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Average warm-start pivot count is solver- and policy-dependent rather than a canonical definition. A supporting source and assumptions ensuring that every LP is solvable and each pivot count is defined are required.
